Why We Exist

Our Mission

Helping every Australian get into — and out of — separation with clarity, dignity, and the information they need.

Separation shouldn't cost you everything

Separation and divorce is stressful in all situation, fear of the unknown, not knowing how to move forward and confusion. Every year, tens of thousands of Australians enter the family law system. Most of them have never seen the inside of a courtroom. They don't know which form to file, what a directions hearing is, or what the court means by "the best interests of the child." They are scared, overwhelmed, and often completely alone. The first thing most people think they need to do, is to go straight to a lawyer.

The legal system was not designed for every day Australians. It was designed for lawyers — written in language only lawyers understand, structured around processes only lawyers are trained to navigate, and priced at rates only some can afford. The result is a two-tier system: those who can pay for representation, and those, who don't qualify for Legal Aid, who are left to figure it out themselves.

CasePath exists to close that gap, through information that is in plain language and offers help with forms and information without the cost of lawyers, especially in the beginning confusing time of separation.

Getting in

The beginning of separation is the hardest part. You don't know what you don't know. You're googling legal terms at midnight, trying to work out whether you need an initiating application or a response, whether you're the applicant or the respondent, and whether you've already missed a deadline you didn't know existed.

CasePath meets you at that moment. We give you a plain-English glossary of every term the court will use. We show you the forms you need, in the order you need them. We walk you through each stage of proceedings — from the first mention to the final hearing — so that when you walk into court, you understand what is happening and why.

We don't replace lawyers. We make sure that when you do speak to one, you understand what they're telling you — and when you can't afford one, you're not left in the dark.

Getting through

Family law cases are not quick. The average contested parenting matter takes 12 to 18 months. During that time, you are expected to file documents, meet deadlines, attend hearings, manage evidence, co-parent under pressure, and somehow keep your life together. The emotional toll is immense — and it is rarely acknowledged by the system itself.

CasePath gives you Your Case to track every phase, chronology and evidence, output workflows that assemble structured drafts from your records, and mental health resources that treat your wellbeing as central to your case — not a footnote. We help you to stay organised, stay informed, and stay standing.

Getting out

The goal of every family law matter should be resolution — not indefinite conflict. Whether that means consent orders, a negotiated property settlement, or final orders after a hearing, the end of proceedings should be the beginning of a new chapter. For you, and especially for your children.

CasePath is built to help you reach that point. We encourage early resolution where possible, help you understand what a realistic outcome looks like, and give you the tools to move forward — not just as a litigant, but as a parent, a person, and a human being who has been through something genuinely hard. Regardless of whether children are involved or not.

Protecting the children 👶 About the Kids →

Children did not choose this. They did not file the application. They did not create the conflict. But they absorb its consequences — every overheard argument, every late changeover, every month the proceedings drag on. The longer a case takes, and the more adversarial it becomes, the more damage is done to the people who matter most.

The research is clear: Children do best when they have a meaningful relationship with both parents. Unless there are genuine safety concerns — family violence, abuse, neglect, or substance issues that put a child at risk — the default outcome should be equal shared care. Both parents. Both homes. Both relationships preserved. That is not a political position. It is what the evidence shows, and it is what the Family Law Act encourages through the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility.

Yet too often, the family court process itself becomes the source of harm. Children are caught between warring parents for months or years. They lose time with a parent not because of any finding of risk, but because proceedings are slow, expensive, and adversarial by design. By the time a final order is made, the damage to the parent-child relationship may already be done.

CasePath is built with a simple principle: get parents to resolution as quickly as possible, preserve both relationships wherever it is safe to do so, and never lose sight of the fact that behind every case number is a child who needs stability, love, and both of their parents.

What we believe

⚖️

Access to justice is not a luxury. Every person deserves to understand the legal process that is reshaping their family, regardless of whether they can afford a lawyer.

🧠

Mental health is not a side issue. The emotional weight of separation affects every decision you make — in court and out of it. Supporting your wellbeing is part of supporting your case.

👶

Children come first. Every parenting decision the court makes — and every tool we build — is grounded in the best interests of the child. Children need stability, routine, and the knowledge that both of their parents love them and are present. That is not a slogan. It is the law, and it should be the practice.

👨‍👩‍👧

Both parents matter. Where it is safe, the default outcome should be equal shared care — 50/50, both parents, both homes. Children thrive when they have a meaningful, ongoing relationship with each parent. The court process should protect that relationship, not erode it through delay and conflict.

🛡️

Safety is non-negotiable. Equal shared care is the starting point — not the outcome in every case. Where there is family violence, abuse, neglect, or genuine risk to a child, the court must act to protect them. CasePath provides information about safety orders, supervised contact, and protective measures because keeping children safe always comes before any presumption.

🤝

Resolution is the goal. We do not help people fight harder. We help people understand their situation clearly so they can reach the best possible outcome — ideally by agreement, as quickly as possible, and in a way that minimises the harm done to children through the family court process.

🔒

Your information is yours. Everything you add to Your Case Workspace is encrypted, private, and under your control. We do not sell data, serve ads, or share your information with anyone — ever.

"Built for every Australian going through separation."

That is not marketing. That is the reason CasePath exists.

Part I — Preliminary
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) · Sections 1–19
9 sections
s 4Interpretation
Defines the key terms used throughout the Act — including "child", "de facto relationship", "family violence", "marriage" and "parenting order".
s 4ABMeaning of family violence
Defines family violence broadly to include physical, sexual, emotional, psychological and economic abuse, and controlling or coercive behaviour.
s 9AObjects of the Act
Sets out the overarching purposes of the Family Law Act, including supporting the welfare of families and ensuring the best interests of children are promoted.
Part VII — Children
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) · Sections 60–70NEB
Most relevant ⭐
s 60BObjects of Part and principles underlying it
Ensures children have the benefit of both parents having a meaningful involvement in their lives…
s 60CAChild's best interests paramount consideration
In deciding whether to make a particular parenting order, the court must regard the best interests of the child as the paramount consideration.
s 60CCHow a court determines what is in a child's best interests
Lists factors the court must consider, including the child's safety, their views, and each parent's capacity to care for them…
s 65DCourt may make parenting order
A court may make a parenting order on the application of a parent, the child, a grandparent, or any other person concerned with the care, welfare or development…
Part VIII — Property, Spousal Maintenance and Agreements
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) · Sections 71–90
24 sections
s 79Alteration of property interests
Empowers the court to make orders altering the interests of parties in property — including transfers, sales, and superannuation splits.
s 79ASetting aside orders altering property interests
Allows a court to set aside a property order in limited circumstances — such as fraud, non-disclosure of assets, or a significant change in circumstances.
s 75Matters to be taken into account for spousal maintenance
Lists the factors a court must consider when deciding whether to award spousal maintenance, including the applicant's ability to support themselves and the payer's capacity to pay.
s 90BFinancial agreements before marriage
Allows parties to a marriage to make a binding financial agreement (sometimes called a "prenup") setting out how property and maintenance will be dealt with if the marriage breaks down.
s 90GWhen financial agreements are binding
Sets out the strict formal requirements that must be met for a financial agreement to be legally binding — including independent legal advice for each party.
Part IV — Divorce and Nullity of Marriage
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) · Sections 48–67
19 sections
s 48Grounds for divorce
Australia has a single ground for divorce: irretrievable breakdown of marriage, established by 12 months of separation. There is no requirement to prove fault.
s 49Separation
Defines what "separation" means, including that parties can be separated while still living under the same roof — the key test is whether the marriage has ended in substance.
s 55ADivorce not to be granted if children under 18 without court satisfaction
Before granting a divorce where there are children under 18, the court must be satisfied that proper arrangements have been made for their welfare.
s 57Rescission of divorce order
A divorce order can be rescinded before it takes effect if the parties reconcile and apply jointly within the prescribed period.
Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Act 2021
FCFCA Act 2021 (Cth) · Establishing legislation for the unified court
Court structure
s 3Objects of the Act
Sets out why the FCFCA was created — to establish a single entry point for family law and federal civil matters, improve efficiency, and reduce delays.
s 10Division 1 — General federal law jurisdiction
Defines the jurisdiction of Division 1 (previously the Family Court of Australia) — complex matters, appeals, and cases involving significant public interest.
s 60Division 2 — Federal Circuit and Family Court jurisdiction
Division 2 (previously the Federal Circuit Court) handles the majority of family law matters including most parenting and property applications.
s 190Appeals
Sets out the appeal pathway — appeals from Division 2 go to Division 1, and from there to the Full Court of the Family Court or the Federal Court.
Family Law Rules 2021
Suborinate legislation · Procedural rules governing all family law proceedings
Procedure
r 1.10Overarching purpose
The overarching purpose of the Rules is to facilitate the just resolution of disputes according to law, as quickly, inexpensively and efficiently as possible.
r 2.01Starting a case — Initiating Application
Sets out the requirements for filing an Initiating Application — the document that formally starts most family law proceedings.
r 2.07Response to Initiating Application
Sets out how and when a respondent must file their response, including timeframes and what the response must contain.
r 8.15Affidavit requirements
Specifies how affidavits must be prepared, sworn, and filed — including formatting, the declaration, and what may and may not be included.
r 10.15Consent orders
Sets out the procedure for applying for consent orders — orders made by agreement between the parties without a contested hearing.
r 12.01Application for divorce
Specifies the procedure for filing a divorce application, including supporting documents, service requirements, and hearing arrangements.
Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989
Commonwealth · Governs the formula assessment of child support
Child support
s 3Objects of the Act
States that the Act's purpose is to ensure children receive adequate financial support from both parents, and that the level of support reflects each parent's capacity to pay.
s 35KFormula assessment — basic formula
Sets out how child support is calculated — based on each parent's income, the costs of raising children, and the amount of time each parent cares for them.
s 98CApplication for departure from formula assessment
Allows either parent to apply to Services Australia (Child Support) for an administrative change from the formula amount in specified circumstances.
s 116Court order for child support
Allows a party to apply to a court for a child support order — for example, where administrative assessment is not available or a party is overseas.
Child Support (Registration and Collection) Act 1988
Commonwealth · Governs registration, collection and enforcement of child support
Enforcement
s 4Objects of the Act
States the Act's purpose: to ensure child support liabilities are registered, collected, and enforced effectively — including through employer deductions, tax intercepts, and overseas enforcement.
s 30Registration of liabilities
Explains how child support liabilities — both administrative assessments and court orders — are registered with Services Australia for collection.
s 72ACDeparture prohibition orders
Allows the Child Support Registrar to prevent a payer from leaving Australia where they owe substantial child support debt and are unlikely to pay.
Family Violence Provisions
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) · Division 11 and related provisions
Protection
s 60CC(2A)Family violence — specific weight in best interests
Requires the court to give particular weight to the need to protect a child from harm, including family violence, in the best interests assessment.
s 60CGCourt to consider family violence orders
Requires the court to consider any family violence order affecting a child or a member of the child's family when making a parenting order.
s 67ZObligation to disclose family violence
Requires a party who is aware of family violence, or risk of family violence, affecting a child to notify the court in prescribed circumstances.
s 68BInjunctions relating to safety of children
Allows the court to make injunctions to protect the safety, welfare and wellbeing of children — including restraining a party from removing a child from Australia.
s 114Injunctions — personal protection
Allows the court to grant injunctions for the personal protection of a party or a child — including to restrain a person from entering premises or approaching within a specified distance.

a42
Administrative Assessment
Orders
The default mechanism by which Services Australia calculates child support payable, based on an administrative formula rather than a court order. It is the standard way child support is assessed for most separated parents in Australia.
When it applies: The administrative assessment is made by Services Australia and applies automatically once an application is lodged. It does not require a court order. The formula considers both parents' adjusted taxable income, a self-support amount, published costs of children, and care percentages. An administrative assessment can be changed through a change of assessment process or replaced by a court-ordered departure order or a Binding Child Support Agreement. Related: child support assessment, child support.
ADVO
Protection
Abbreviation for Apprehended Domestic Violence Order. See Apprehended Domestic Violence Order.
When it applies: Used widely in court documents, police reports, and everyday speech. When reading documents, ADVO and AVO are often used interchangeably in the domestic violence context. Technically, ADVO refers specifically to domestic relationships; APVO (Apprehended Personal Violence Order) refers to non-domestic relationships. Both are made under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW).
Agreed Facts
Evidence
Factual matters that both parties formally accept as true for the purposes of the proceedings, removing the need for those facts to be proved by evidence at a hearing.
When it applies: Parties can prepare a document called a Statement of Agreed Facts that is filed with the court before a hearing. This narrows the issues in dispute, saves court time, and can reduce legal costs. Courts encourage parties to identify agreed facts early in proceedings. Facts that cannot be agreed remain in dispute and must be proved by evidence. Related: evidence bundle, affidavit.

Preparing a Statement of Agreed Facts

Before any hearing, review the other party's position carefully and identify areas of genuine agreement. Common agreed facts include: dates of marriage and separation, children's dates of birth, existence of property and its approximate value, and procedural history.

Agreed facts should be stated neutrally and specifically. Avoid agreeing to characterisations or legal conclusions — agree to facts only. For example: 'The parties separated on or about 1 March 2023' is an agreed fact.

Even partial agreement on facts assists the court significantly. Courts often comment favourably on parties who have made genuine efforts to narrow the issues before hearing.

Alienation
High Conflict
A pattern of behaviour in which one parent attempts to undermine or destroy the child's relationship with the other parent, causing the child to reject or fear the target parent without legitimate justification. Courts treat alienating conduct very seriously.
When it applies: Evidence of alienation may include: a child refusing contact that was previously positive; the child using adult language and concepts to explain their refusal; one parent making negative statements about the other in the child's presence; interfering with contact; and making false allegations. Courts must distinguish genuine estrangement (where the child's negative feelings are a legitimate response to the other parent's conduct) from alienation (where the feelings are unjustly manipulated). In serious cases, courts have ordered changes of residency to protect the child's relationship with the alienated parent. Related: parental responsibility, best interests of the child, family report.

Responding to Alienation Concerns

In court, what matters is documented conduct and how it affects the child — not whether anyone uses the words "parental alienation" or similar labels. Section references on CasePath are for orientation; always check the current Family Law Act and obtain independent legal advice.

If you believe alienation is occurring, document every instance carefully: what was said or done, when, and who was present. Consistency and specificity are essential — courts are alert to generalised or exaggerated allegations.

Raise alienation concerns through your affidavit and, if appropriate, by requesting that an ICL be appointed and that a family report be ordered. Family consultants are specifically trained to assess family dynamics and identify alienating patterns.

Alienation allegations are sensitive and contested. Courts assess them carefully and require evidence. Making unsubstantiated alienation claims can damage your own credibility. Focus on specific, documented behaviours rather than broad characterisations.

CasePath provides general information only — seek independent legal advice about your own proceedings.

Amended Application
Court Process
A modification to the original application filed with the court, changing the orders sought, the facts relied upon, or other details of the original filing.
When it applies: When circumstances change or new evidence emerges, a party may need to amend their application to reflect the current position. Court permission may be required, particularly late in proceedings.

Amending Your Application

An amended application modifies the original orders sought. This may be necessary where circumstances have changed since filing, new evidence has emerged, or the original application was incomplete.

Early in proceedings, amendment is usually straightforward. Closer to a hearing, you will need the court's permission — and the other side may be entitled to additional time to respond to new matters.

💡 Act early

If you know you need to change what you are seeking, do it as early as possible. Late amendments can disrupt the timetable, attract costs orders, and damage judicial goodwill.

Amending Your Application

An amended application modifies the orders originally sought. Amendments may be needed where circumstances change, new evidence emerges, or the original application was incorrectly drafted. Court permission may be required, particularly late in proceedings.

⚠️ Don't amend without purpose

Every amendment creates an opportunity for the other party to respond and for hearings to be adjourned. Amend when genuinely necessary — not to widen the scope of the dispute or to raise issues you should have raised originally.

Alienation Allegations
Parenting
Claims that one parent is systematically undermining the child's relationship with the other parent — through negative comments, blocking contact, coaching the child, or other conduct designed to damage the child's attachment to the other parent. The court examines such allegations carefully due to their complexity and the risk they are misused.
When it applies: Relevant where a parent alleges the other is intentionally damaging the child's relationship with them. The term "parental alienation syndrome" is not accepted as a clinical diagnosis in Australia, but the underlying conduct is taken seriously where supported by specific evidence.

Alienation Allegations — Handle With Care

In court, what matters is documented conduct and how it affects the child — not whether anyone uses the words "parental alienation" or similar labels. Section references on CasePath are for orientation; always check the current Family Law Act and obtain independent legal advice.

Alienation allegations involve claims that one parent is systematically undermining the child's relationship with the other parent. Courts examine these carefully due to their complexity and the risk of misuse — they are sometimes raised to deflect from legitimate safety concerns.

The concept of "parental alienation syndrome" is not accepted as a clinical diagnosis in Australia. However, the underlying behaviour — a parent acting to damage a child's relationship with the other — is taken seriously if supported by evidence.

⚠️ Evidence is everything

Alienation claims without specific documented evidence are often dismissed. If raising alienation, be specific: dates, conduct, impact on the child. If responding to it, address it directly with your own evidence of the child's authentic relationship with you.

CasePath provides general information only — seek independent legal advice about your own proceedings.

Abuse Allegations
Protection
Claims that a child or parent has been subjected to physical, emotional, or sexual harm. The court treats such allegations seriously and may require evidence before making findings.
When it applies: Raised in parenting proceedings where a party alleges harm to a child or themselves. The court must consider these allegations and may order a family report, child impact report, or protective interim orders. A civil standard of proof applies — the court does not require a criminal conviction.
Abuse of Process
Court Process
The misuse of court procedures for an improper purpose — such as to harass the other party, delay proceedings, obtain a tactical advantage, or relitigate matters already decided. Courts have inherent jurisdiction to prevent and sanction abuse of process.
When it applies: May result in summary dismissal of an application, a permanent stay of proceedings, significant costs orders, or referral to appropriate authorities. Courts take abuse of process seriously as it undermines the administration of justice and imposes unjustified burden on the other party and the court system.
Access Time
Parenting
An older term referring to the time a child spends with a parent who does not live with them. Now replaced in Australian family law by the term 'spend time with' or simply 'time with' a parent.
When it applies: You may encounter this term in older court orders or documents. Under current legislation and practice, the equivalent concept is expressed as 'time with' orders under a parenting arrangement. The substance is the same — the language has been modernised.
Additional Conditions
Protection
Optional restrictions added to an AVO beyond the mandatory conditions that apply in every AVO. Additional conditions are tailored to the specific circumstances of the case and the risk posed by the defendant.
When it applies: Courts may add conditions such as: no contact by any means (phone, email, social media), no approach within a set distance, not entering the protected person's suburb, surrendering firearms, not approaching the protected person's workplace or children's school, and not publishing material about the protected person online. The applicant or police may request specific conditions; the court decides what is appropriate. Related: mandatory conditions, no contact condition, no approach condition.

Requesting Additional Conditions

When applying for an AVO, you can specify the additional conditions you are seeking. Explain why each condition is necessary by reference to past conduct. Courts are more likely to grant conditions that are proportionate and directly connected to the risks you face.

Common additional conditions in domestic violence matters include social media restrictions (preventing the defendant from posting about the protected person), and firearms surrender orders (mandatory if the defendant holds a firearms licence).

Additional conditions can be varied or removed at a later court date if circumstances change. If a condition is proving unworkable — for example, because it prevents necessary communication about children — you can apply to vary it while keeping the core protection in place.

Adjourned Hearing
Court Process
A hearing that has been postponed from its original listed date and rescheduled to a new date by the court. Any interim orders in place at the time of the adjournment typically remain operative until the adjourned date.
When it applies: Arises when a party is unprepared, documents have not been filed, or settlement negotiations require more time. Parties must notify the court promptly if they anticipate difficulty meeting a hearing date.
Adjournment
Court Process
A postponement of a court hearing to a later date. An adjournment suspends the current listing and reschedules the matter, with all existing orders and obligations remaining in force in the interim.
When it applies: Applies when a party needs more time to prepare, file documents, or when negotiations are ongoing. Either party may seek an adjournment, or the court may adjourn of its own motion. The court has discretion to grant or refuse.
Adjournment Application
Court Administration
A formal request to the court to postpone a scheduled court listing or hearing to a later date. An adjournment application may be made by consent (both parties agree) or on notice (one party seeks an adjournment over the other's objection).
When it applies: Adjournment applications arise when a party is not ready to proceed, a key witness is unavailable, new evidence has emerged, or settlement negotiations are ongoing. Courts do not grant adjournments as a matter of course — you must show genuine cause. Repeated or last-minute adjournment applications can attract costs orders. If both parties agree, contact the court registry in advance rather than waiting until the hearing day. Related: adjournment, court listing.

Applying for an Adjournment

An adjournment application should be made as early as possible. If you wait until the day of the hearing, the court may refuse or impose costs. Where possible, get the other party's agreement in writing before approaching the court.

You will need to explain: why the adjournment is needed, how long you need, and what steps you will take in the intervening period. A vague or last-minute application is likely to be refused.

💡 Contact the registry first

Many adjournments can be arranged by contacting the registry before the hearing date and filing a consent minute. This saves court time and avoids an in-person application.

Administrative Mention
Court Administration
A brief court event, usually before a registrar, used to manage administrative steps in a proceeding — such as confirming that documents have been filed, checking service has been completed, or setting the next court date. It is not a hearing on the merits of the case.
When it applies: Administrative mentions are common in busy registries and allow the court to monitor case progress without occupying judicial time. Parties are expected to attend or be represented. Come prepared to confirm the status of all filing obligations and to propose or agree on a timetable for the next steps. Related: directions hearing, court listing.
Adverse Inference
Evidence
A negative conclusion drawn by the court from a party's failure to produce evidence, call a witness, or provide an explanation that would be expected if their version of events were true.
When it applies: Relevant where a party fails to disclose documents, refuses to answer questions, or fails to call a witness who would be expected to support their case. Courts do not automatically draw adverse inferences — they assess whether the omission or failure is genuinely unexplained and whether an inference is warranted.

Adverse Inference in Family Law

May be drawn where a party fails to produce evidence within their control. The court may infer the missing evidence would not have assisted that party.

Common examples: withholding financial records, refusing access to medical reports, not calling a corroborating witness.

📌 Silence is rarely neutral

If you have evidence that supports your case, produce it. Withholding material the court knows exists may lead to an inference that it would have hurt you.

When Courts Draw Adverse Inferences

An adverse inference may be drawn where a party fails to produce evidence that is within their control and which they could reasonably be expected to produce. The court may infer that the missing evidence would not have assisted that party's case.

Common examples include failing to call a witness who was present, refusing to produce documents in response to subpoena, or declining to provide financial records.

📌 Use it strategically

If the other party fails to produce relevant evidence they clearly have access to, raise it in submissions. Ask the court to draw the inference that the evidence would have been unfavourable to them. Courts recognise this principle and will apply it where it is properly argued.

Aggravated Breach
Protection
A breach of an Apprehended Violence Order involving aggravating circumstances such as the presence of a child, prior AVO convictions, use of a weapon, or causing physical harm. Penalties are significantly more severe than standard breach.
When it applies: Charged by police where one or more aggravating factors are present. The most common aggravating circumstance in family violence contexts is the presence of a child during the breach.

Aggravated Breach of an AVO

Involves additional factors that increase severity — presence of a child, prior AVO convictions, use of a weapon, or causing injury. Penalties are significantly more severe than standard breach.

⚠️ Child present = aggravated

In most states, breaching an AVO in the presence of a child automatically elevates the offence. These findings carry significant weight in parenting risk assessments.

What Makes a Breach Aggravated?

An aggravated breach involves additional factors that increase the seriousness — such as prior AVO breaches, committing an act of violence during the breach, or breaching the order in the presence of a child. Penalties are significantly more severe than a standard breach.

Aggravated findings often carry significant weight in parenting risk assessments, particularly where children were present during the breach or were otherwise exposed to the conduct.

📌 Impact on parenting proceedings

A criminal conviction for aggravated breach is powerful evidence in family law. The family court is not bound by the criminal findings but will give them significant weight when assessing risk and parenting arrangements.

Affidavit
Evidence
A written statement of facts that a person (the deponent) swears or affirms to be true, signed before an authorised witness such as a lawyer or Justice of the Peace. In family law proceedings, affidavits are the primary method of placing evidence before the court, replacing oral testimony in many pre-hearing stages and forming the factual foundation of most applications.
When it applies: Required when filing most applications in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia. Used to support interim applications, respond to the other party's claims, and present evidence at a final hearing. Each party is generally required to file and serve their affidavit materials within court-ordered timeframes.

Affidavit Evidence in Family Law

Affidavits are sworn written evidence forming the foundation of most family law cases. They must:

  • Contain facts, not argument
  • Be structured and chronological
  • Avoid hearsay where possible

Inconsistencies between affidavits, documents and oral evidence can significantly damage credibility. The tone and clarity of affidavit material often influence early judicial impressions.

💡 Practical tip

Write your affidavit as if telling a judge the story of what happened, in order. Describe specific incidents with dates, locations, and what was said or done — not legal conclusions. Judges form their impressions from the detail.

Affidavit in Reply
Evidence
An affidavit filed in response to another party's affidavit, addressing matters raised in their evidence. It is confined to replying to the other party's evidence and should not introduce entirely new issues.
When it applies: Filed within the court-ordered timeframe after the other party's affidavit has been served. Courts generally do not permit reply affidavits to raise matters that should have been included in the original affidavit. A reply that strays beyond responding to the other party's evidence may be struck out or limited.
Affidavit of Service
Court Process
A sworn statement made by the person who served court documents, confirming when, where and how service was effected.
When it applies: Required whenever the other party fails to appear at a hearing — the court will not proceed in their absence without proof of service.

Affidavit of Service

A sworn statement confirming when, where and how documents were served. Required before the court will proceed in the absence of the other party.

Must be made by the person who actually served the documents — including date, time, location, and description of what occurred.

💡 File it promptly

File as soon as service occurs. Without it, if the other party fails to appear, the hearing may be adjourned.

What an Affidavit of Service Contains

An affidavit of service confirms when and how documents were served on a party. It proves procedural compliance and is required before certain applications can proceed — particularly where the other party has not appeared or has not acknowledged receipt.

It should specify the date, time, location, method of service, and the person served. Where personal service was used, describe the interaction briefly.

💡 Always keep these

File your affidavit of service promptly after serving documents. Courts regularly require proof of service before proceeding — having it ready avoids delays and demonstrates compliance with procedural obligations.

Amicable Resolution
Court Process
Agreement reached cooperatively between parties without the need for a contested hearing, typically through negotiation, FDR, or settlement conference.
When it applies: The preferred outcome of family law proceedings. Amicable resolution is faster, cheaper, and typically produces more durable arrangements than court-imposed outcomes. Courts actively encourage resolution at every stage of proceedings.

Why Amicable Resolution Is Worth Pursuing

Amicable resolution refers to agreement reached cooperatively without contested hearing. It is faster, significantly cheaper, and typically produces more durable arrangements than court-imposed outcomes — because both parties had a hand in crafting them.

Research consistently shows that children have better outcomes when their parents resolve arrangements cooperatively. Courts actively encourage and facilitate settlement at every stage of proceedings.

💡 You can negotiate at any stage

It is never too late to resolve proceedings by agreement — even on the morning of a final hearing. Formalise any agreement as consent orders. A negotiated outcome where both parties give something is almost always better for children than a binary judicial decision.

Reaching Amicable Resolution

Amicable resolution refers to agreement reached cooperatively without the need for a contested hearing. It can occur at any stage — through FDR, direct negotiation, a settlement conference, or on the steps of the court.

Agreements reached cooperatively are more durable than imposed orders. Parties who design their own arrangements are more likely to comply with them and less likely to return to court.

💡 Stay open to resolution

Even in deeply contested matters, the circumstances that made resolution seem impossible often shift. Stay open to negotiation at each stage. Most matters that settle do so after significant preparation — preparation that also sharpens your position if you don't settle.

Affidavit Drafting
Evidence
The process of preparing a sworn written statement of facts to be filed as evidence in court proceedings.
When it applies: Required whenever a party needs to place factual evidence before the court. Poor drafting — argumentative tone, irrelevant material, hearsay, or lack of structure — weakens the evidence and may be struck out or ignored.

Drafting Affidavits That Work

Affidavit drafting requires factual, structured and relevant presentation. Every paragraph should contain a fact within your personal knowledge that is relevant to the issues in dispute. Common mistakes:

  • Including argument instead of fact
  • Attacking the other parent's character rather than describing specific behaviour
  • Referring to events you did not personally witness without attribution
  • Extensive irrelevant history
📌 The test for every paragraph

Ask yourself: is this a fact I personally know? Is it relevant to the orders I am seeking? Could it be cross-examined? If you can't answer yes to all three, consider removing it.

Courts read large volumes of affidavits. Clarity, brevity, and organisation matter. A well-structured 15-page affidavit is more effective than a disorganised 50-page one. Each paragraph should contain a single factual matter within your personal knowledge, stated clearly and chronologically.

💡 Structure: chronology then issues

Open with your background and the child's circumstances. Then address each issue in dispute in a separate section with specific, dated evidence. Close with the orders you seek and why they serve the child's interests. Judges can follow this structure easily.

Affirmation
Court Process
A solemn promise to tell the truth made by a witness who objects to taking a religious oath, or who does not hold a religious belief. An affirmation has the same legal force as an oath — giving false evidence after affirming carries the same consequences as perjury.
When it applies: Witnesses are asked at the start of giving oral evidence whether they wish to take an oath or make an affirmation. Both options are equally valid and carry equal legal weight. In affidavit proceedings, the equivalent is an affirmation instead of swearing before a Justice of the Peace. Lying after affirming constitutes perjury, which is a serious criminal offence. Many self-represented litigants choose to affirm rather than swear on a religious text — this is entirely acceptable and does not affect how your evidence is received.

Oath vs Affirmation: What to Choose

There is no legal difference between swearing an oath and making an affirmation. Choose whichever you are most comfortable with. Some people prefer affirmation because it does not involve a religious text; others prefer the traditional oath.

When having an affidavit witnessed, tell the authorised witness whether you wish to swear or affirm. They will use the appropriate form of words. Either is acceptable for all family court documents.

The critical point is that you are bound to tell the truth in either case. Courts are not more or less likely to believe your evidence based on whether you swore or affirmed.

Age-Appropriate Parenting
Parenting
The expectation that a parent's care decisions, routines, and arrangements reflect the developmental stage, maturity, and emotional needs of the child at their current age rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.
When it applies: Considered by courts and family consultants when assessing proposed parenting arrangements — for example, whether overnight stays are appropriate for infants, or whether a teenager should have greater input into their schedule.
Age-Appropriate Weight
Parenting
The principle that the significance given to a child's expressed preferences about parenting arrangements should reflect the child's age, maturity, and capacity to understand the issues involved.
When it applies: Applied when the court considers a child's views as part of the best interests assessment. A teenager's clear and consistent preference is typically given substantial weight. A young child's expressed preference, which may reflect parental influence, is given less determinative weight but is still relevant to the court's assessment.
Allegation Escalation
High Conflict
The pattern of increasingly serious accusations made as proceedings progress, often in response to the other party's filings rather than new events.
When it applies: Recognised by courts and family consultants as a sign of high-conflict litigation. Where allegations appear to escalate in seriousness with each affidavit, courts may scrutinise credibility and question whether the claims reflect genuine concern or tactical positioning.
Allegations of Abuse
Protection
Formal claims made in family court proceedings that a child or another party has been subjected to physical, sexual, emotional, or psychological abuse. A criminal conviction is not required — the family law court applies a civil standard of proof.
When it applies: When raised, the court must treat the child's safety as the paramount consideration and may order investigations, family reports, or protective interim orders. False allegations carry serious consequences, but courts are equally vigilant about not dismissing genuine concerns.
Allocation of Parental Responsibility
Parenting
The court's determination of how decision-making authority for a child's major long-term issues will be divided between parents or others. Responsibility may be sole (one parent) or shared (both parents).
When it applies: Determined in all contested parenting matters and can also be agreed upon in consent orders or a parenting plan. The allocation is always based on the child's best interests, with safety as the primary consideration.
Allocation to Division 1
Court Process
Assignment of a case to Division 1 of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA) — the superior division handling the most complex, legally novel, or serious family law matters. Division 1 was formerly known as the Family Court of Australia.
When it applies: A matter may be allocated or transferred to Division 1 where it involves significant legal complexity, serious family violence, international elements, or novel legal questions. A judge in Division 2 may also transfer a matter up where appropriate.
Allocation to Division 2
Court Process
Assignment of a case to Division 2 of the FCFCOA, which handles the majority of standard family law applications including parenting and property matters. Division 2 was formerly the Federal Circuit Court.
When it applies: Most applications are initially filed in and remain in Division 2. The matter may be transferred to Division 1 if complexity warrants it. Division 2 aims to resolve matters efficiently and at lower cost.
Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)
Dispute Resolution
A broad term covering processes used to resolve disputes outside of a contested trial, including mediation, conciliation, arbitration, and collaborative law. ADR is actively encouraged by the court as a faster and less costly alternative to litigation.
When it applies: Available at any stage of proceedings. Courts may order parties to attempt ADR before proceeding to hearing. ADR is particularly suitable for financial matters and for parenting disputes where the parties have capacity to negotiate. It is not appropriate where there is a significant safety risk or power imbalance.
Annexure
Evidence
A document attached to an affidavit as supporting evidence. Annexures are labelled alphabetically (Annexure A, B, C…) and are identified and referenced within the body of the affidavit. Common examples include text messages, emails, financial statements, and medical records.
When it applies: Used whenever a party wishes to rely on a document as evidence. The affidavit must specifically refer to the annexure and explain its relevance. Annexures not referenced in the affidavit body may be disregarded by the court.
Anton Piller Order
Orders
An urgent ex parte court order (made without notice to the other party) requiring the respondent to permit the applicant to enter specified premises to search for, inspect, and seize documents or items. Named after the English case Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976].
When it applies: Anton Piller orders are granted in exceptional circumstances — where there is strong evidence that the respondent holds relevant items and would destroy or conceal them if given notice. In family law, they are sometimes used to secure documentary evidence of hidden assets or financial records before they can be destroyed. They must be executed in a prescribed manner and the respondent has the right to seek legal advice before permitting entry. Courts make these orders rarely and impose strict conditions. Related: asset pool, property settlement.
Appeal
Appeals
A formal request to a higher court to review and overturn a decision made by a lower court. An appeal is not a re-hearing of the facts — the appellant must demonstrate the original judge made an error of law or a material error of fact that affected the outcome.
When it applies: Available after a final or appealable interim order is made. Leave (permission) of the court is generally required, and strict time limits apply — typically 28 days from the date of the order. Appeals from Division 2 are heard by the Full Court of the FCFCOA.

Appeals in Family Law

An appeal is not a rehearing — it challenges whether the original judge:

  • Applied the wrong legal principle
  • Made a significant factual error
  • Exercised discretion improperly

Disagreement with the outcome alone is insufficient. Appeals are complex, expensive and time-limited.

⚠️ Time limits are strict

Appeals must generally be filed within 28 days. Missing this requires a separate leave application. Get legal advice immediately if considering an appeal.

What Grounds Support an Appeal?

An appeal challenges a judicial decision on the basis of legal error — not because you disagree with the outcome. The appellate court examines whether the original judge applied the wrong legal principle, made a significant factual error, or exercised discretion improperly.

Appeals are complex and time-limited. Strict filing deadlines apply, and leave to appeal may be required. Disagreement with the outcome alone is insufficient.

✓ Arguable grounds include
  • Wrong legal principle applied
  • No evidence for a factual finding
  • Improper exercise of discretion
  • Denial of procedural fairness
✗ Not sufficient grounds
  • Simply disagreeing with the result
  • Wanting to re-litigate the facts
  • A different judge might have decided differently
Appellant
Appeals
The party who brings an appeal — the person challenging a court decision they believe was legally wrong. The opposing party in an appeal is called the respondent.
When it applies: Becomes relevant once a party decides to challenge a court order. The appellant must file a Notice of Appeal within the required timeframe, identify specific grounds of error, and obtain leave if required before the appeal will be listed for hearing.
Applicant
Protection
The person seeking protection under an AVO.
When it applies: Used throughout AVO proceedings to identify the party who initiated the application. In police-initiated AVOs, the police are the applicant even if the protected person is someone else.
Application (Initiating / Response)
Court Process
The formal documents used to commence or respond to family court proceedings. An Initiating Application starts the case and sets out the orders sought. A Response to Initiating Application is filed by the other party and outlines their own position and the orders they seek.
When it applies: Filed at the outset of all contested family law proceedings. The initiating application triggers service obligations, filing fees, and court listing processes. Both documents must be filed in accordance with the court's rules and practice directions.

Initiating Application vs Response — What's the difference?

The Initiating Application is the document that starts family court proceedings. It sets out who is applying, what orders are being sought (parenting, property, or both), and the basic facts relied on. It must be filed with a supporting affidavit, a Notice of Risk form (if parenting orders are sought), and payment of the court filing fee.

The Response to Initiating Application is filed by the other party — the respondent — after being served. It sets out the respondent's own position: which of the applicant's orders they agree or disagree with, and any orders the respondent seeks in their own right. A response is not mandatory, but failing to file one limits the respondent's ability to seek their own orders at hearing.

⏱️ Time limits

The respondent generally has 28 days from the date of service to file a Response. If the matter is listed for a first hearing sooner, the Response must be filed before that date. Missing this deadline does not end the case, but it limits what orders the respondent can seek.

⚠️ Notice of Risk is mandatory

If parenting orders are sought, both the applicant and respondent must file a Notice of Child Abuse, Family Violence or Risk with their application or response. Filing this form is a legal requirement — the proceedings cannot proceed without it.

Application for AVO
Protection
The formal request lodged with a court seeking protection from another person.
When it applies: When you are seeking an AVO against someone who has threatened, harassed, or harmed you. The application can be made at your local court registry or, in urgent situations, through police.
Application to Vary
Court Process
A formal application made to a court seeking to change the conditions of an existing order without cancelling it entirely. It is the procedural vehicle for seeking a variation of orders.
When it applies: In family law, an Application to Vary is filed as an Application in a Case or a new Initiating Application depending on whether the original proceedings remain on foot. You must demonstrate a significant change in circumstances to justify reopening final orders. In AVO matters, an Application to Vary is made directly at the relevant Local Court. Related: variation, change of circumstances.

Filing an Application to Vary

For parenting orders: file an Initiating Application or Application in a Case at the FCFCOA. Attach a supporting affidavit explaining the changed circumstances and what orders you are seeking.

For AVO matters: attend the Local Court registry and complete a Variation/Revocation Application form. A mention date will be listed and the other party will be notified.

Bringing a variation application prematurely — before there has been a genuine change in circumstances — can work against you. Courts may infer that you are not accepting the original orders.

How to make an AVO application

You can apply at your local court registry in person. Bring any evidence you have — photos, messages, medical records, or a written account of incidents. If you are in immediate danger, contact police — they can apply on your behalf and seek an urgent interim AVO.

What happens after you apply?

The court will usually list the matter for a first mention date. If needed, an interim AVO can be granted on the same day without the defendant present. The defendant will then be served and given a chance to respond at a later hearing. You do not need a lawyer to make a private application, but legal advice is recommended.

Who can be the applicant?

Any person aged 16 or over can apply for an AVO at their local court. For children under 16, an adult — usually a parent — applies on their behalf. Where police attend a domestic violence incident, they will often apply for an AVO themselves, making the police the applicant even though they are not the person at risk.

Applicant vs Protected Person

The applicant and the protected person are not always the same. In a police-initiated AVO, the protected person may not have wanted the AVO at all — but police are empowered to apply regardless. Once the order is made, it protects the named person whether they sought it or not.

Apprehended Domestic Violence Order
Protection
An AVO made in circumstances of domestic violence — that is, where the parties are in a domestic relationship (current or former intimate partners, family members, or people living in the same household).
When it applies: An ADVO is subject to the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW). Police have a positive duty to apply for an ADVO on behalf of a victim of domestic violence if they believe the person needs protection. The ADVO includes mandatory conditions and may include additional conditions tailored to the specific risk. An ADVO can protect the applicant and children named in the order. Related: AVO, interim AVO, breach of AVO.

ADVO vs APVO

An ADVO (Apprehended Domestic Violence Order) applies where the parties are in a domestic relationship — such as current or former partners, family members, or people sharing a household. An APVO (Apprehended Personal Violence Order) covers all other relationships, such as neighbours or work colleagues.

Police duty to apply

Under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW), police have a positive duty to apply for an ADVO where they believe a person is in a domestic violence situation and needs protection — even if the protected person does not want the order. This reflects the serious public interest in protecting victims of domestic violence.

Apprehended Violence Order
Protection
A civil court order in NSW that prohibits a person from engaging in conduct that threatens or harasses another person. An AVO can be made by the applicant (or police on their behalf) in the Local Court.
When it applies: An AVO is a civil order — it is not a criminal conviction. It places restrictions on the defendant's behaviour, such as no contact conditions and no approach conditions. Breaching an AVO is, however, a criminal offence. There are two main types: an Apprehended Domestic Violence Order (ADVO) (for domestic relationships) and an Apprehended Personal Violence Order (APVO) (for non-domestic relationships). Related: ADVO, interim AVO, mandatory conditions, breach of AVO.

AVO vs Family Law Orders

An AVO operates independently of family law parenting orders. Both can exist at the same time, and they must be read together. If your AVO prohibits contact but parenting orders require it, seek legal advice immediately about how to reconcile them.

An AVO does not make findings of fault in any family law proceedings, but it is a relevant document. Courts in family proceedings are entitled to know that an AVO exists and may draw inferences from it — particularly about risk to children.

If you are served with an AVO application, do not ignore it. Attend court. Consider seeking Legal Aid or a duty lawyer. You can consent without admissions, which ends the matter without a finding of wrongdoing.

Arbitration
Dispute Resolution
A private dispute resolution process in which parties agree to submit their dispute to an independent arbitrator (who is not a judge) for a binding decision. In Australian family law, arbitration is available for financial matters but not parenting matters.
When it applies: Family law arbitration under the Family Law Act 1975 allows parties to resolve financial disputes (property settlement, superannuation, and maintenance) outside of court with a binding outcome. The arbitrator's award can be registered with the FCFCOA and enforced as a court order. Arbitration is generally faster and more private than court proceedings. Both parties must consent to arbitration, and the arbitrator must be a family law arbitrator accredited by the Law Council of Australia. Arbitration is not available for parenting or child support matters. Related: family dispute resolution, conciliation conference, mediation.

Arbitration vs Mediation

Mediation produces a negotiated agreement — the mediator facilitates but the parties decide. Arbitration produces a decision made by the arbitrator — similar to a judgment but without going to court.

Arbitration is binding and final (subject to very limited grounds of appeal). It gives the parties more control over timing, process, and the identity of the decision-maker than litigation.

Arbitration costs are shared between the parties and include the arbitrator's fees (typically $300-$600/hour) plus lawyer fees. It is usually cheaper and faster than contested court proceedings, but more expensive than mediation.

Arbitration (Family Law)
Dispute Resolution
A private dispute resolution process where an independent arbitrator hears both parties and makes a binding decision called an arbitral award. The process is more formal than mediation but less costly and faster than court.
When it applies: Available for financial and property disputes in family law, but not parenting matters. Both parties must agree in writing to arbitrate. The arbitral award can be registered with the court and enforced as a court order. Particularly suited to parties who want a binding outcome without court delays.
Asset Pool
Orders
The total collection of assets, liabilities, superannuation interests, and financial resources of both parties that a court considers when making a property settlement. Everything owned by either party (jointly or individually) is generally included.
When it applies: The asset pool is the starting point for any property settlement. It includes: real estate, vehicles, bank accounts, investments, superannuation, business interests, inheritance (in some circumstances), and any debts. Assets held in companies or trusts may also be included if the court is satisfied a party effectively controls them. Both parties have a duty of full and frank disclosure — deliberately hiding assets is a serious breach that can result in orders being set aside and costs penalties. Related: property settlement, contributions, future needs.

Disclosure and Hidden Assets

Each party must provide full financial disclosure: bank statements (typically 12 months), superannuation statements, tax returns, mortgage statements, vehicle valuations, and business financials. This is not optional.

If you suspect the other party is hiding assets — transferring property to relatives, undervaluing a business, not disclosing bank accounts — raise this with your lawyer early. Courts can order subpoenas to financial institutions and compel production of records.

Deliberately hiding assets or providing false disclosure is contempt of court and can result in orders being reopened, adverse costs orders, and in serious cases, criminal sanctions.

Attachment Disruption Claim
Parenting
An allegation that a parenting arrangement or a parent's conduct is interfering with the development or maintenance of the child's attachment bond with one or both parents. Secure attachment is recognised as fundamental to healthy child development.
When it applies: Relevant in proceedings involving very young children, cases of long separation, or where one parent has been restricting the child's contact with the other. Expert evidence from a psychologist or family consultant is often required to assess attachment disruption. Courts take attachment concerns seriously in designing parenting arrangements.
b64
Balance of Probabilities
Evidence
The civil standard of proof applied in family law and AVO proceedings. A court applies this standard when deciding whether a fact is established — it asks whether it is more likely than not (greater than 50% probable) that the fact occurred.
When it applies: This is the standard used in all family law proceedings — parenting, property, and AVO matters. It contrasts with the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt. The practical implication is significant: conduct that was never proven in criminal court (because the criminal standard was not met) can still be accepted as proven in family proceedings. For example, a court can find that family violence occurred — and shape parenting orders accordingly — even if police did not charge the perpetrator, or charges were dismissed. See also: standard of proof, Briginshaw standard.

Why This Matters for Your Case

Many litigants mistakenly believe that because police did not charge the other party, or charges were dropped, the conduct cannot be raised in family court. This is incorrect. Family court applies its own lower standard and makes its own findings.

Similarly, a criminal acquittal does not prevent the family court from finding that violence occurred on the balance of probabilities. The family court is not bound by the criminal court's conclusion.

This works both ways: you do not need a police record or conviction to prove family violence in family proceedings. But it also means allegations against you can be accepted even without a criminal finding. Quality evidence is important on both sides.

Behaviour Pattern Evidence
Evidence
Evidence showing a repeated pattern of conduct over time, rather than relying on a single incident. Pattern evidence is often more persuasive in establishing the nature of a relationship or a risk.
When it applies: Particularly relevant in family violence, coercive control, and parenting capacity cases. Courts recognise that a single incident may be ambiguous, but a documented pattern of conduct can establish a clear picture. Behaviour pattern evidence is best presented through a structured, chronological account with specific examples.

Pattern Evidence in Family Law

Demonstrates consistent behaviour over time. Particularly relevant in family violence and coercive control — a documented pattern is far more persuasive than a single incident.

💡 How to present it

Structure your affidavit to show the pattern, not just incidents. Use dates, quote messages directly, show how the behaviour repeated. A chronological incident table can be more compelling than paragraphs of narrative.

Best Interests of the Child
Parenting
The overarching principle guiding all parenting decisions in Australian family law. The court must consider what outcome will best promote the child's safety, wellbeing, and development — including their right to a meaningful relationship with both parents where it is safe to do so.
When it applies: Applies to every parenting decision made by the court. Since the 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act, the child's safety is the primary consideration. Courts assess a range of factors including the child's views, their relationships, and each parent's capacity to care for them.

The Best Interests Framework

The "best interests" principle is the central decision-making framework in Australian parenting law. The court does not determine what outcome is fair to parents — it determines what outcome best promotes the child's safety, welfare and developmental needs.

The legislation sets out primary and additional considerations. Safety from harm carries significant weight. Even where both parents are loving and capable, practical realities — geography, schooling, conflict levels, parental capacity — often determine the outcome.

Importantly, the best interests assessment is discretionary. Two cases with superficially similar facts can produce different results depending on credibility findings, risk assessment, and the child's specific circumstances.

🔑 Key insight

The court's focus is forward-looking: what arrangement best protects and promotes the child's long-term wellbeing. Every argument you make should connect back to your child's specific needs — not to fairness between adults.

Binding Financial Agreement
Orders
A formal written agreement between parties to a marriage or de facto relationship that deals with the division of property and financial matters — either before the relationship begins (a 'pre-nup'), during it, or after separation. When properly executed, it is binding on both parties and can exclude the court's jurisdiction.
When it applies: A BFA must comply with strict requirements under the Family Law Act 1975 (ss 90B, 90C, 90D for married couples; ss 90UB, 90UC, 90UD for de facto couples). Each party must receive independent legal advice before signing, and both lawyers must sign certificates. A BFA can be set aside by a court in limited circumstances: fraud, duress, unconscionable conduct, or a material change in circumstances relating to a child. Related: consent orders, property settlement, financial agreement.

BFA vs Consent Orders

A BFA does not require court approval — it takes effect once signed. Consent orders, by contrast, require court approval but carry the benefit of judicial scrutiny. For complex property matters, consent orders are generally preferred.

The technical requirements for a valid BFA are strict. If the agreement does not comply — for example, if the certificate of independent advice is insufficient — it can be voided. Courts have set aside BFAs on procedural grounds even where both parties intended to be bound.

Pre-relationship BFAs (sometimes called 'pre-nups') are enforceable in Australia but must meet the same technical requirements. They are most valuable in relationships where one party has substantially greater assets or there are family business interests to protect.

Blocking Allegation
High Conflict
A claim that one party obstructed or prevented contact between the child and the other parent, whether by blocking calls, refusing changeovers, or making the child unavailable for scheduled time.
When it applies: Raised in contravention and enforcement proceedings. To support a blocking allegation, a party should document each incident — including date, time, method of attempted contact, and the response received. Repeated blocking without reasonable excuse may result in enforcement orders or variation of the parenting arrangements.
Breach Application
Orders
An application filed by one party alleging that the other has failed to comply with existing court orders. Also known as a contravention application. The court can impose sanctions, make compensatory orders, or refer the matter to police where the breach is serious.
When it applies: Filed when a party has not complied with a parenting or financial order without reasonable excuse. The applicant must identify the specific order breached and how. In parenting matters, the court may order make-up time, impose a fine, or in serious cases, impose a community service or imprisonment order.

How to Bring a Breach Application

A breach application alleges that a party has failed to comply with court orders without reasonable excuse. The applicant bears the burden of proving non-compliance on the balance of probabilities.

The court will ask: was the order clear? Did the respondent understand it? Was there a reasonable excuse? Was there any attempt to make up the time? A strong application addresses all four questions with evidence.

⚠️ Choose your battles

Not every breach warrants a formal application. Courts expect parties to attempt resolution first. Bringing minor technical breach applications repeatedly signals litigation abuse. Reserve formal applications for serious or persistent breaches that genuinely affect the child.

Courts expect breach applications to be genuine, not tactical. Filing for minor breaches without good cause may attract a costs order.

💡 Use a clear table format

Present each breach in a table: date, what the order required, what happened instead, and any communication about it.

Breach of AVO
Protection
The criminal offence of contravening a condition of an AVO — either an ADVO (domestic) or APVO (personal). Breach is a standalone criminal charge, separate from any underlying conduct.
When it applies: Any breach of any condition — including mandatory conditions and additional conditions — is a criminal offence regardless of whether the underlying conduct would itself be criminal. The maximum penalty is 2 years imprisonment and/or a fine of 50 penalty units. Courts treat breach seriously, particularly repeated breaches or those involving violence. Police can charge for breach without the protected person's consent. Evidence of breach includes call logs, messages, CCTV, witness accounts, and police attendance records. Related: AVO, contravention.

Reporting a Breach

If the defendant breaches the AVO, call police immediately. Do not engage with the defendant or attempt to resolve the situation yourself. Police can arrest the defendant and charge for breach without your consent to prosecute.

Document the breach thoroughly: photographs, timestamps, screenshots of messages, names of any witnesses. The more specific and contemporaneous your records, the stronger the breach charge.

Repeated breaches escalate the criminal consequences significantly. Courts imposing sentence for breach consider the total history of non-compliance, the nature of each breach, and the vulnerability of the protected person.

Breach of Orders
Orders
Failure by a party to comply with a court order — most commonly a parenting order. Breach of family law orders can result in contravention proceedings, with penalties including fines, community service, make-up time for the child, or imprisonment in serious cases.
When it applies: Under Div 13A of the Family Law Act 1975, a person who breaches a parenting order without a reasonable excuse can face contravention proceedings. The court may: adjourn and require the parties to attend family dispute resolution; make a further parenting order; order make-up time; impose a fine; order community service; or in serious/repeated cases, impose imprisonment. A reasonable excuse includes: the order was not practicable to comply with; the breach was necessary to protect the child from harm. Related: contravention application, parenting order.

When to File a Contravention Application

Before filing, consider whether the breach was serious or a one-off. Contravention proceedings add cost and conflict. For minor or isolated breaches, a letter from a lawyer noting the breach and requesting compliance may be more effective.

For repeated or serious breaches — particularly withholding of children — contravention proceedings are appropriate. Courts take persistent non-compliance with orders very seriously.

Document every breach: date, what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, any communications about it. The clearer your evidence, the stronger your application.

c12
Case Assessment Conference (CAC)
Court Process
An early court event managed by a registrar or senior family consultant designed to identify the issues in dispute, explore the possibility of resolution, and set procedural directions for how the case will progress.
When it applies: Typically scheduled shortly after proceedings commence and before the matter is listed for a hearing. If resolution is possible, consent orders may be made at the CAC itself, avoiding the need for further litigation.

Case Assessment Conference in Practice

A case assessment conference is an early procedural event to identify issues, encourage resolution and set directions. It shapes the case pathway and is one of the first opportunities for the matter to resolve without a hearing.

If the parties reach agreement at the CAC, consent orders can be made on the spot. If not, the registrar will set timetables for filing evidence and list the matter for a hearing.

💡 Come prepared

Know your key issues, what orders you are seeking, and whether there are any urgent safety concerns. The more clearly you can articulate your position, the more productively the conference will run. Bring a summary of your case, not your full affidavit.

Case Management
Court Process
The process by which the court oversees the progress of a matter from filing to resolution. A judicial officer issues directions, sets deadlines, and monitors compliance to ensure the matter moves efficiently toward resolution without unnecessary delay or cost.
When it applies: Applies throughout proceedings. Case management hearings are scheduled regularly to review compliance, set next steps, and ensure both parties are progressing their case. Failure to comply with case management directions can result in costs orders, striking out of pleadings, or dismissal.

How Case Management Works

Case management refers to judicial oversight of procedural steps to ensure efficient progression. It includes setting timetables, identifying the real issues in dispute, and limiting unnecessary evidence. Strong case management reduces delay and cost for all parties.

Courts actively manage family law cases to prevent them from becoming protracted. If you are not complying with case management directions, expect to be called on it.

⚠️ Comply with all directions

Missing court-ordered deadlines without seeking a variation in advance is one of the most common and easily avoided mistakes. If you cannot meet a deadline, file a request to vary the timetable before the deadline passes — not after.

Courts also expect cooperation on procedural steps — late filing, unnecessary applications, or ignoring directions can attract adverse costs even when you believe you are substantively in the right.

💡 Work with the process, not against it

Courts expect parties to cooperate on procedural matters even when the substantive dispute is bitter. Agreeing on timetables and directions where possible demonstrates reasonableness and reduces your costs.

Case Pathway
Court Process
The procedural route a matter follows from initial filing through to final hearing, including all intermediate events and timetable milestones.
When it applies: Determined early in proceedings at case assessment or directions hearings. The pathway affects how quickly the matter progresses, what evidence must be filed and when, and the overall cost and duration of the proceedings.

Understanding the Case Pathway

The case pathway determines procedural progression from filing to final hearing. It shapes timing and evidence requirements. Understanding your pathway helps you plan resources, manage expectations, and identify upcoming milestones.

Matters may be placed on different tracks — dispute resolution, short hearing, or long hearing — depending on complexity. The pathway can be varied if circumstances change significantly.

💡 Know your milestones

At your first court event, ask for a clear timetable with all key dates. Diary every deadline immediately. Missing milestones delays the case, attracts adverse comment, and can have costs consequences.

Common pathways include the standard track, the specialist list (for complex cases), and the fast track (for matters capable of early resolution). The court assigns pathways based on complexity, risk, and the nature of the dispute.

💡 Understand your pathway early

Ask the registry or check the court's procedural guide to understand which pathway applies to your matter. Missing a milestone on your pathway — a filing deadline, a listed conference — can delay your entire case significantly.

Case Management Conference
Court Administration
A structured procedural hearing at which the court reviews the progress of a matter and issues directions to keep it moving toward resolution. The case management system in the FCFCOA means most matters will have at least one case management conference before a final hearing is allocated.
When it applies: Case management conferences are usually before a registrar rather than a judge. Parties should be ready to confirm: what documents have been filed and served; whether disclosure is complete; whether a family report is needed; and realistic timeframes for finalising the matter. Courts use these conferences to identify matters that can be resolved without trial and to ensure the parties are not delaying. Related: directions hearing, case management.

Preparing for a Case Management Conference

Before a case management conference, review what directions have been made and whether you have complied. If you have not, have an explanation ready and be prepared to propose a revised timetable.

The registrar will want to know whether the matter is on track, what issues remain genuinely in dispute, and whether any interim orders are needed. Raising settlement at a conference is appropriate and encouraged.

💡 Narrow the issues before you attend

Contact the other party before the conference to agree on as many directions as possible. Parties who arrive having already resolved procedural disputes are viewed favourably. Courts dislike having to referee disagreements about filing dates that could have been sorted out by email.

Case Management Pathway
Court Administration
The structured route a family law matter follows from initial filing through to final resolution, as determined by the case management framework of the FCFCOA. The pathway allocates the matter to an appropriate track — fast, standard, or complex — based on the nature and urgency of the issues.
When it applies: Your matter's pathway determines the pace and type of events you will attend. Fast-track matters (urgent parenting or safety concerns) move quickly. Standard matters follow a set timetable of directions, conferences, and hearings.
