Economic Abuse
High Conflict
A form of family violence involving the control, exploitation, or sabotage of a person's financial resources, income, or economic activity. Economic abuse is recognised as family violence under Australian law and is relevant to both protection orders and family law proceedings.
When it applies: Examples include: controlling access to bank accounts; preventing a partner from working or studying; accumulating debt in the other person's name without their knowledge; forcing a partner to sign financial documents; denying money for basic necessities; sabotaging employment; and taking the other person's income. Under s 4AB of the Family Law Act 1975, economic abuse is a defined form of family violence. It is increasingly recognised in property settlement — a party who suffered economic abuse may receive a greater share of the asset pool to recognise both the conduct and its financial impact. Related: family violence, coercive control, property settlement.

Economic Abuse and Property Settlement

If you experienced economic abuse during the relationship, document it carefully: bank statements showing denied access, communications about financial control, evidence of debts incurred in your name, and impact on your career or education.

Courts can take into account conduct during the relationship, including economic abuse, in determining what is just and equitable in property settlement. This is separate from the contributions analysis.

The Australian Banking Association has a financial hardship protocol for victims of financial abuse. If the other party controlled your finances and you have credit damage as a result, seek specialist financial counselling through the National Debt Helpline.

Electronic Filing
Court Administration
The submission of court documents through the Commonwealth Courts Portal (CCP) — the online system used by the FCFCOA for receiving, processing, and managing family law filings.
When it applies: Mandatory for most document filings in FCFCOA proceedings. Applies to both represented and self-represented parties. Technical difficulties do not automatically extend filing deadlines — apply promptly for an extension if needed.

Electronic Filing in Practice

Electronic filing allows documents to be lodged through the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia's online portal. Strict formatting and compliance requirements apply — PDFs must meet size and naming conventions, and forms must be completed correctly before the system will accept them. Documents that do not meet technical requirements may be rejected without being processed.

Improper filing may result in rejection without notice, causing you to miss deadlines without realising it. Always check for a confirmation receipt after filing. Filing fees apply to most documents; fee waivers are available for financial hardship — apply before filing, not after.

💡 Always save your confirmation

Screenshot or save the filing confirmation immediately after each submission. If the portal later shows no record of your filing, your confirmation is evidence that you lodged it. File early — portal issues on the day of a deadline are not accepted as an excuse.

💡 Common rejection reasons

Incorrect PDF formatting, missing signatures, wrong document type selected, and file size limits are the most common causes of rejection. Check the court's electronic filing guide before lodging for the first time.

Electronic Service
Court Process
Service of court documents via approved digital means such as email, where permitted by court rules or agreed between the parties.
When it applies: Increasingly common in family law proceedings. Requires either the other party's consent or a court order permitting electronic service. Documents served electronically must comply with the same content and timing requirements as physical service.

Electronic Service in Practice

Electronic service allows documents to be served via approved digital means — most commonly email. The recipient's agreement or a court order is required for electronic service to be valid for most document types.

Keep delivery receipts and read receipts where possible. If service is later disputed, your evidence of sending is not sufficient — you may need to show the email was received.

💡 Agree on an email address in writing

At the start of proceedings, confirm in writing the email address both parties will use for service. Disputes about whether service was effective are common and easily avoided by clear early agreement.

Electronic service of documents may be via email or the court's online portal. The court's rules specify which documents may be served electronically and when service is deemed to have occurred. Service by email is generally taken to occur at the time of sending if sent during business hours, or at the start of the next business day if sent after hours.

💡 Keep delivery receipts

Always request read receipts or keep email delivery confirmations for documents served electronically. If the other party later claims non-receipt, your delivery records are your proof of service.

Emergency Protection Order
Protection
A short-term protective order made urgently — sometimes without notice to the respondent — when a person or child faces an immediate and serious risk of harm.
When it applies: Issued by police or state courts when there is insufficient time to file a standard protection order application. It is a temporary measure, typically lasting a short number of days, until a full hearing can be listed to determine whether a longer-term protection order is warranted.
Emotional Regulation Concern
Parenting
A concern about a parent's capacity to manage their own emotional responses in a way that does not harm the child — particularly in high-conflict situations, during changeovers, or when discussing the other parent in the child's presence.
When it applies: Raised in family reports, risk assessments, and parenting proceedings. Evidence of emotional dysregulation — such as hostile communication, incidents at changeover, or children reporting distress about a parent's anger — can influence the court's assessment of parenting capacity and may result in more structured or supervised arrangements.
Enforcement Hearing
Court Process
A hearing convened specifically to address alleged non-compliance with court orders. The court considers the evidence of breach, any reasonable excuse, and determines what enforcement measures are appropriate.
When it applies: Scheduled when a contravention application is filed and cannot be resolved by consent. Both parties present evidence and submissions. Courts have broad powers at enforcement hearings including making compensatory orders, imposing fines, ordering community service, or varying the underlying orders.

What Happens at an Enforcement Hearing

An enforcement hearing examines alleged breaches of court orders and determines appropriate consequences. The applicant must prove the breach; the respondent can raise a reasonable excuse. The court considers whether the orders were clear, whether the breach occurred, and whether there was a reasonable excuse — the burden shifts to the breaching party to explain their conduct.

Outcomes range from a formal finding and make-up time through to fines, bonds, community service, or in serious cases, imprisonment. The court may vary the underlying orders if that would better serve the child.

📌 Document every breach

Keep a contemporaneous log: date, time, what was ordered, exactly what happened, and any communications from the other party. Your evidence must prove both that the order was clear and that it was not followed.

📌 Prepare your evidence carefully

For the applicant: document every breach specifically with dates, what was ordered, and what happened. For the respondent: gather everything that supports your reasonable excuse — communications, medical records, witness accounts.

Enforcement Order
Orders
An order made by the court to compel compliance with an existing court order that has been breached. In parenting matters, enforcement orders can include make-up time, compensatory time, or sanctions against the non-complying party.
When it applies: Applied for by the aggrieved party after a contravention has occurred. The court must be satisfied that a contravention occurred and that there was no reasonable excuse for it before making enforcement orders.

Enforcement Orders

The court may impose:

  • Make-up time for missed contact
  • Bonds requiring good behaviour
  • Fines payable to the other party
  • Variation of existing arrangements

Persistent non-compliance may justify altering primary arrangements — including reversing who the child lives with.

🚨 Document every breach

Keep a dated log of each incident. A pattern of contraventions carries far more weight than individual complaints.

Enforcing parenting orders

Before applying for enforcement, document each breach clearly — date, what was ordered, what happened instead. Courts expect you to have attempted to resolve the issue before bringing an application.

⚠️ Serious non-compliance

Where a party repeatedly withholds a child in breach of orders, the court has the power to reverse primary living arrangements. Sustained non-compliance is one of the strongest grounds for a major variation at final hearing.

Escalation Behaviour
Litigation Conduct
A pattern of increasing conflict, applications, or breaches that intensifies the adversarial nature of proceedings over time.
When it applies: Recognised by courts as a harmful dynamic that damages children and often reflects an inability or unwillingness to prioritise their wellbeing. Escalation behaviour — filing repeated applications, making new allegations each time previous ones fail, or responding to every perceived slight with a court application — may influence judicial assessment of parenting capacity.

Escalation Behaviour — What Courts See

Escalation behaviour involves increasing conflict through repeated applications or breaches. It may influence judicial assessment of parenting capacity — courts view escalation as evidence of an inability to prioritise the child over personal grievance.

Both parties may escalate. The parent who demonstrates the ability to de-escalate, stay focused on the child, and avoid unnecessary conflict will generally present better to the court.

💡 De-escalation as a litigation strategy

Consciously choosing not to respond to provocation, not filing applications for minor issues, and keeping communications business-like and child-focused is not weakness — it is strategically smart. It demonstrates parenting maturity and protects your credibility with the court.

Escalation behaviour may also involve disproportionate responses to minor issues, breaches of orders, or aggressive litigation tactics. A parent who escalates conflict — even in response to genuine provocation — may find that the court treats them as contributing to an unsafe environment for the child, regardless of who started the conflict.

📌 De-escalate wherever possible

Every time you respond proportionately to provocation, you demonstrate maturity and child-focus. Document the provocation so the court knows it occurred, but show through your own conduct that you are the stable parent.

Ex Parte Order
Court Process
A court order made without the other party being present or notified, usually due to urgency or where notification would defeat the purpose of the order.
When it applies: Available in urgent circumstances where the risk is immediate and giving notice to the other party could cause harm or allow the situation to be worsened before the order is made. The other party is notified after the order is made and given an opportunity to be heard at the return date.

Ex Parte Orders — What They Are

An ex parte order is made without the other party present, usually due to urgency. The absent party is not given notice before the order is made — they are served after and given the opportunity to be heard at a return date, usually within days or weeks.

Because they are made on one side's evidence only, the court applies a high duty of candour — you must disclose all relevant facts, including those that might assist the other party's position, or the order may be set aside.

⚠️ Full disclosure required

Failure to disclose material facts when seeking an ex parte order can result in the order being set aside and a costs order against you. When making an ex parte application, you must disclose facts that may weigh against granting the orders — even if they help the other party.

Ex parte orders are subject to a return date where the other party can be heard. Courts scrutinise the basis for ex parte applications carefully.

⚠️ Full and frank disclosure

Omissions can lead to the order being set aside and adverse consequences for you.

Equal Shared Parental Responsibility
Parenting
A former statutory presumption (removed by 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act) that both parents would share equal responsibility for major long-term decisions about their child. Courts now assess what arrangement best serves the child in each individual case.
When it applies: No longer presumed — courts make orders based on the specific circumstances of each family. Shared parental responsibility remains possible and common where it serves the child's interests. It should not be confused with equal time, which concerns where the child lives rather than who makes decisions.

Parental Responsibility vs. Time

Equal shared parental responsibility concerns decision-making authority — not time spent with the child. There is a legislative presumption that it is in a child's best interests for parents to share major long-term decision-making, unless evidence of family violence or abuse rebuts that presumption.

If the presumption applies, the court must then consider whether equal time or substantial and significant time is appropriate — but only if reasonably practicable and in the child's best interests.

🔑 Key distinction

Evidence of coercive control, sustained conflict, or inability to cooperate can undermine the presumption. Major long-term decisions include schooling, medical treatment, and religious upbringing — not day-to-day parenting decisions.

Equal Time
Parenting
A parenting arrangement where a child spends approximately equal time living with each parent, typically structured as alternating weeks. Equal time is about the child's physical living arrangements, not decision-making authority.
When it applies: Ordered only where the court finds it to be in the child's best interests and reasonably practicable — having regard to the parents' proximity, their ability to communicate and cooperate, and the child's needs and preferences. Equal time is not automatic.
Escalating Enforcement
Orders
The progressive increase in legal consequences imposed by a court for repeated failures to comply with orders. As breaches accumulate, the court's response becomes more severe, potentially including fines, community service, or imprisonment.
When it applies: Applied in serious or repeated contravention cases. Courts use escalating enforcement to signal that continued non-compliance will have increasingly serious consequences. It is intended to achieve compliance rather than simply punish, but the court retains full discretion to impose significant sanctions.
Escalation Risk
Protection
The risk that an existing pattern of concerning behaviour — such as conflict, family violence, or non-compliance — will intensify if not addressed by the court. Escalation risk informs the protective orders a court considers necessary.
When it applies: Assessed by family consultants and courts in proceedings involving family violence or high conflict. Evidence of escalating behaviour, such as increasingly serious incidents over time, strengthens the case for protective orders. De-escalation — such as completed behaviour change programs — can be relevant to reducing supervision requirements.
Evidence
Court Process
Information presented to the court in a prescribed form to help establish facts in dispute. In family law, evidence is given through affidavits, oral testimony, exhibits, and expert reports. Not all information is admissible — the court applies rules about relevance, reliability, and form.
When it applies: Required at every contested hearing. Parties must file and serve their evidence within court-ordered timeframes. Evidence filed late may be excluded. The court weighs the totality of the evidence when making findings and orders.
Evidence Bundle
Evidence
A compiled and indexed collection of documentary evidence that a party intends to rely on at a hearing. Also called a court book or trial bundle. It typically includes affidavits, exhibits, reports, correspondence, financial records, and other supporting documents.
When it applies: Parties are usually directed to prepare and exchange evidence bundles before a hearing date. The bundle should be paginated, indexed, and organised logically (chronologically or by topic). Both parties and the judge work from the same bundle during the hearing, which ensures everyone is referring to the same document when it is discussed. Failing to properly prepare your evidence bundle can result in documents not being admitted. Related: affidavit, exhibits, annexure.

Preparing Your Evidence Bundle

Start compiling your evidence bundle early. Obtain copies of all relevant documents — bank statements, school reports, medical records, photographs, text messages — and organise them chronologically.

Each document in the bundle should be referenced in your affidavit as an exhibit (Exhibit A, Exhibit B, etc). The judge will cross-reference your sworn evidence with the documents in the bundle.

For self-represented litigants: use dividers or tabs to separate categories of documents. File three copies — one for the court, one for the other party, one for yourself. Courts appreciate organised, legible bundles.

Evidence Flooding
High Conflict
The submission of an excessive volume of documents, annexures, or affidavit material that is disproportionate to the issues in dispute, making it difficult for the court and the other party to identify what is truly relevant.
When it applies: Courts regularly criticise evidence flooding as contrary to the overarching purpose and as a potential abuse of process. Affidavit material should be focused, proportionate, and confined to matters that genuinely assist the court. Excessive annexures are often disregarded or the party is directed to file a reduced set of documents.
Evidence Objection
Evidence
A formal challenge to the admissibility of evidence on grounds such as relevance, hearsay, opinion, or procedural non-compliance.
When it applies: Raised during a hearing when a party attempts to rely on evidence that the objecting party believes should not be admitted. Successful objections may exclude damaging material. Objections must be raised promptly — if you allow evidence in without objection, you may lose the right to challenge it.

Evidence Objections — How and When

An evidence objection challenges admissibility based on relevance, hearsay, opinion evidence, or procedural defects. Successful objections may exclude damaging material. Raise objections promptly — waiting until after the evidence is in may be too late.

Family law courts have more flexible evidentiary rules than criminal courts, so objections on pure technical grounds are less likely to succeed. Focus objections on material that is clearly irrelevant or that would be genuinely unfair to admit without prior notice.

💡 Common valid objections

Documents not produced in discovery that are sprung at trial; expert reports not served in time; evidence relating to matters not in issue; material that is purely scandalous or designed to embarrass rather than inform.

Raise objections before the material is read into evidence if possible. State the specific ground — for example relevance — rather than a general objection. Courts expect precision.

💡 Object early and specifically

Family law has more flexible evidentiary rules than criminal proceedings, but courts still exercise discretion to exclude unreliable, prejudicial, or irrelevant material.

Evidence in Chief
Evidence
The primary evidence a party relies on to establish their case, typically contained in their affidavit. In family law proceedings, evidence in chief is almost always given in writing before the hearing rather than orally, and the affidavit stands as the witness's evidence unless they are called to be cross-examined.
When it applies: Filed and served within court-ordered timeframes before a hearing. If a party fails to file evidence in chief on time, the court may refuse to allow reliance on late evidence, which can significantly undermine their case. At the hearing, the affidavit is formally tendered and the deponent may be cross-examined on its contents.

Evidence in Chief in Family Law

The primary evidence a party presents — typically through affidavit. It forms the foundation of the case. Clarity, consistency and credibility are central.

A focused, chronological affidavit with specific detail is far more persuasive than a sprawling complaint. Courts read hundreds of affidavits — concise, factual evidence stands out.

💡 Structure matters

Lead with who you are, the children, and the key issues. Tell the story chronologically. End with the orders you seek and why they serve the child's best interests. Avoid legal argument — that is for submissions.

Evidence in Chief in Practice

Evidence in chief refers to the primary evidence presented by a party, typically through affidavit in family law proceedings. It forms the foundation of the case — everything else (cross-examination, rebuttal) responds to it.

Clarity, consistency and credibility are central. A well-constructed affidavit tells a coherent, factual narrative that anticipates the other party's likely challenges and addresses them directly.

📌 What makes strong evidence in chief

Specificity beats generality every time. "On 14 March he arrived 3 hours late, smelling of alcohol, and the children were visibly distressed" is far stronger than "he was often unreliable and seemed to be drinking." The more specific your evidence, the harder it is to dismiss.

Ex Parte Application
Court Process
An application made to the court by one party without notifying the other party. Any orders made ex parte are temporary, and the absent party must ordinarily be given an opportunity to be heard shortly afterwards.
When it applies: Reserved for situations of genuine urgency where notifying the other party in advance would defeat the purpose of the application or put a person at immediate risk. The applicant must make full and frank disclosure of all relevant facts, including facts that may favour the other party.
Exclusion from Home
Protection
A condition in an AVO or a family law injunction prohibiting a person from entering or remaining at the family home, regardless of whether they own or co-own the property.
When it applies: Courts can exclude a person from their own home where necessary to protect the safety of the other occupants. Property ownership is not a defence. In AVO proceedings, an exclusion condition is one of the additional conditions courts can impose. In family law proceedings, a similar result can be achieved through an injunction under s 114 of the Family Law Act 1975. Related: protected address, injunction.

Exclusion and Property Ownership

Courts are clear: property ownership does not override safety. If the court is satisfied that remaining in the home poses a risk, the defendant can be excluded even if they own the property outright.

A party excluded from the home may need to arrange alternative accommodation urgently. They retain their property rights and can raise the property division in separate proceedings. Exclusion from the home does not mean they forfeit their interest in the property.

Exclusion orders in AVO matters are enforceable by police. If the excluded person returns, police can remove them and charge for breach of the AVO.

Exhibit
Evidence
A document or item formally tendered to the court and accepted as evidence during a hearing. Exhibits are marked sequentially and form part of the official court record.
When it applies: Documents become exhibits when formally tendered and accepted during a hearing. The opposing party may object on admissibility grounds. Unlike annexures to affidavits, exhibits are tendered orally at the hearing itself and numbered as they are accepted.
Exhibits
Evidence
Documents or physical objects formally tendered as evidence in court proceedings and given an exhibit number or letter. Exhibits become part of the court record and can be referred to by the court in making its decision.
When it applies: In affidavit proceedings, exhibits are documents attached to an affidavit — typically labelled Exhibit A, Exhibit B, etc — and referenced in the body of the affidavit. At oral hearings, documents are formally tendered by one party and the other party may object. Once admitted, an exhibit is part of the evidence. Each exhibit should be clearly paginated, titled, and cross-referenced in the relevant affidavit paragraph. Related: affidavit, evidence bundle, annexure.
Expert Report
Evidence
A report prepared by a specialist — such as a psychologist, psychiatrist, accountant, or property valuer — to assist the court with matters requiring professional expertise. An expert's primary duty is to the court, not to the party who engaged them.
When it applies: Ordered or agreed upon when the court needs expert opinion to resolve a disputed issue — for example, a parent's mental health, the value of a business, or a child's therapeutic needs. Expert reports require court approval before being commissioned in most cases. The opposing party may seek leave to file their own expert report in response.
Expert Witness
Evidence
A witness qualified by reason of their specialised knowledge, training, or experience to give opinion evidence in court proceedings. Expert witnesses can give opinions on matters outside the knowledge of the average person — such as medical, psychological, financial, or engineering matters.
When it applies: In family law proceedings, common expert witnesses include: child and adolescent psychologists (providing family reports or psychological assessments), forensic accountants (valuing businesses or tracing assets), property valuers, occupational therapists, and medical specialists. Expert evidence must comply with strict court requirements — the expert's report must set out their qualifications, the material they relied on, their reasoning, and the opinion itself. Parties may engage their own expert or the court may appoint a single expert. Related: single expert, family report.

Expert Evidence Rules

Under the Evidence Act 1995 (Cth) and Family Law Rules 2021, an expert's duty is to the court, not to the party who engaged them. Experts must be independent — they should not advocate for a party's position.

Each party may call their own expert, creating a 'battle of experts.' Courts then assess which expert opinion is more persuasive based on their reasoning, methodology, and independence.

Where the parties have separate experts whose opinions significantly differ, the court may direct the experts to confer and prepare a joint report identifying areas of agreement and disagreement. This often significantly narrows the issues.

f45
Court Filing Fee
Court Administration
The fee payable to the court upon lodging certain documents, including initiating applications and responses. Fees are set by Commonwealth regulations and updated periodically. Different fees apply to different types of applications.
When it applies: Payable at the time of filing. Fee waivers are available for parties who qualify on financial hardship grounds and for legal aid recipients. Non-payment may result in documents not being accepted by the registry. Fee amounts should be confirmed with the registry as they are subject to change.
Fact-Based Framing
Evidence
The practice of presenting events in an affidavit through specific, observable facts rather than through opinion, interpretation, or characterisation. It is the preferred approach in effective affidavit drafting.
When it applies: Fact-based framing makes an affidavit more credible and more difficult to attack in cross-examination. It involves saying 'On [date], he said [specific words]' rather than 'He was always aggressive.' Courts respond better to affidavits grounded in specific, dated, factual accounts.
Family Consultant
Court Administration
A psychologist or social worker employed by the FCFCOA whose role is to assist the court with child-focused assessments. Family consultants conduct interviews, prepare reports, facilitate dispute resolution sessions, and provide independent recommendations about parenting arrangements.
When it applies: Involved in most contested parenting matters, particularly at the case assessment and dispute resolution stages. A family consultant is not an advocate for either party — their duty is to the child and to the court. Their reports carry significant weight in proceedings.
Family Counselling
Dispute Resolution
A confidential therapeutic process to help individuals and families manage the emotional, relational, and practical impacts of separation. It is distinct from legal dispute resolution — its goal is psychological support and improved communication, not reaching legal agreements.
When it applies: Can be accessed at any stage of separation, independently of court proceedings. Courts and family consultants sometimes recommend family counselling as part of a broader plan to improve parenting outcomes. Communications made in family counselling are generally confidential and cannot be used in court.
Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)
Legislation
The primary Commonwealth legislation governing family law in Australia. It establishes the framework for divorce, parenting orders, property settlements, and financial agreements, and sets out the principles and considerations courts must apply in all family law proceedings.
When it applies: Applies to all family law proceedings in Australian courts, covering married and (in most states and territories) de facto couples. Most recently amended in 2023 to prioritise child safety and reform parenting presumptions. All practitioners and parties must comply with its provisions.
Additional Considerations
Legislation
Secondary legislative factors a court may consider when determining the best interests of a child. These supplement the primary considerations and allow the court to weigh a broader range of circumstances relevant to the child's welfare.
When it applies: Considered alongside primary considerations in parenting proceedings. Unlike primary considerations, these factors carry less weight but may be decisive where the primary considerations do not clearly favour one outcome.
Coercive Control
Legislation
A pattern of controlling behaviour recognised in legislation that may constitute family violence. It includes acts designed to isolate, humiliate, intimidate, monitor, or restrict a person's freedom, finances, or movement — even in the absence of physical violence.
When it applies: Relevant in all family law proceedings where family violence is alleged. Courts consider patterns of coercive control when assessing risk to children and adults. Evidence of coercive control can rebut the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility.
Family Law Pathways Network
Court Administration
A national network of community-based organisations that provide information, referral, and support services to families experiencing relationship breakdown. Pathways Networks operate in most regions of Australia and bring together legal, family support, and community services.
When it applies: Family Law Pathways Networks aim to help families access the right service at the right time — whether that is legal advice, mediation, financial counselling, domestic violence support, or mental health services. The National Family Law Pathways Network website provides a service finder for your local area. These networks are particularly valuable for self-represented litigants who may not know what services are available. Related: family dispute resolution, legal aid.
Family Violence Definition (Statutory)
Legislation
The formal definition of family violence as set out in legislation. Under section 4AB of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), family violence includes behaviour that is violent, threatening, or coercive, as well as a broader range of conduct including physical, emotional, psychological, financial, and coercive behaviour that causes a family member to fear for their safety.
When it applies: Applies whenever family violence is raised in proceedings. The statutory definition is intentionally broad — it is not limited to physical acts. Courts are required to consider the impact of family violence on children even where it is not directly directed at them.

Family Violence — the Statutory Definition

The statutory definition of family violence is intentionally broad. It includes not only physical harm, but also threatening, coercive, controlling, emotionally abusive and financially restrictive conduct.

Exposure of a child to family violence — even if not directly targeted — is legally relevant. The court must consider:

  • Patterns of behaviour over time
  • Impact on the child
  • Ongoing safety risk

Findings of family violence can affect parental responsibility, supervision requirements, and time arrangements.

⚠️ Important

The absence of criminal charges does not prevent the family court from making findings of family violence. The civil standard of proof — balance of probabilities — applies.

Family Violence Order
Protection
A civil protection order available in states and territories outside NSW — such as a Family Violence Intervention Order (FVIO) in Victoria, a Domestic Violence Order (DVO) in Queensland, or a Family Violence Safety Notice (FVSN) in Victoria. Equivalent to an ADVO in NSW.
When it applies: While the name differs by jurisdiction, the purpose is the same: to protect a person from family violence through court-imposed conditions on the perpetrator's conduct. All states and territories have mutual recognition of family violence orders — an order made in one state is automatically recognised and enforceable in all others. This is critical where parties move interstate after separation. Related: ADVO, AVO, family violence.
Federal Circuit Court
Court Administration
Formally merged with the Family Court of Australia in 2021 to create the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA). The former Federal Circuit Court handled the majority of family law matters. Its jurisdiction and functions continue within the FCFCOA Division 2.
When it applies: Before 1 September 2021, the Federal Circuit Court of Australia (FCCA) was a separate court that handled most family law applications at the base level. It merged with the Family Court of Australia to form the FCFCOA. Division 2 of the FCFCOA broadly corresponds to what was the Federal Circuit Court — handling most parenting and property applications. Division 1 (formerly the Family Court) handles the most complex matters. Related: judge, registrar, full court.
Financial Agreement
Orders
A written agreement between parties to a relationship (married or de facto) that deals with how their property and financial resources will be divided — either before, during, or after the relationship. Financial agreements are the broader category of which Binding Financial Agreements (BFAs) are the formal, court-enforceable type.
When it applies: Financial agreements range from informal understandings to legally binding instruments. For an agreement to be binding and to exclude the court's jurisdiction, it must comply with the requirements of the Family Law Act 1975 (ss 90B–90D for marriage; ss 90UB–90UD for de facto). Informal financial agreements have no binding legal effect in family law — they can be set aside by the court. Related: binding financial agreement, consent orders, property settlement.
Firearms Prohibition
Protection
A condition in an AVO or family violence order requiring the defendant to surrender any firearms and prohibited weapons, and prohibiting them from acquiring, possessing, or using firearms during the currency of the order.
When it applies: This condition is automatically included in any ADVO in NSW under the Firearms Act 1996 (NSW). When an ADVO is made, the defendant's firearms licence is automatically suspended, and any firearms held must be surrendered to police within 24 hours. This applies regardless of whether the defendant is a licensed firearm owner. Firearms surrendered under an AVO are held by police and can be returned when the AVO expires or is revoked. Related: mandatory conditions, ADVO.

Automatic firearms prohibition

When an AVO is made, the defendant is automatically prohibited from acquiring, possessing, carrying, or using any firearm or prohibited weapon for the duration of the order. The defendant must surrender all firearms and licences to police within 24 hours of being served with the order.

What this means in practice

Failure to surrender firearms is a separate criminal offence. The prohibition applies even if the AVO is made on a consent without admissions basis. Firearms licences are automatically suspended. Reinstatement of a licence after an AVO expires requires a separate application to the firearms registry.

Full Court
Appeals
The appellate division of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, constituted by three judges, that hears appeals from decisions of single judges of the FCFCOA and, in some cases, from the Federal Circuit Court.
When it applies: An appeal to the Full Court requires leave (permission) unless the decision is of a category that attracts an appeal as of right. The Full Court does not rehear evidence — it reviews the trial judge's decision for legal error or, in limited cases, error in the exercise of discretion. The Full Court's decisions are binding on all lower courts in the family law jurisdiction. Further appeal lies to the High Court of Australia by special leave. Related: appeal, leave to appeal.
Future Needs
Orders
One of the two main adjustments a court makes in property settlement — the other being contributions. Future needs reflect the fact that parties may emerge from a relationship with different earning capacities, caring responsibilities, health challenges, or financial resources.
When it applies: Courts consider: the age and health of each party; their income, earning capacity, and financial resources; the care of children; the impact of the relationship on career and earning capacity; and the standard of living during the relationship. A party who gave up a career to raise children and now faces re-entry challenges will receive a future needs adjustment. Superannuation, pension entitlements, and likely inheritances may also be considered. Related: property settlement, spousal maintenance, contributions.

How Future Needs Affect Your Settlement

Future needs adjustments typically benefit the primary carer of children, the lower-earning partner, and anyone whose earning capacity was materially impacted by their role in the relationship.

Evidence that supports a future needs adjustment includes: expert vocational evidence about re-employment prospects, superannuation projections, medical evidence about health limitations, and evidence of the costs of sole parenting.

The interaction between property settlement and spousal maintenance is important. If a party receives a larger property share on future needs grounds, a separate spousal maintenance order may be less likely.

Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL) Appointment Power
Legislation
The legislative authority allowing the court to appoint an Independent Children's Lawyer to represent a child's interests in proceedings. Under section 68L of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the court may make this appointment on its own initiative or on application, where it is in the interests of the child to do so.
When it applies: Most commonly ordered in high-conflict parenting matters, cases involving allegations of abuse or family violence, or where the child's wishes need to be independently conveyed to the court. The ICL acts in the child's best interests, not necessarily according to the child's expressed wishes.
Jurisdiction
Legislation
The legal authority of a particular court to hear and decide a matter. In Australian family law, jurisdiction is conferred by the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) and related legislation. Without jurisdiction, a court has no power to make orders.
When it applies: Jurisdiction must exist before any proceedings can commence. The FCFCOA has jurisdiction over divorce, parenting, and property matters for married couples and (by referral) most de facto couples. If jurisdiction is disputed, a preliminary hearing may be required.
Legislative Amendment
Legislation
A formal change made to an Act of Parliament that alters how the law operates. Amendments may add, remove, or modify provisions. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) has been amended many times, most significantly in 2006 and again in 2023, each time substantially changing how parenting matters are decided.
When it applies: When researching your rights or obligations, always confirm you are reading the current version of the legislation at legislation.gov.au — older versions or summaries may not reflect recent amendments.
Mandatory Reporting Obligations
Legislation
Legal requirements imposed on certain professionals — including teachers, doctors, nurses, and social workers — to report suspected child abuse or neglect to the relevant authority. Mandatory reporting laws are set by state and territory legislation, not the Family Law Act, but reports made under these laws can intersect significantly with family law proceedings.
When it applies: If a mandatory report is made about your child or your household, this may trigger a child protection investigation that runs parallel to your family law matter. Mandatory reports can also generate evidence that becomes relevant in family court proceedings.
Paramountcy Principle
Legislation
The foundational legal principle that the child's best interests are the most important — or paramount — consideration in all parenting decisions made by the court. Enshrined in section 60CA of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the paramountcy principle overrides other considerations, including the preferences of either parent.
When it applies: Applies in every parenting decision made by the court. When presenting your case, all arguments should be framed around what is best for the child — not what is most convenient or fair to either parent. Courts are not interested in parental disputes for their own sake.
Presumption of Equal Shared Parental Responsibility
Legislation
A starting legal assumption — formerly in the Family Law Act — that both parents should share equal responsibility for major long-term decisions about a child's life. This presumption was repealed by the 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act and no longer applies. Courts now consider parental responsibility as part of the broader best interests assessment without any presumption.
When it applies: The presumption no longer applies to proceedings commenced after 6 May 2024. If your matter was commenced before that date, transitional provisions may apply. If you encounter references to "equal shared parental responsibility" in older court documents or advice, confirm whether the new framework applies to your case.
Primary Considerations
Legislation
The most important factors a court must consider under legislation when determining a child's best interests. Under the amended Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), the primary considerations are: (1) the benefit to the child of having a meaningful relationship with both parents; and (2) the need to protect the child from harm, including family violence, abuse, and neglect. Where these considerations conflict, safety takes priority.
When it applies: Every parenting decision by the court is guided by these considerations. If there is a safety concern, it will generally outweigh the benefit of a relationship with the other parent. You should address both primary considerations directly in any affidavit or submission.
Procedural Fairness
Legislation
The legislative and common law requirement that parties be given a fair opportunity to present their case and respond to allegations before a decision is made. Also called natural justice. A decision made without procedural fairness can be set aside on appeal.
When it applies: Applies at every stage of proceedings. If you have not been given adequate notice of a hearing, have not seen evidence relied on against you, or have not had a reasonable opportunity to respond, raise this with the court immediately. Failure to raise it promptly can be taken as waiver.

Procedural Fairness in Practice

Requires that parties have the opportunity to present their case and respond to adverse material before a decision is made. Failure to provide it may justify appeal.

If you become aware of material the other party intends to rely on that you haven't seen, raise it with the court immediately.

📌 Raise it early

Failing to raise a procedural fairness objection promptly can be treated as a waiver. Say so at the time — not after the decision is made.

This includes being informed of allegations against you, having a fair opportunity to respond, and having decisions made by an impartial decision-maker. If you believe you have not been given a proper opportunity to respond, raise it with the court immediately — not after the hearing has concluded.

💡 Raise it promptly

Courts are more receptive to fairness concerns raised in real time.

Procedural Threshold
Court Process
A minimum legal requirement that must be satisfied before a court will proceed with an application or consider varying existing orders.
When it applies: Examples include the material change in circumstances threshold for varying final parenting orders, and the arguable grounds requirement for leave to appeal. Procedural thresholds act as gatekeepers preventing the court from being burdened with applications that do not meet minimum legal requirements.

Why Procedural Thresholds Exist

A procedural threshold must be met before a matter proceeds. Examples include jurisdictional requirements, the material change in circumstances test for varying final orders, and the requirement for leave to appeal. They prevent the court from being used for applications without proper foundation.

Failing to satisfy a threshold doesn't just end the application — it can result in a costs order. Understand what threshold applies to your application before filing.

💡 Address it head on in your application

Where a procedural threshold applies, your application should specifically address how it is satisfied — don't assume the court will read between the lines. If you are seeking to vary final orders, explain the material change. If appealing, identify the legal error.

Examples include jurisdictional thresholds, the requirement to attempt FDR before filing, and the material change of circumstances test before varying final orders. Failing to address the threshold in your application is a common reason for early dismissal.

💡 Address the threshold explicitly

In your application or affidavit, address every threshold that applies — don't assume the court will overlook it. State why the threshold is satisfied.

Rebuttable Presumption
Legislation
A legal assumption that applies as the starting position in a matter but can be displaced if sufficient evidence is provided to disprove it. In family law, rebuttable presumptions operate as defaults that shift the burden of proof — a party who wishes to displace the presumption must adduce evidence that outweighs it.
When it applies: Relevant wherever a legal presumption operates in your matter. Understanding whether a presumption applies — and what evidence is needed to rebut it — is critical to structuring your case effectively.
Risk of Harm Threshold
Legislation
The minimum level of risk required under legislation before protective intervention — such as supervised contact, a no-contact order, or removal from a parent's care — is legally justified. The threshold is not absolute harm but a real and substantial risk that cannot be adequately managed without court intervention.
When it applies: Considered whenever a party seeks protective parenting orders. Vague or unsubstantiated concerns are unlikely to meet the threshold. Courts look for evidence of actual incidents, patterns of behaviour, or expert opinion that establishes a real and present risk.
Standard of Proof
Evidence
The threshold of evidence required for a court to make a finding in favour of a party. Family law and AVO proceedings use the civil standard — the balance of probabilities. Criminal proceedings use the higher standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
When it applies: In family law and AVO proceedings, the balance of probabilities means the court must be satisfied that it is more likely than not that a particular fact is true — essentially, more than 50% probable. This is a lower threshold than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt. It means allegations of family violence, child abuse, or other serious conduct can be accepted by a civil court even if the conduct was never proven in criminal proceedings. Courts still scrutinise serious allegations more carefully the more serious their potential consequences: see the principle from Briginshaw v Briginshaw.

The Briginshaw Principle

The High Court in Briginshaw v Briginshaw (1938) held that courts should not make findings of serious misconduct lightly, even on the civil standard. The more serious the allegation (e.g. child sexual abuse), the more cogent the evidence must be before the court is satisfied.

This does not change the standard — it is always the balance of probabilities. But it means that the quality and weight of evidence required increases with the gravity of the allegation.

Practically: if you are making serious allegations, gather strong corroborating evidence — medical reports, police records, witness statements, photographs. Courts are appropriately cautious about making life-altering findings based solely on uncorroborated assertions.

Unacceptable Risk Test
Legislation
A legal test applied by courts to determine whether a child would face an unacceptable risk of harm if particular parenting arrangements were ordered. The test requires the court to weigh the probability and magnitude of the alleged harm against the benefit of the child maintaining a relationship with both parents.
When it applies: Applied in contested parenting matters where one party alleges the other poses a risk to the child. The test originated in M v M (1988) and is now applied routinely in cases involving allegations of abuse, family violence, or substance misuse. The alleged risk need not be certain — it must be real and not remote.
False Allegations
Evidence
Untrue or fabricated claims made in proceedings, ranging from honest mistakes to deliberate fabrication for tactical purposes.
When it applies: The court distinguishes between allegations made in genuine but mistaken belief and deliberate fabrication. Fabricated or knowingly exaggerated allegations affect credibility, may attract costs orders, and in extreme cases may amount to contempt. The existence of allegations that are not proven does not automatically mean they were false.

False Allegations — What Courts Look For

False allegations may affect credibility and costs. Courts distinguish between allegations made in genuine but mistaken belief and deliberate fabrication — the consequences are very different. An unproven allegation is not automatically false.

Courts are experienced at identifying fabricated or exaggerated claims. Inconsistencies, implausibility, and contradictory evidence are the markers. Bringing allegations the court finds were fabricated may result in adverse costs and will significantly damage your standing throughout the proceedings.

📌 If you are facing false allegations

Respond calmly and specifically. Address each allegation with evidence — documents, records, witnesses. Emotional denials without supporting evidence are less persuasive than a methodical, documented response that exposes specific inconsistencies in the other party's account.

False Allegations — the Court's Approach

False allegations in family law proceedings are taken seriously. The court distinguishes between genuine mistakes or misperceptions (where a party genuinely believed what they alleged) and deliberate fabrication (where a party knowingly made false claims to gain advantage).

Making serious allegations the court finds to be deliberately false — particularly regarding abuse or family violence — can result in adverse credibility findings, costs orders, and reduced prospects in future applications.

⚠️ Mistaken belief is different from fabrication

Courts understand that trauma can distort perception, and that people sometimes genuinely misinterpret events. If you have made allegations you are now uncertain about, taking a measured and honest position is better than doubling down. Consistency with earlier accounts matters.

Family Dispute Resolution
Court Process
A mediation process aimed at resolving parenting and other family law disputes without or before litigation, conducted by accredited practitioners.
When it applies: Generally required before filing parenting applications. A section 60I certificate is issued following participation. FDR encourages cooperative resolution and is less adversarial, less costly, and faster than court proceedings. Exemptions apply for family violence, urgency, and where the other party refuses to participate.

Family Dispute Resolution in Practice

Family Dispute Resolution is mediation aimed at resolving parenting disputes. Participation is generally required before filing parenting applications — you need a section 60I certificate to commence most proceedings.

FDR is facilitated by a neutral accredited practitioner. It is confidential and without prejudice — what is said cannot be used in court. The goal is a negotiated agreement; the practitioner does not impose a decision.

💡 Come prepared with proposals

FDR is most productive when you arrive with clear, realistic proposals focused on the child's needs. Know your bottom line, be flexible on details, and keep the conversation child-focused. Agreements reached in FDR and then formalised as consent orders are usually more durable than court-imposed outcomes.

FDR — Before You File

Family Dispute Resolution is mediation aimed at resolving parenting disputes without court proceedings. Participation is generally required before filing most parenting applications — you must obtain a Section 60I certificate first.

FDR is run by accredited practitioners at organisations such as Relationships Australia, Interrelate, and Legal Aid. It is confidential. What is said in FDR cannot be used as evidence in court, except in limited circumstances.

✓ FDR works well when
  • Both parties can engage safely
  • Issues are about arrangements, not safety
  • There is some goodwill remaining
  • Each party can speak without fear
✗ FDR may not be suitable when
  • There is a history of family violence
  • One party is in fear of the other
  • Child abuse allegations are present
  • One party refuses to participate
Family Report
Evidence
A comprehensive report prepared by a family consultant or independent expert assessing the family's circumstances, each parent's capacity to care for the child, the child's needs and views, and the risks and benefits of proposed parenting arrangements. It includes recommendations for the court.
When it applies: Ordered in contested parenting matters, typically before the final hearing. The preparation process involves interviews with both parents, the child (if old enough), and relevant third parties. Family reports carry significant weight and courts rarely depart from their recommendations without good reason. Both parties receive a copy before the hearing.

Family Reports — What to Expect

A family report is prepared by a court-appointed expert to assist in determining parenting arrangements. The report writer assesses parenting capacity, child attachment and risk factors through interviews with both parents, the child (if old enough), and relevant third parties.

While influential, the court is not bound by its recommendations. Courts rarely depart from a family report without good reason — but it does happen, particularly where new evidence emerges at trial or credibility findings differ from the report writer's assessment.

⚠️ How to approach the interview

Be honest, child-focused and composed. Report writers are trained to detect coaching of children and will note it. Avoid speaking negatively about the other parent during interviews — focus on your child's needs. What you say and how you behave is all observed and may appear in the report.

Family Safety Plan
Protection
A written plan developed with the assistance of a family violence service that details the steps a person and their children can take to protect themselves from harm. It typically includes warning signs, emergency contacts, escape routes, and safe places.
When it applies: Relevant in parenting proceedings involving family violence risk. Courts and family consultants may consider whether a family safety plan is in place when assessing the adequacy of protective measures. Having a plan demonstrates a proactive approach to safety.
Family Violence
Protection
Under the Family Law Act, family violence is broadly defined to include physical, sexual, emotional, and psychological abuse; economic abuse; harassment; stalking; and exposing a child to any of these behaviours. The definition extends well beyond physical violence.
When it applies: Must be considered by the court in all parenting proceedings. Where allegations are raised, the court must give them serious weight and may take protective steps including interim orders, referral to child protection, or ordering a family report addressing risk. A criminal conviction is not required for the court to act.
Family Violence Allegations
Protection
Claims raised by one party in proceedings that the other has engaged in conduct constituting family violence. Allegations may relate to conduct toward the other party, the children, or both, and must be particularised with specific dates and descriptions wherever possible.
When it applies: When made, the court must respond appropriately — including by considering whether interim protective orders are needed. The court applies a civil standard of proof (balance of probabilities) and must also consider the unacceptable risk test when assessing whether safety measures are required.
Family Violence Narrative
Protection
The structured account of alleged abusive behaviour provided in an affidavit or application, describing the nature, frequency, and impact of family violence. A well-structured narrative includes specific dates, descriptions, and consequences.
When it applies: Forms the evidential foundation of protection order applications and parenting proceedings involving safety concerns. Vague or generalised narratives are given less weight than specific, particularised accounts. Courts benefit from a clear, chronological description of individual incidents, including what was said or done and its effect.
Filing
Court Administration
The formal submission of documents to the court registry, either in person, by post, or electronically via the Commonwealth Courts Portal. Filing creates an official court record and triggers the court's procedural obligations, including allocation of a court date where required.
When it applies: Required at every procedural step of proceedings — initiating application, response, affidavits, notice of risk, consent orders, and so on. Documents must be in the correct form, accompanied by any required fee, and filed by the prescribed deadline. Late filing requires leave of the court and can jeopardise a party's case.

Filing Documents with the Court

Formally lodges documents with the registry. Documents are not legally effective until filed — serving a document before filing does not make it valid.

Most documents can be filed through the Commonwealth Courts Portal. Filing fees apply to most applications. The court stamps documents with the date of filing.

💡 Keep sealed copies

Always keep a court-sealed copy of everything you file. You'll need it to serve on the other party. Unfiled drafts have no legal status.

Filing formally lodges documents with the court registry. Documents are not legally effective until filed. Filing is now primarily done online through the FCFCOA portal; fee exemptions and waivers are available in hardship cases.

💡 Check deadlines carefully

If you have a court-ordered filing deadline, file early — not on the day. Technical issues with the portal, registry delays, or rejected documents can cause you to miss a deadline even if you submit on time. Missing a court-ordered deadline without explanation is taken seriously.

Court Attendance
Court Administration
The obligation of a party to physically appear at a listed court event. Court attendance is generally mandatory for all parties unless the court has excused attendance in advance or permitted a representative to appear on the party's behalf.
When it applies: Failing to attend a listed hearing without excuse can have serious consequences: the court may proceed in your absence, make orders against you, strike out your application, or issue a warrant. If you cannot attend, contact the court registry as early as possible and apply for the matter to be adjourned or for leave to appear by telephone or video link. Related: court listing, adjournment.

What to Do if You Cannot Attend

If you are unable to attend a scheduled court event, do not simply fail to appear. Contact the other party and the registry as soon as possible. Courts generally permit phone or video appearances for procedural matters if proper notice is given.

If it is an emergency (illness, accident), contact the registry immediately on the morning of the hearing and be prepared to provide supporting documentation (e.g. a medical certificate) at the next event.

⚠️ Orders can be made in your absence

If you do not appear and the court is not satisfied with the explanation, the other party's application may be granted without you having the opportunity to be heard. This is very difficult to undo later.

Court Etiquette
Court Administration
The expected standards of conduct and behaviour for parties, witnesses, and representatives appearing before a court. Proper court etiquette includes dressing appropriately, addressing the judge or magistrate correctly, standing when the judge enters or leaves, not speaking over others, and silencing mobile phones.
When it applies: Court etiquette is not merely formality — failure to observe it can prejudice your case and, in serious cases, lead to a contempt finding. For self-represented litigants in family law, the key obligations are: address the judge as 'Your Honour'; speak only when invited to do so; stand when addressing the court; do not argue with the judge; and treat the other party and their legal representative respectfully. Related: your honour.

How to Conduct Yourself in Court

Arrive early — at least 15–20 minutes before the listed time. Go through security without delay. Find the correct courtroom from the daily list posted at the registry or entrance. Sit in the public gallery until your matter is called.

When your matter is called, approach the bar table (the long table in front of the bench). Introduce yourself by stating your name and that you are self-represented. Speak clearly, calmly, and directly to the judge — not to the other party.

💡 Emotion vs argument

Family law proceedings are emotionally charged. Judges understand this but remain most influenced by calm, focused, evidence-based submissions. Raising your voice, making personal attacks on the other party, or becoming visibly distressed rarely assists your case and can harm it.

Court Leave
Court Administration
Permission granted by a court to take a step that would not otherwise be permitted under the rules or existing orders. Applying for court leave (or 'seeking leave') is required in situations such as: filing a document out of time; bringing a further application where proceedings have been finalised; or adducing fresh evidence on appeal. Also referred to as leave of the court.
When it applies: If you need to do something that the rules do not ordinarily allow — including filing late, amending an application, or asking to call additional witnesses — you must formally seek the court's leave. Simply proceeding without leave risks the court rejecting what you have done. Courts apply different tests depending on the type of leave sought. Related: leave of the court, appeal.
Court Registry
Court Administration
The administrative office of a court where documents are filed, sealed, and processed. The court registry is the first point of contact for parties seeking to start or progress proceedings. Registry staff can assist with procedural and administrative questions but cannot provide legal advice.
When it applies: The court registry handles: acceptance and stamping of filed documents; issuing sealed copies; scheduling matters on the court's list; processing subpoenas; and providing information about court procedures. For the FCFCOA, documents can be filed electronically via the Commonwealth Courts Portal or, where permitted, in person at the relevant registry. Registry hours and locations vary — check the FCFCOA website for your nearest registry. Related: Commonwealth Courts Portal, filing deadline.

Using the Court Registry

The registry is the administrative gateway to the court. You interact with it at every stage — when filing your initiating documents, when checking your court date, when requesting sealed copies of orders, and when seeking procedural information.

Registry staff are not judges and cannot tell you whether your application will succeed, how to run your case, or what orders to seek. If you ask for legal advice, they will politely decline and direct you to a lawyer or legal aid service.

💡 Always keep sealed copies

When you file a document, request a sealed (stamped) copy for your records. Sealed copies are essential proof that a document was filed and are required when serving the other party. Always keep copies of everything you file.

Filing Deadline
Court Administration
The date by which a party must lodge specified documents with the court. Filing deadlines are set by court orders, practice directions, or rules and are strictly enforced to ensure proceedings progress efficiently.
When it applies: Applies throughout proceedings at each procedural step. Missing a deadline without leave can result in documents being excluded, the matter being adjourned, or an adverse costs order. A party must apply promptly for an extension if they cannot comply.
Final Hearing
Court Process
The hearing at which a judge receives all evidence and legal arguments and makes final binding orders to resolve the matter. A final hearing may last from one day to several weeks depending on complexity. It is equivalent to a trial in other jurisdictions.
When it applies: Occurs when all attempts at resolution have failed. Both parties present their affidavit evidence, cross-examine witnesses, and make submissions. The judge may give judgment immediately or reserve it to a later date. Thorough preparation — including all affidavits, subpoenaed documents, and written submissions — is essential.

What to Expect at a Final Hearing

A final hearing resolves all contested issues after full evidence and cross-examination. Both parties present their evidence in chief (via affidavit), are cross-examined, and make final submissions. The judge then makes findings of fact and applies the best interests framework.

Final hearings can run from one day to several weeks depending on complexity. After the hearing, judgment may be reserved — meaning the decision is delivered at a later date. It is the most significant event in family law proceedings; the judge hears all evidence, makes credibility findings, and applies the full best interests framework. Most matters settle before final hearing — but thorough preparation often makes settlement possible.

📌 Preparation is everything

Know your evidence thoroughly. Anticipate the questions you will be asked in cross-examination and prepare honest, consistent answers. Know what orders you are seeking and why they serve your child's best interests. A judge who has read hundreds of affidavits will notice genuine care and preparation.

✓ Preparing well means
  • Consistent affidavit evidence across the case
  • Independent corroborating evidence gathered
  • Witnesses identified and briefed
  • Realistic understanding of the likely outcome
⚠️ Common final hearing mistakes
  • Raising new issues not in your affidavit
  • Contradicting your own earlier evidence
  • Emotional rather than factual testimony
  • Losing composure under cross-examination
Final Order
Protection
A protection order made after a hearing or agreement.
When it applies: A final AVO is made either after a contested hearing or when the defendant consents to the order. It replaces any interim or provisional order and remains in force for the period specified — usually two years, but can be longer.
Final Orders
Orders
Court orders made at the conclusion of proceedings intended to resolve the matter on a long-term or permanent basis. Final orders replace all interim orders previously in force and set out the parties' rights and obligations going forward.
When it applies: Made either by consent or after a contested trial. Parenting final orders remain in force until the child turns 18 unless varied. Property final orders are generally not varied once made. They can only be changed by further court order, consent of all parties, or on appeal.

The Effect of Final Orders

Final orders are made after full hearing of evidence and submissions. They are intended to provide long-term stability. The court makes detailed credibility findings and applies the full best interests framework.

Once final orders are made, they cannot be easily revisited. A party seeking to change them must satisfy the Rice & Asplund threshold — demonstrating a material change in circumstances. The principle promotes finality and stability for children.

📌 Why finality matters

Prepare thoroughly before final hearing — the threshold to reopen is high. Once orders are made, the expectation is that parties will comply and move forward.

Gatekeeping
Parenting
Behaviour by one parent that restricts, controls, or undermines the child's access to and relationship with the other parent.
When it applies: Can range from justified protective gatekeeping (limiting access where genuine risk exists) to unjustified restrictive gatekeeping that harms the child's relationship with the other parent without cause. Excessive unjustified gatekeeping is a factor the court considers when assessing parenting capacity and may influence parental responsibility and time arrangements.

Gatekeeping — Protective vs. Restrictive

Gatekeeping involves restricting or controlling the child's access to the other parent. There is an important distinction: justified protective gatekeeping (based on genuine safety concerns) is appropriate; unjustified restrictive gatekeeping harms the child and damages your credibility with the court.

Courts view excessive gatekeeping as evidence of an inability to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent — a relevant consideration in parenting arrangements.

✓ Justified gatekeeping
  • Limiting contact due to safety risk
  • Refusing time during active DV incident
  • Child ill and medical attention needed
✗ Unjustified gatekeeping
  • Refusing contact because of relationship conflict
  • Using the child to punish the other parent
  • Blocking communication without cause
Final AVO
Protection
An Apprehended Violence Order made after a contested hearing or by consent. Provides ongoing protection and typically runs for one to two years. May include conditions restricting contact, approach, communication, or residence.
When it applies: Made at the final court date for the AVO application. Findings of family violence associated with a final AVO can affect related parenting proceedings.

Final AVOs and Family Law

Made after a contested hearing or by consent. May include conditions restricting contact, approach, communication, or residence. Typically runs 1–2 years.

Findings of family violence associated with a final AVO can significantly affect parenting arrangements in the family court.

📌 Consent without admissions

Many respondents consent without admitting the allegations are true. Whether to contest or consent is a strategic decision — get advice before the hearing date.

Final Parenting Determination
Parenting
The conclusive court decision on all outstanding parenting arrangements, made at the conclusion of a final hearing or trial. It resolves the dispute on a long-term basis and replaces all prior interim orders.
When it applies: Made after all evidence and submissions have been received and the judge has delivered judgment. Final parenting determinations are intended to provide certainty and stability. They can only be varied by further court order if there is a significant change in circumstances. Parties should plan for compliance from the moment final orders are made.
First Mention
Court Process
The initial court appearance in a matter after an application has been filed. At the first mention, the court confirms the parties are present, determines whether the matter is defended or undefended, and gives directions for the next steps.
When it applies: The first mention is usually brief — typically 5 to 15 minutes. The court will note appearances, make any urgent orders if needed, and direct the parties on what to do before the next date (for example, filing affidavits or a response). In AVO proceedings, the defendant may also enter an appearance and indicate whether they consent to the AVO or intend to contest it. Related: directions hearing, court listing.

Preparing for Your First Mention

Arrive early and check the daily court list. Bring all filed documents, your court file number, and identification. Know in advance whether you intend to consent, seek an adjournment, or contest.

The first mention is not usually the time to argue your case. It is a procedural step. If you are self-represented, you may simply say: 'Your Honour, I am [name] and I am self-represented. I would like [time to get legal advice / to contest the application / to consent without admissions].'

If you cannot attend the first mention, contact the registry as soon as possible. Failing to appear can result in orders being made against you in your absence.

Focused Determination
Court Process
A judicial decision addressing a specific, defined question within broader proceedings — rather than all outstanding issues — where resolving that question may facilitate settlement or reduce the scope of the dispute.
When it applies: Used where one question is identified as the central issue that, if resolved, will allow the parties to reach agreement on everything else. Courts can list matters for a focused determination hearing as a cost-effective alternative to a full trial on all issues.
g3
Gatekeeping Allegation
High Conflict
A claim that one parent is limiting or obstructing the child's relationship with the other parent, whether through scheduling, negative commentary, emotional pressure on the child, or outright refusal of contact.
When it applies: Taken seriously by courts as a potential form of family violence or parenting failure. If established, gatekeeping can result in reduced time for the gatekeeping parent, transfer of primary care, or enforcement orders. Courts distinguish between protective gatekeeping (genuine safety concerns) and alienating gatekeeping (motivated by conflict).
Geographic Restriction Order
Orders
A court order prohibiting a parent from relocating a child beyond a defined area — whether a suburb, city, state, or country — without the other parent's consent or further court order.
When it applies: Made when the court determines that relocation would not be in the child's best interests, or as an interim measure while relocation proceedings are on foot. Also commonly issued as part of a broader package of protective orders in family violence matters where the abuser's location poses a risk.
Guardian ad Litem
Parenting
A person appointed by the court to represent and protect the interests of a child in legal proceedings, acting in the child's best interests rather than on the child's instructions. In Australian practice, this role is largely fulfilled by the Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL).
When it applies: Appointed in exceptional circumstances where no other adequate representation exists for the child, or in some international child abduction matters. The guardian ad litem has standing to take procedural steps in the proceedings and must act solely in the child's best interests.
h10
Hague Convention
Parenting
Short for the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (1980). An international treaty, implemented in Australia by the Family Law (Child Abduction Convention) Regulations 1986, that provides a mechanism for the prompt return of children wrongfully removed or retained across international borders.
When it applies: Under the Convention, a parent whose child has been taken to another Convention country without consent can apply for the child's return. The central question is whether the removal was wrongful — that is, in breach of custody rights under the law of the child's habitual residence. Courts hearing Hague applications do not consider the merits of the underlying parenting dispute — they focus on whether the child should be returned for custody proceedings to continue in the country of habitual residence. Australia is a signatory, as are most Western countries. Related: international relocation, mirror order, overseas order.

If Your Child Has Been Taken Overseas

Act immediately. Contact the Australian Central Authority (Department of Attorney-General) which administers Hague Convention applications in Australia. The sooner you apply, the better — courts are more likely to order return where proceedings are commenced quickly.

Not all countries are signatories. If the child has been taken to a non-Convention country, different legal processes apply and recovery is significantly more difficult.

Hague proceedings are heard urgently. They focus on whether the removal was wrongful and whether any of the narrow exceptions apply (such as the child having settled in the new country, or grave risk of harm on return). They do not determine who should have long-term care.

Harassment
Protection
