Courts allow parties to explain apparent inconsistencies or ambiguities in their evidence. Parties should be prepared to provide clear, calm explanations during cross-examination rather than becoming defensive or evasive.
Order for Attendance
Court Process
A court order requiring a specified person to appear before the court at a particular time and place. It compels attendance and may be enforced by warrant if the person fails to comply.
When it applies: Issued when a party cannot be reached through ordinary means, or when the court requires a particular person — such as a child protection officer or health professional — to appear and give evidence. Failure to comply without a reasonable excuse may constitute contempt of court.
Orders Made by Consent
Orders
Court orders made with the agreement of all parties, without the need for a contested hearing. Consent orders are binding and enforceable in the same way as orders made after a hearing.
When it applies: Consent orders in family law are made by filing an Application for Consent Orders and a minute of orders with the FCFCOA. A registrar reviews the proposed orders for compliance with the law and the interests of any children. If satisfied, orders are made in chambers without the parties attending. Consent orders for property settlement stamp duty exemptions in most states. Related: consent orders, property settlement, parenting order.

Why Consent Orders Matter

Consent orders provide certainty and finality. Unlike informal agreements, they are enforceable by the court — breach can result in contravention proceedings.

For property matters, consent orders are generally preferred over Binding Financial Agreements for most couples because they receive judicial scrutiny and provide a greater level of legal certainty.

Always seek independent legal advice before signing any consent orders, even if you and your partner have agreed on everything. Small errors in drafting can create big problems down the track.

Orders Sought
Court Process
The specific outcomes a party is asking the court to make. Every application filed in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia must state the orders sought — the precise legal relief or directions the applicant wants the court to grant.
When it applies: Orders sought must be stated when filing an Initiating Application, Response, or any other court document seeking relief. They frame the entire proceedings — the court can only grant what has been asked for. Courts expect orders sought to be clear, specific, and capable of being complied with.

What Are Orders Sought?

When you file a document in the family court, you must tell the court exactly what you want it to do. These are your orders sought — a numbered list of specific directions you are asking a judge or registrar to make. Think of them as the "asks" of your case. The court can only make orders that have been properly sought; it cannot go beyond what is in front of it.

Orders sought must be drafted precisely. Vague requests like "I want to see my children more" are not orders — they are wishes. A properly drafted order sought might read: "That the child X live with the applicant and spend time with the respondent each alternate weekend from Friday at 5:00pm to Sunday at 5:00pm." The clearer and more specific the order, the easier it is for the court to grant it and for both parties to comply.

Tip: Orders sought can be interim (temporary, until the final hearing) or final (permanent). Many applicants ask for both in the same document — for example, asking for interim living arrangements while the case proceeds, and final orders at trial.

10 Examples of Orders Sought

The following examples show how orders sought are drafted in practice across different types of family law applications:

Example 1 — Parenting: Live With

"That the child Emily Jane Smith, born 12 March 2019, live with the applicant mother/father."

Establishes the child's primary residence. Often paired with a time order specifying when the child spends time with the other parent.

Example 2 — Parenting: Time & Communication

"That the child spend time with the respondent father/mother each alternate weekend from Saturday at 10:00am to Sunday at 5:00pm, and each Wednesday from 4:00pm to 7:30pm during school terms."

Specifying exact days and times removes ambiguity and makes the order enforceable. Courts prefer precision over general phrases like "reasonable time".

Example 3 — Property: Sale of the Family Home

"That the property at 14 Maple Street, Parramatta NSW 2150 be listed for sale within 28 days of these orders, with the net proceeds divided 60% to the applicant and 40% to the respondent after payment of the mortgage and reasonable costs of sale."

Property orders must identify the asset precisely and specify how the proceeds or transfer are to occur, including timeframes.

Example 4 — Interim: Urgent Injunction

"On an interim basis, that the respondent be restrained from removing the children from the State of New South Wales pending further order of the court."

Interim orders sought must clearly state they are interim and explain why urgency is required. These are often sought at the same time as final orders when there is an immediate risk.

Example 5 — Costs Order

"That the respondent pay the applicant's costs of and incidental to this application, to be agreed or assessed."

A costs order asks the court to require one party to pay the other's legal costs. While costs orders are uncommon in family law (each party usually pays their own), they can be sought where a party has acted unreasonably or caused unnecessary delay.

🧒 Child-Focused Orders — Examples 6–10 below focus specifically on orders centred on children's safety, welfare, and best interests.

Example 6 — Child-Focused: Supervised Time

"That the child Liam Robert Brown, born 5 June 2017, spend supervised time with the respondent father/mother for a period of two hours each Saturday between 10:00am and 12:00pm at the XYZ Children's Contact Service, until further order of the court."

Supervised time orders are sought where there are safety concerns — such as a history of family violence, substance abuse, or risk of harm — but the court recognises the child's right to a meaningful relationship with both parents. The order should name the contact service or supervisor and specify duration and frequency.

Example 7 — Child-Focused: Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL)

"That an Independent Children's Lawyer be appointed pursuant to section 68L of the Family Law Act 1975 to represent the best interests of the children in these proceedings."

An ICL is a lawyer appointed by the court to represent the child's best interests (not the child's wishes). This order is commonly sought in cases involving allegations of abuse, high conflict, or where a child's views need independent assessment. Either party can request the appointment, or the court can make it on its own initiative.

Example 8 — Child-Focused: Family Report / Child Assessment

"That a family consultant prepare a family report pursuant to section 62G of the Family Law Act 1975, addressing the parenting arrangements that would be in the best interests of the children, including each parent's capacity to provide for the children's emotional and developmental needs."

A family report order directs a qualified professional (usually a psychologist or social worker) to interview both parents, the children, and sometimes other relevant people, then provide the court with an expert assessment. These reports carry significant weight in parenting decisions.

Example 9 — Child-Focused: Parental Responsibility for Major Long-Term Decisions

"That the applicant mother/father have sole parental responsibility for major long-term decisions in relation to the child's education, health, and religious and cultural upbringing."

While the court presumes equal shared parental responsibility, this presumption is rebutted where there is family violence or abuse. Sole parental responsibility orders allow one parent to make major long-term decisions without needing the other's agreement — reducing conflict and protecting the child from deadlocked decision-making.

Example 10 — Child-Focused: Restraint on Relocation

"That neither party relocate the child Ava Grace Nguyen, born 22 September 2020, more than 50 kilometres from the child's current residence without the written consent of the other party or further order of the court."

Relocation restraint orders protect the child's stability and ensure that both parents remain geographically accessible. They are commonly sought where one parent is likely to move interstate or to a remote area, which would disrupt the child's existing time arrangements, schooling, and relationship with the other parent.

Important: You can change or add to your orders sought by filing an amended application. If circumstances change — for example, a child's needs evolve or a property issue arises — you should update your orders sought before the next hearing rather than raising new issues for the first time at trial.

Over-Litigation
High Conflict
The filing of excessive, disproportionate, or unnecessary applications, affidavits, and procedural steps in a way that drives up cost and complexity without advancing the genuine issues in dispute.
When it applies: Courts have express powers to address over-litigation under the overarching purpose provisions of the FCFCOA Act. Consequences include costs orders, summary dismissal of applications, and judicial criticism in judgments. Courts increasingly expect parties to focus proceedings on the core issues rather than litigating every peripheral matter.
Overarching Purpose
Court Process
A statutory obligation under the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Act 2021 requiring all parties and their lawyers to conduct proceedings in a way that is efficient, proportionate, and timely, facilitating the just resolution of disputes at minimum cost.
When it applies: Applies throughout all proceedings in the FCFCOA from commencement to conclusion. Lawyers have a specific duty to assist their clients in complying with the overarching purpose. Courts may impose costs orders or other sanctions on parties who unnecessarily increase complexity, cost, or delay.
Overseas Order
Parenting
A parenting or family law order made by a court in a foreign country. An overseas order may be registered and enforced in Australia under the Family Law Act 1975 if it meets certain requirements.
When it applies: Australia has reciprocal arrangements with many countries for the registration and enforcement of overseas family law orders. Once registered, an overseas order has the same force as an Australian order. Registration is not automatic — a party must apply to the FCFCOA for registration. The court will not register an order that is contrary to Australian public policy or inconsistent with existing Australian orders for the same child. Related: mirror order, Hague Convention.
p34
Parallel Parenting
Parenting
A structured post-separation parenting model designed for high-conflict situations, in which each parent operates independently in their own domain with minimal direct communication. It reduces conflict by limiting the need for cooperative co-parenting.
When it applies: Recommended by courts and practitioners in high-conflict cases where direct communication consistently results in harm to the children or parties. Under a parallel parenting arrangement, detailed orders specify each parent's responsibilities and decision-making authority to minimise the need for ongoing interaction.

Parallel Parenting in High-Conflict Cases

Parallel parenting allows parents to operate independently during their own time with minimal direct cooperation — limiting interaction and protecting the child from exposure to hostility.

Communication is usually limited to essential matters via written channels (apps or email); changeovers may be neutral or via school or third parties.

💡 Tools and mindset

Co-parenting apps create a dated record; clear orders reduce disputes. The aim is a business-like focus on the child — reducing conflict, not avoiding parental responsibility.

Parental Responsibility
Parenting
The full set of duties, powers, responsibilities, and authority which, by law, parents have in relation to their children. It relates principally to major long-term decisions rather than day-to-day care decisions, which fall to the parent who has the child at the time.
When it applies: Relevant in all parenting proceedings. Courts can allocate responsibility solely to one parent or jointly to both. Where shared parental responsibility is ordered, both parents must consult and endeavour to agree on major long-term decisions. Failing to do so can constitute a breach of the order.
Parenting App Order
Orders
A court order requiring parties to use a structured, monitored parenting communication platform — such as Our Family Wizard or Cozi — for all co-parenting communication. The platform records all exchanges and can provide evidence of conduct.
When it applies: Ordered in high-conflict cases where unstructured communication has repeatedly led to conflict or evidence disputes. Using a parenting app creates an auditable record of communication, reduces the risk of disputed messages, and can facilitate compliance monitoring. Parties should be aware that all communications on the platform may be accessed by the court.
Parenting Coordination Agreement
Dispute Resolution
An agreement by which a trained parenting coordinator is engaged to assist high-conflict parents implement their parenting orders, manage day-to-day disputes, and improve communication. Within their agreed scope, a parenting coordinator may make recommendations or minor decisions.
When it applies: Used in high-conflict parenting situations where ongoing disputes about implementation of orders would otherwise result in repeated court applications. The parents and coordinator sign a participation agreement. Parenting coordination significantly reduces the need for court intervention in routine disputes.
Parenting Order
Parenting
A legally binding court order setting out the arrangements for a child — including who the child lives with, how much time they spend with each parent, how parental responsibility is exercised, and any other conditions relevant to the child's welfare.
When it applies: Made either by consent or after a contested hearing whenever a court is required to formalise a child's arrangements. Parenting orders are enforceable — a breach can give rise to a contravention application and enforcement orders. They remain in force until the child turns 18 or are otherwise varied by the court.
Parenting Coordinator
Parenting
A professional appointed to assist parents in implementing parenting orders, resolving day-to-day disputes, and reducing ongoing conflict without returning to court.
When it applies: Typically a psychologist or social worker with family law experience. The parenting coordinator does not make binding decisions (unless given specific powers by the court) but facilitates resolution of practical disputes — school issues, holiday scheduling, medical decisions — that arise under existing orders.

What a Parenting Coordinator Does

A parenting coordinator assists parents in implementing orders and reducing conflict. Their role is practical rather than judicial — they help parents navigate day-to-day disputes that orders may not specifically address, without requiring court intervention.

Common in high-conflict cases where parents struggle to communicate. Using a parenting coordinator can significantly reduce legal costs by resolving disputes informally before they escalate into applications.

💡 A practical alternative to returning to court

If you find yourself in repeated minor disputes — holiday arrangements, medical decisions, school issues — a parenting coordinator can provide a structured process to resolve them at a fraction of the cost of court applications.

A parenting coordinator assists high-conflict parents in implementing existing orders and navigating day-to-day disputes — school decisions, medical appointments, holiday scheduling, and communication protocols. Their role is practical and interpersonal rather than judicial.

Parenting coordinators are typically psychologists or social workers. They do not have authority to vary court orders, but can help resolve disputes that would otherwise return to court.

💡 Use them to reduce legal costs

Every dispute you can resolve through a parenting coordinator costs a fraction of what a court appearance costs. High-conflict co-parenting relationships often benefit significantly from this structured support.

Parenting Orders
Parenting
Legally binding court orders setting out the arrangements for a child following parental separation, including who the child lives with, the time spent with each parent, how parental responsibility is exercised, and any other conditions the court considers necessary for the child's welfare.
When it applies: Made either by consent or after a contested hearing in all parenting proceedings. Parenting orders are enforceable and can be varied if there is a significant change in circumstances. They remain in force until the child turns 18 unless otherwise varied or discharged by the court.

What Parenting Orders Can Cover

Parenting orders are binding court orders determining arrangements for a child's care, time and parental responsibility. They may address:

  • Living arrangements (who the child lives with)
  • Time schedules (when the child is with each parent)
  • Communication (phone, video, messages)
  • Travel restrictions and passport controls
  • Decision-making authority
📌 Clarity is critical

Ambiguity in parenting orders is one of the most common sources of post-order disputes. Orders should be specific enough that both parties know exactly what is required without needing to negotiate. Vague terms like "reasonable time" are an invitation to conflict.

Parenting Plan
Parenting
A written agreement between parents about their child's living arrangements and related matters, made without court involvement. Parenting plans are flexible and can be amended by written agreement, but they are not legally enforceable as they have not been approved by a court.
When it applies: Used when parents can agree on arrangements without court proceedings. A parenting plan is a practical and cost-effective option but carries no enforcement mechanism. The existence of a prior parenting plan can be considered by the court as evidence of the parties' intentions if a dispute later arises.

Parenting Plans vs. Consent Orders

A parenting plan is a written, signed agreement between parents. It is not legally enforceable like court orders. However, it may override earlier parenting orders in certain circumstances and may be considered by the court in later proceedings.

Because it is flexible and amendable by agreement, it is often used where cooperation exists.

✓ Use a parenting plan when
  • You have a cooperative co-parenting relationship
  • You want flexibility as children grow
  • You want to avoid court costs and formality
⚠️ Consider consent orders when
  • There is any history of non-compliance
  • You need legal enforceability
  • The other parent is unpredictable
Party-Party Costs
Costs
The standard basis for costs orders in family law proceedings, under which the paying party contributes to — but does not fully cover — the other party's legal costs. Party-party costs are typically 60-70% of actual legal costs.
When it applies: In family law proceedings, the general rule is that parties bear their own costs. However, courts can make costs orders where the conduct of a party has been unreasonable. Party-party costs (also called ordinary costs) are the default level of any costs order — they represent a reasonable contribution, not full indemnity. For full reimbursement, a party must obtain indemnity costs. Courts assess costs orders against: the reasonableness of the parties' conduct; whether offers to settle were made; and the financial circumstances of the parties. Related: indemnity costs, costs order.
Prima Facie Case
Evidence
A sufficient body of evidence to support a legal claim if left uncontradicted — the minimum evidentiary threshold required to proceed.
When it applies: Must be established before certain orders can be made or applications can proceed. It does not guarantee success but demonstrates that the claim is not baseless. Courts assess whether, on the applicant's evidence alone, the case could succeed before requiring the respondent to answer.

Establishing a Prima Facie Case

A prima facie case exists where initial evidence supports the legal claim if uncontradicted. It does not guarantee success but satisfies a preliminary threshold — it shows the application is not without foundation.

Relevant in interim hearings, urgent applications, and summary dismissal contexts. If you cannot establish even a prima facie case, the application may be dismissed without hearing the other side's response.

📌 Evidence first

Before filing, ask yourself: do I have enough evidence to support this claim if the other party says nothing? If the answer is no, gather more evidence before filing. An application without a prima facie evidentiary foundation will fail at the first hurdle.

What a Prima Facie Case Requires

A prima facie case exists where initial evidence, if uncontradicted, is sufficient to support the legal claim. It satisfies a preliminary threshold — enough to justify the matter proceeding or an order being made on an interim basis.

It does not guarantee success at final hearing, but demonstrates that the application is not baseless. In urgent or ex parte applications, establishing a prima facie case is often a minimum requirement before orders are made.

💡 What this means practically

When making an urgent application, your first job is to show the court that you have a real case — not a perfect case, but one with sufficient substance to justify the court's intervention. Lead with your strongest, most specific evidence.

Particulars
Evidence
Specific factual details provided in support of a claim or allegation — including dates, places, descriptions of incidents, and their alleged effects. Particulars give substance and precision to allegations that might otherwise be too vague to respond to or assess.
When it applies: Required for all serious allegations, particularly of family violence or abuse. Unparticularised allegations are given less weight and may limit a party's ability to rely on them at hearing. A party may be ordered to provide further particulars if their allegations are not sufficiently specific.
Pattern of Intimidation
Protection
Repeated behaviour — such as threats, aggressive communication, physical presence, property damage, or surveillance — that causes a person to fear for their safety. A pattern is more probative than isolated incidents.
When it applies: Relevant in protection order applications and parenting proceedings involving family violence. Courts look for evidence of repeated conduct across a period of time. Documentary evidence — screenshots, police attendance records, medical records — significantly strengthens intimidation claims.
Pattern of Non-Compliance
Orders
A series of failures to comply with court orders over time, demonstrating an entrenched disregard for the court's authority. Courts treat a pattern more seriously than an isolated breach.
When it applies: Established in contravention proceedings through evidence of multiple individual breaches. The existence of a pattern significantly affects the sanctions the court imposes and may result in variation of the underlying orders to reduce the opportunity for further breach.
Pattern Evidence
Evidence
Evidence demonstrating a consistent course of behaviour over time rather than relying on a single incident. Particularly significant in family violence and coercive control contexts.
When it applies: Used to establish that alleged behaviour was deliberate and sustained. Documentary evidence — texts, emails, incident logs, police records — provides the most reliable foundation.

Pattern Evidence in Family Law

Demonstrates consistent behaviour over time. Particularly relevant in family violence and coercive control — a documented pattern is far more persuasive than a single incident.

💡 How to present it

Structure your affidavit to show the pattern, not just incidents. Use dates, quote messages directly, show how the behaviour repeated. A chronological incident table can be more compelling than paragraphs of narrative.

Why Pattern Evidence Matters

Pattern evidence demonstrates consistent behaviour over time. It is particularly relevant in family violence and coercive control allegations, where no single incident may seem severe but the cumulative pattern reveals the true nature of the conduct.

Isolated incidents carry less weight than demonstrated patterns. A single incident can be explained away; a documented pattern is much harder to dismiss.

💡 How to build pattern evidence

Keep a contemporaneous journal — dated entries recording incidents as they occur carry far more weight than a retrospective account written years later. Supplement with communications (texts, emails), photographs with timestamps, and consistent third-party witnesses.

PINOP
Protection
"Person In Need of Protection." The person the AVO is designed to protect.
When it applies: The PINOP may or may not be the same as the applicant. In police-initiated AVOs, police are the applicant but the PINOP is the person at risk. The PINOP's address and identifying details can be kept confidential.
Police-Initiated AVO
Protection
An AVO application made by police on behalf of a protected person.
When it applies: Police are obligated to apply for an AVO if they attend a domestic violence incident and believe a person needs protection. The protected person does not need to agree to or support the application.

Police-Initiated AVOs

Sought by police where they believe a person needs protection. The protected person does not control whether proceedings continue — once police initiate, they are the prosecuting party.

These orders may impact parenting proceedings, particularly where allegations overlap. The police AVO record and the grounds alleged will typically be available to the family court.

If you are the protected person
  • You can express a view but cannot withdraw the AVO
  • The order can still be made against your wishes
If you are the respondent
  • You can consent without admissions
  • You can contest at a hearing
  • Get legal advice before the court date
Post-Separation Parenting
Parenting
The arrangements, communication, and practical cooperation by which separated parents continue to raise their children. It encompasses both the legal framework (parenting orders and plans) and the day-to-day reality of managing a child's life across two households.
When it applies: Relevant from the point of separation and throughout the child's upbringing. Courts and practitioners consider the quality of post-separation parenting when assessing what orders will best serve the child. Interventions such as parenting coordination and therapeutic programs are often recommended to support it.
Private Application
Protection
An AVO application made directly by an individual rather than police.
When it applies: If police have not applied for an AVO on your behalf, you can apply at your local court registry. You will need to complete an application form and may be required to attend a mention date to explain why the order is needed.
Probative Value
Evidence
The capacity of a piece of evidence to prove or disprove a fact in issue. High probative value means the evidence significantly advances the case on a material point. Courts weigh probative value against other considerations such as prejudice and reliability.
When it applies: Relevant whenever courts assess the weight to give evidence. Where evidence has low probative value relative to its prejudicial effect, the court may limit or exclude it. Parties should focus their evidence on material with genuine probative value rather than including everything available.
Procedural Fairness
Court Process
The fundamental legal principle that each party must be given a fair opportunity to know the case against them, to present their own evidence and arguments, and to have their case genuinely considered before a decision is made. Also known as natural justice.
When it applies: Applies throughout all court proceedings. A denial of procedural fairness is a ground of appeal. It is breached, for example, when a party is not given adequate notice of a hearing, when evidence is relied upon without being put to the affected party, or when a decision-maker is biased.
Procedural Fairness (Natural Justice)
Court Process
The fundamental legal requirement that each party in proceedings is given a fair opportunity to be heard and to have their evidence and arguments genuinely considered before a decision is made. It also requires the court to act without bias.
When it applies: Applies in all proceedings before the court. A failure to accord procedural fairness is a ground of appeal. It is breached, for example, when a judge makes orders based on information not put to the parties, or when a party is denied a reasonable opportunity to respond to the other's case.

Natural Justice (Procedural Fairness)

Requires impartial decision-making and a fair hearing. Two core rules:

  • The hearing rule — a fair opportunity to present your case and respond to adverse material
  • The bias rule — the decision-maker must be, and appear to be, impartial
📌 Raising a bias concern

Applications for judicial disqualification (recusal) are serious and require clear grounds. Unsubstantiated bias applications can damage your credibility.

Procedural Fairness at Interim Stage
Court Process
The obligation on the court to ensure both parties have a meaningful opportunity to be heard before interim orders are made, even when time is limited. It includes adequate notice and the chance to file responding material.
When it applies: Applies to all interim hearings. Where orders are sought without notice (ex parte), the absent party must be given the earliest possible opportunity to be heard and to challenge the orders. Courts are alert to procedural fairness arguments as grounds of appeal in interim decisions.
Procedural Obstruction
High Conflict
Deliberate non-cooperation or obstruction of the court's procedural steps — such as refusing to file documents on time, failing to attend conferences, or withholding disclosure — in a way that impedes the progress of proceedings.
When it applies: Treated seriously by courts as conduct that undermines the administration of justice. Courts may impose costs orders, unless the obstructing party, or refer serious cases to the court's disciplinary processes. Procedural obstruction by a self-represented party does not receive any more tolerance than by legally represented parties.
Procedural Order
Court Process
A court order managing the steps and timetable for a case — including filing deadlines, exchange of documents, attendance at conferences, or commissioning expert reports. Procedural orders organise proceedings rather than determining their outcome.
When it applies: Made at every directions hearing and case management event throughout proceedings. Parties must comply with procedural orders or risk having their case disadvantaged. Repeated non-compliance can result in costs orders or summary dismissal.
Proof of Service
Court Process
Documentary evidence that a party has been formally served with court documents — such as an application, orders, or a subpoena. Proof of service is usually an affidavit of service sworn by the person who effected service.
When it applies: Before a court will proceed in a matter where the other party has not appeared, it will require proof that they were properly served. Without proof of service, the court cannot be satisfied the other party had notice of the proceedings. Service must comply with the rules — personal service, substituted service, or electronic service as directed. An affidavit of service should state: who was served, how they were identified, when and where service occurred, and what documents were given. Related: service, substituted service, affidavit of service.

What to Include in an Affidavit of Service

Your affidavit of service should be specific: 'On Tuesday 14 May 2024 at approximately 3:45pm I attended 12 Smith Street, Parramatta NSW 2150. A man who identified himself as John Smith opened the door. I handed him a sealed envelope containing the initiating application and notice of listing and said These are court documents for you.'

If service was effected by email or post as directed by the court, attach copies of the sent email or Australia Post tracking confirmation as exhibits.

Keep a copy of every proof of service in your court file. If the other party fails to appear on a listing date, you will need to produce it to the court.

Property Settlement
Orders
The legal process by which the property, assets, debts, and financial resources of a separating couple are divided. A property settlement can be reached by agreement (formalised as consent orders or a binding financial agreement) or, if parties cannot agree, determined by the court.
When it applies: The court has broad discretion to make orders altering property interests under s 79 of the Family Law Act 1975. The process involves: identifying and valuing the asset pool; assessing contributions (financial and non-financial); considering future needs; and asking whether a proposed division is just and equitable. There is no automatic 50/50 split — outcomes vary widely depending on the length of the relationship, contributions, and the parties' future circumstances. Property settlements must be formalised to be binding. Related: consent orders, binding financial agreement, asset pool.

When to Formalise Your Settlement

Many couples reach informal agreements about property after separation but never formalise them. This is a significant risk — an informal agreement can be undone years later. Either party can apply to court for a property settlement until the statutory time limit expires.

The time limit for applying is: 12 months after a divorce order takes effect (for married couples) and 2 years from the end of a de facto relationship (for de facto couples). After this, leave of the court is required.

Formalise your agreement as consent orders through the FCFCOA or as a binding financial agreement (BFA). Both require careful legal drafting — a poorly drafted property settlement can create ongoing disputes.

Proportional Response
Court Process
The principle that legal steps taken in proceedings should be appropriate in scale and cost to the nature and significance of the issue in dispute. Disproportionate litigation responses are contrary to the overarching purpose of the FCFCOA Act.
When it applies: Assessed throughout proceedings. A party who files extensive material, multiple applications, and lengthy submissions in response to minor issues may be criticised by the court and exposed to costs orders. Self-represented parties should ask themselves whether each proposed step is genuinely necessary and proportionate to what is at stake.
Protected Address
Protection
The residential, work, or other address of the protected person that is named in the AVO as a location the defendant must not approach or enter.
When it applies: The protected address is typically the protected person's home. It may also include their workplace, children's school, a parent's home, or any other location significant to the protected person's safety. The defendant is prohibited from approaching within the specified distance of each listed address. If the protected person moves, they should apply to vary the AVO to update the protected address — the defendant is bound by the address listed in the order, not a new one they may not know about. Related: no approach condition, exclusion from home.

Updating a Protected Address

If you move home after an AVO is made, you should apply to vary the order to include your new address. Until the order is varied, it only protects the addresses specifically named.

Keep a copy of your AVO with you at all times. If the defendant approaches a protected address, call police immediately and provide them with a copy of the order. The order number and defendant's details will allow police to act quickly.

Courts take violations of protected address conditions seriously. Even a single visit — particularly one that appears calculated or intimidating — is likely to result in criminal charges and may influence any associated family law proceedings.

Protected Person
Protection
The individual — or individuals — named in an AVO as the person or persons whose safety the order is designed to protect. The AVO imposes restrictions on the defendant's conduct specifically in relation to the protected person.
When it applies: The protected person is usually the applicant (or the person on whose behalf police applied). Children can also be named as protected persons, in which case the defendant's restrictions extend to conduct towards those children as well. The protected person does not need to have suffered physical harm — fear of harm is sufficient to establish the need for protection. The protected person has standing to appear in AVO proceedings, vary the order, or apply for revocation. Related: defendant, applicant.

Rights of the Protected Person

As the protected person, you do not need to attend every court date in AVO proceedings — police and prosecutors handle the matter. However, you may attend and may be asked to give evidence, particularly if the defendant contests the AVO.

You can apply to vary or revoke an AVO if your circumstances change. If you no longer wish to be protected — for example, because you have reconciled — a magistrate will still assess whether revocation is appropriate. You cannot be forced to continue the AVO, but the court has discretion.

If you have children with the defendant, the AVO and any parenting orders need to be read together carefully. A family lawyer or Legal Aid can help you understand how the two sets of orders interact — particularly around changeovers and communication.

Protective Capacity
Parenting
A parent's demonstrated ability to recognise and respond to risks to their child's safety and wellbeing. Protective capacity includes insight into the risks posed by the other parent, by third parties, and by the parent's own conduct or circumstances.
When it applies: Assessed in parenting proceedings involving safety concerns. A parent who minimises or denies risks to the child — including risks arising from their own behaviour — may be found to have limited protective capacity. Courts consider protective capacity when determining primary care and the need for supervised arrangements.

Demonstrating Protective Capacity

Protective capacity refers to a parent's ability to recognise risk, take appropriate action, and keep the child safe from harm. It is central in cases involving family violence — a parent who minimises or denies risk to a child is viewed as having poor protective capacity.

A parent who acknowledges a risk and has taken concrete steps to address it demonstrates stronger protective capacity than one who denies the problem exists.

📌 Show, don't just tell

Saying "I will protect my child" is not enough. Document the specific steps you have taken — leaving a violent relationship, engaging with support services, completing courses, restricting the child's exposure to risk. Concrete actions demonstrate capacity; words alone do not.

Courts also weigh whether a parent recognises documented risks — including from a new partner, their own conduct, or the other parent — and what concrete steps they have taken (police, AVO, separation, counselling for the child).

⚠️ Protective capacity is observable

Courts look at what you have actually done to protect your child, not just what you say. Evidence of protective capacity includes contacting police, obtaining an AVO, separating from a harmful relationship, or seeking counselling for the child.

Provisional Order
Protection
An urgent order made by police before the matter reaches court.
When it applies: Police can issue a provisional AVO at the scene of an incident when they believe a person needs immediate protection. The order is temporary and must be confirmed by a court at the first mention date.
Pseudonym Order
Court Process
An order permitting a party, witness, or child to be identified by a pseudonym rather than their real name in court documents and proceedings. Pseudonym orders protect privacy and safety, particularly in sensitive or high-risk matters.
When it applies: Pseudonym orders are most commonly made to protect victims of family violence or sexual abuse, to protect children, or in matters involving witness safety concerns. Once a pseudonym order is made, all court documents use the pseudonym. The real identity is known to the court, the parties' lawyers, and specified parties only. Breach of a pseudonym order — such as publishing the real identity — can result in criminal sanctions. Related: suppression order, non-publication order.
Psychological Abuse
High Conflict
A form of family violence involving the use of threats, humiliation, intimidation, and emotional manipulation to control or harm another person. Psychological abuse does not require physical contact and is recognised as family violence under Australian law.
When it applies: Recognised forms of psychological abuse include: threats of harm to the victim, children, pets, or property; persistent belittling or humiliation; controlling social interactions and isolating from support networks; monitoring communications; gaslighting (causing the victim to question their own perception of reality); and threatening self-harm to coerce compliance. Under s 4AB of the Family Law Act 1975, psychological abuse is expressly included in the definition of family violence. Evidence of psychological abuse is highly relevant to parenting proceedings, property settlement, and AVO applications. Related: family violence, coercive control, economic abuse.
Psychological Safety Consideration
Protection
The court's evaluation of a child's or party's emotional wellbeing and psychological security in the context of proposed parenting or protective arrangements. It extends beyond physical safety to include mental health and emotional stability.
When it applies: Increasingly prominent in parenting decisions since the 2023 Family Law Act amendments. Courts consider whether arrangements will protect a child's emotional development and minimise anxiety, fear, and distress. Expert evidence from psychologists or family consultants often informs this assessment.
r94
Re-Examination
Evidence
The questioning of a witness by the party who called them, conducted after that witness has been cross-examined by the other side. Re-examination is confined to matters arising from cross-examination and cannot introduce new topics.
When it applies: Occurs at contested hearings and trials as the third stage of witness examination. It is used to clarify ambiguous or misleading answers given during cross-examination or to rehabilitate the witness's credibility. Leave of the court is required to raise entirely new matters.
Reactive Allegation
High Conflict
An allegation made in direct response to a claim filed by the other party, rather than arising independently from the facts.
When it applies: Courts are alert to patterns of reactive allegations, which can indicate tactical litigation rather than genuine safety concerns. Where allegations appear to mirror or respond to the other party's claims, courts may assess whether they are genuinely held or strategically motivated.
Reasonable Excuse
Orders
A justification for non-compliance with a court order that the court accepts as sufficient to excuse or mitigate the breach. What constitutes a reasonable excuse depends on the circumstances of each case.
When it applies: Raised as a defence in contravention proceedings. Common examples include illness, emergency, or genuine misunderstanding of the order's requirements. The burden is on the party in breach to establish a reasonable excuse. Strategic or after-the-fact reasons are scrutinised carefully.
Reasons for Judgment
Court Process
The written explanation provided by a judge setting out the facts found, the law applied, and the reasons for the orders made. Reasons for judgment are a fundamental requirement of procedural fairness — parties are entitled to know why the court decided as it did.
When it applies: In family law proceedings, reasons for judgment are delivered either orally at the conclusion of a hearing or in writing at a later date. Written reasons are more common in complex or significant matters. Reasons form the basis of any appeal — an appeal is generally confined to errors of law or fact identified in the reasons. If you believe the judge made an error, the reasons are the starting point for advice about whether to appeal. Related: appeal, leave to appeal.
Recovery Order
Orders
A court order requiring the return of a child to the person with whom they are supposed to be living, following a contravention of a parenting order by the other parent or a third party. Federal Police may be authorised to locate and return the child.
When it applies: Applied for urgently when a child has been taken or withheld in breach of a parenting order. The court can hear recovery order applications on a same-day basis in sufficiently urgent circumstances. May be combined with a passport order and a request to border agencies if removal from Australia is suspected.

Recovery Orders Explained

A recovery order authorises law enforcement to locate and return a child who has been wrongfully removed or retained. The court considers urgency, risk, and the child's immediate safety.

Recovery orders can be sought without notice in urgent cases. The court's focus is on restoring lawful arrangements while assessing any underlying risk concerns.

🚨 If a child has been taken

Contact the court registry immediately for urgent listing. If there is risk of international removal, also contact the Australian Federal Police to flag the child on the Movement Alert List. Do not attempt to physically recover the child yourself.

Restraint Order
Protection
A court order restricting a party from taking specific actions, such as removing a child from a geographic area, disposing of assets, or contacting certain individuals.
When it applies: Used to preserve the status quo or prevent anticipated harm pending further determination. Common examples include travel restraints (preventing international removal of a child), asset preservation orders in financial matters, and restraints from approaching a residence.

Types of Restraint Orders

A restraint order restricts specific behaviour to protect a party or child. Common examples in parenting matters include prohibiting a parent from removing the child from a defined area, travelling internationally, or approaching the family home.

Restraint orders can be sought urgently — if you have reason to believe the other parent may attempt to take the child overseas, contact the court and the Australian Federal Police (Movement Alert List) immediately.

🚨 International child abduction risk

If you have genuine reason to fear international removal, seek a passport restraint order and contact the AFP's Liaison for International Family Abduction (LIFE) unit. Act before it happens — recovering a child from overseas is significantly harder and more costly than preventing removal.

Restraint orders can be made as standalone orders or as conditions within broader parenting or property orders. Breach is a serious matter.

📌 Be specific about what you seek

When applying for a restraint order, describe precisely what behaviour you need restricted and why. Vague orders are harder to enforce. The more specific the order, the clearer the obligation — and the clearer the breach if it occurs.

Recovery Order Application
Orders
An application to the court seeking orders for the immediate return of a child who has been wrongfully retained or removed — whether interstate or internationally — in breach of existing parenting orders or without consent.
When it applies: Filed urgently when a child has been taken or is being withheld. The court can make recovery orders on the same day in sufficiently urgent cases. Federal Police may be authorised to locate and return the child. Where international removal is suspected, applications under the Hague Convention may also be needed.
Registrar
Court Administration
A judicial officer of the FCFCOA with delegated jurisdiction to determine certain procedural and administrative matters, including approving consent orders, conducting case management hearings, and presiding over dispute resolution conferences.
When it applies: Involved at many points in proceedings, particularly at early case management stages. Decisions made by a registrar can be reviewed by a judge on application. Registrars cannot determine final contested hearings, which must be presided over by a judge.
Registry
Court Administration
The administrative office of the court responsible for receiving and processing filed documents, allocating case numbers, collecting fees, managing listings, and providing general information about court procedures to parties and the public.
When it applies: The first point of contact when commencing or responding to family court proceedings. Registry staff cannot give legal advice but can provide information about how to file, current fees, and court locations. Most interactions now occur through the Commonwealth Courts Portal.

Working With the Registry

The registry manages administrative aspects of court proceedings — filing, listings, document processing, and fee collection. Registry staff cannot give legal advice but are your first point of contact for procedural questions.

Being polite, organised, and having your court file number ready will make every registry interaction smoother. They process high volumes and clear, efficient requests get faster responses.

💡 Practical tip

Keep a copy of everything you file and note the date and time. If there is ever a dispute about whether a document was received or processed, your records are your protection.

What the Registry Does

The registry manages the administrative side of court proceedings — receiving filed documents, listing matters, processing applications, and maintaining court records. Registry staff cannot give legal advice, but they can explain procedural requirements and filing processes.

💡 Build a good relationship with the registry

Be polite, organised and prepared. Registry staff deal with hundreds of litigants. If you come with documents in order, know what you're filing, and have the right forms, things move faster. Calling to clarify requirements before you arrive saves everyone time.

Adjournment
Court Administration
The postponement of a court hearing or matter to a later date. Adjournments may be granted by consent of both parties or on application, and the court must be satisfied there is a good reason — such as late service, illness, or unavailability of a witness.
When it applies: Sought when a party or their lawyer cannot attend on the listed date, or when additional time is needed to prepare. Repeated adjournments may draw judicial criticism and cost orders.
Case Management
Court Administration
The court's ongoing supervision of proceedings to ensure they progress efficiently toward resolution. Includes setting timetables, making procedural orders, directing parties to dispute resolution, and listing matters for hearing.
When it applies: Active throughout proceedings. Parties are expected to comply with case management orders; failure to do so may result in the matter being struck out or costs ordered against the non-compliant party.
Chambers
Court Administration
The private office of a judge, as distinct from the open courtroom. Interlocutory or procedural matters may be heard in chambers, meaning they are not open to the public. Chambers hearings are typically brief and deal with administrative or preliminary issues.
When it applies: Procedural applications — such as requests for timetable extensions or adjournments — may be determined in chambers on the papers without requiring physical attendance.
Chambers Correspondence
Court Administration
Written communications addressed directly to the judge's associate or chambers regarding procedural or administrative matters. It must be brief, factual, and — unless the court directs otherwise — copied to the other party.
When it applies: Used to request urgent listings, notify the court of settlement, or flag an administrative issue. Self-represented parties may send chambers correspondence but must always copy the other side.
Commonwealth Courts Portal
Court Administration
The online filing and case management system used by the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA). Parties use the Portal to file documents, pay fees, access court orders, and view hearing dates.
When it applies: Required for all electronic filings in the FCFCOA. Self-represented parties can register directly on the Portal. Paper filing remains available but is the exception rather than the rule.
Compliance and Readiness Hearing
Court Administration
A hearing conducted to check that both parties have complied with all pre-trial orders and are ready for a final hearing. The court reviews whether affidavits have been filed, subpoenas served, experts engaged, and other preparatory steps completed.
When it applies: Scheduled before a final hearing. Parties who are not ready risk having the hearing adjourned and costs ordered against them.
Court Date
Court Administration
A specific day on which a matter is listed before the court. Court dates may be for procedural hearings, mention dates, interim hearings, conciliation conferences, or final hearings. Attendance is mandatory unless excused by the court.
When it applies: Parties must attend every listed court date. Failure to appear without prior leave can result in the matter being determined in the absent party's absence or a warrant issued for attendance.
Court Fees
Court Administration
Fees charged by the FCFCOA for filing applications, issuing subpoenas, requesting hearings, and other court services. Fee amounts are set by the Family Law (Fees) Regulation 2012 and are indexed periodically.
When it applies: Payable at the time of filing. Fee reduction or waiver is available for holders of certain concession cards and in cases of financial hardship — apply using the appropriate court form before filing.
Court Record
Court Administration
The official file of documents, orders, and transcripts maintained by the court in relation to a matter. Access to the court record by persons other than the parties is restricted under the Family Law Act and court rules.
When it applies: Parties may request copies of documents from their own court file. Third parties — including journalists — must obtain leave of the court before accessing family law records.
Delay Strategy
Litigation Conduct
The deliberate use of procedural mechanisms to slow down proceedings, typically to gain tactical advantage, wear down the other party financially, or maintain a favourable status quo.
When it applies: A recognised form of litigation abuse where one party repeatedly seeks adjournments, files unnecessary applications, or fails to comply with timetables to extend the proceedings. Courts may penalise unreasonable delay with costs orders or adverse findings.

Identifying and Responding to Delay Tactics

Delay strategy refers to intentional procedural delay to gain advantage. Courts may penalise unreasonable delay through costs orders, adverse comment, or by making the orders sought by the other party.

Common delay tactics include: repeatedly seeking adjournments without good reason, filing late, raising new issues just before hearings, and failing to comply with timetable directions.

💡 If it's happening to you

Document the pattern and raise it with the court. Ask for a peremptory timetable where failure to comply still lists the matter for hearing. Courts may penalise unreasonable delay with costs or adverse comment.

⚠️ Document delay tactics

Keep correspondence showing adjournments, late filings, and missed timetable steps — courts respond when the pattern is clear.

Directions Hearing
Court Administration
A procedural hearing at which the court gives directions about the steps each party must take before the next listing. Directions may include filing affidavits, exchanging financial statements, engaging a family report writer, or attempting mediation.
When it applies: Common in the early stages of contested proceedings. The court expects parties to have discussed directions before the hearing and to agree on a timetable where possible.

What Happens at a Directions Hearing

A directions hearing manages procedural steps — filing evidence, issuing subpoenas, engaging experts, and setting timetables. It does not determine final outcomes. The court expects parties to have discussed directions beforehand and to agree on a timetable where possible.

Directions hearings are usually brief. The judge or registrar will review the status of the matter, resolve any procedural disputes, and issue orders setting out what each party must do before the next event.

💡 Be ready to propose directions

Come to a directions hearing knowing what steps you believe are needed and realistic timeframes for completing them. If you need more time to file evidence, say so — but have a reason. Courts dislike adjournments caused by lack of preparation.

Docket System
Court Administration
A case management system in which each matter is assigned to a specific judge who manages it from commencement to resolution. The FCFCOA uses a docket system to promote consistency and judicial familiarity with complex matters.
When it applies: Matters allocated to a docket judge are generally heard by that judge at all stages. Parties may apply to transfer if there is a conflict of interest or case management reason.
Appeal Book
Court Administration
A bound or paginated compilation of documents required for an appeal, including the orders appealed from, the reasons for judgment, relevant affidavits, and the transcript of the proceedings below. The appeal book is prepared by the appellant and provided to the court and the respondent.
When it applies: The appeal book must be filed and served within the time set by the appeal court's rules. Its preparation can be complex and expensive — mistakes in pagination or omission of relevant documents can delay the appeal. If you are self-represented, contact the appeal registry for guidance on the required format. Related: appeal, notice of appeal.

Preparing an Appeal Book

The appeal book must include every document the appeal court needs to understand and decide the appeal. Courts are strict about format — missing pages, incorrect numbering, or omitted transcripts are common grounds for delay or costs orders.

In the Full Court of the FCFCOA, the appellant's solicitor (or the self-represented appellant) is responsible for compiling and filing the appeal book. The registry can provide a checklist of required documents.

💡 Get the transcript early

Transcripts of hearings must be ordered from the court reporting service and can take several weeks. Order them as soon as you decide to appeal to avoid missing the filing deadline.

Appeal Hearing
Court Administration
A hearing before an appellate court — in family law, usually the Full Court of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia — at which the appellant argues that the primary judge made an error of law or fact, and the respondent defends the original orders. Appeal hearings are generally conducted on the papers and transcript, not by calling fresh evidence.
When it applies: An appeal hearing is not a retrial. The Full Court considers whether the primary judge made a legal error, exercised a discretion incorrectly, or made factual findings not supported by the evidence. Fresh evidence is rarely permitted. Parties typically present written submissions in advance and brief oral argument on the day. Related: appeal, notice of appeal, appeal book.

What Happens at an Appeal Hearing

Appeal hearings in family law are heard by a panel of three judges (Full Court). Each party is allocated time — typically 30 to 90 minutes — to present oral argument. Judges frequently ask questions, so be prepared to address the specific errors you allege, not simply to repeat your case.

Written submissions must be filed before the hearing in accordance with the court's timetable. They are the foundation of your argument — oral argument supplements but does not replace them.

💡 Know the standard of review

The Full Court cannot simply substitute its view for that of the primary judge. You must identify a specific error — a wrong legal principle, a finding with no evidentiary basis, or a failure to consider a relevant factor. Without identifying an error, an appeal is very unlikely to succeed.

Appeal Period
Court Administration
The time limit within which a party must file a notice of appeal to challenge a court order or judgment. In the FCFCOA, the standard appeal period for final orders is 28 days from the date the orders were made or the judgment was delivered.
When it applies: Missing the appeal period means you lose the automatic right to appeal. You must then apply for an extension of time, which is discretionary and not always granted. Act quickly if you believe orders are wrong — do not wait until the deadline is near. Related: appeal, notice of appeal.
Appeal Record
Court Administration
The complete official record of the proceedings at first instance that is before the appeal court. It includes the documents filed, orders made, reasons for judgment, and transcripts of hearings. The appeal record is distinct from the appeal book, which is the condensed working document prepared for the appeal.
When it applies: The appeal record is the authoritative source of what occurred below. If there is a dispute about what was said or filed in the original proceedings, the appeal record is determinative. Parties who wish to rely on material not in the record must apply to adduce fresh evidence, which courts grant rarely and only in defined circumstances.
Electronic Filing
Court Administration
The submission of court documents via the Commonwealth Courts Portal rather than in person or by post. Documents must be in the prescribed format (typically PDF) and filed by the relevant deadline to be accepted.
When it applies: The standard method of filing in the FCFCOA. The Portal timestamps each filing, which is important when deadlines are measured in days. A filing is only complete once a confirmation receipt is received.
Ex Parte Application
Court Administration
An application made to the court by one party without notifying or serving the other party. Ex parte orders are only granted in urgent situations — typically where notifying the other party would put a person or child at risk before the order can be made.
When it applies: Used for urgent interim injunctions, recovery orders, or family violence orders. The court will usually require full disclosure of all relevant facts, including any that favour the other side. A return date is set promptly so the other party can respond.
Filing Deadline
Court Administration
The date by which a document must be lodged with the court. Filing deadlines are set by court rules, procedural orders, or legislation. Missing a deadline without leave of the court can have serious consequences, including the document being rejected or a hearing being vacated.
When it applies: Every court document has an associated deadline. If you cannot meet a deadline, apply to the court for an extension before the deadline passes — not after.
Hearing List
Court Administration
The daily or weekly schedule of matters listed before a court or judicial officer. The hearing list is published by the court and indicates the time, location, and presiding judge or registrar for each matter.
When it applies: Parties should check the hearing list before each court date to confirm their matter is still listed and to identify the correct courtroom. Listing times are indicative — matters may be called earlier or later.
Hearing Allocation
Court Administration
The process by which the court assigns a specific date, time, and judge or registrar to hear a matter. A hearing allocation is granted after the case management process identifies that the matter is ready for a substantive hearing — whether interim or final.
When it applies: Getting a hearing allocation is a significant step — it means the court has determined the matter cannot resolve without judicial determination and is ready for hearing. Once allocated, parties must comply with all pre-hearing directions (filing evidence, exchanging submissions, preparing a court book) by the set dates. Vacating an allocated hearing date is strongly discouraged and will generally require court leave and a good explanation. Related: final hearing, interim hearing, directions hearing.

After You Receive a Hearing Allocation

Once a hearing date is set, treat every pre-hearing direction as a firm deadline. Courts have limited hearing time and take a serious view of parties who are not ready when their allocated date arrives.

In the period between allocation and hearing: finalise your affidavit evidence; prepare your submissions; organise your documents into a court book or bundle; and consider whether a last-minute settlement attempt is realistic.

💡 Settlement discussions before a hearing

Even after a hearing is allocated, many matters settle in the days or hours before the hearing begins. Being prepared for the hearing and being open to a fair resolution are not mutually exclusive — preparation actually puts you in a stronger negotiating position.

In Camera Proceedings
Court Administration
Proceedings held in private, closed to the public and the media. Family law proceedings are presumptively in camera under section 97 of the Family Law Act to protect the privacy of children and parties.
When it applies: Most FCFCOA hearings are in camera by default. The court may allow specific persons — such as a support person or student observer — to attend with leave.
Interlocutory Application
Court Administration
An application made during the course of proceedings for interim orders or procedural directions, as distinct from the final orders sought in the primary application. Interlocutory applications are used to deal with urgent or temporary matters while the main proceedings continue.
When it applies: Filed when a party needs an order before the final hearing — for example, interim parenting orders, a property injunction, or a requirement for the other party to produce documents.

What Interlocutory Applications Cover

An interlocutory application seeks temporary or procedural orders before the final hearing — urgent parenting, disclosure, subpoenas, or interim protective measures.

Outcomes are usually decided on affidavit material without full cross-examination; they shape the case but do not determine final rights.

💡 Use sparingly, prepare affidavits well

Repeated minor applications cost goodwill and money. Front-load clear, factual, child-focused affidavits — early credibility matters.

Listing
Court Administration
The scheduling of a matter for a particular hearing type on a specific date. A matter may be listed for a mention, a directions hearing, an interim hearing, a conciliation conference, or a final hearing. Listings are managed by the court registry.
When it applies: After filing, the registry will notify parties of the first listing. Further listings are generally made at each hearing for the next event in the proceeding.

How Listings Affect Your Case

Listing refers to scheduling a matter for a hearing or court event. Court lists are often under significant pressure — delays in obtaining hearing dates are common and can substantially affect interim arrangements and overall case strategy.

If your matter is urgent, apply for an urgent listing rather than waiting in the general queue. The court will assess urgency based on the risk and circumstances you disclose.

💡 Listing delays are real

In many registries, final hearings are listed 12–24 months out. This means interim orders often govern a child's life for an extended period. It is important to get interim arrangements right — they may operate longer than you expect.

Listings and Hearing Dates

Listing refers to scheduling a matter for a hearing or procedural event. Court lists are managed by the registry and can be affected by judicial availability, complexity, and urgency. Delays in listing may significantly affect interim arrangements.

⚠️ Urgency listings exist for a reason

If your matter has a genuine urgent element — safety risk, imminent relocation, removal threat — you can apply to be listed urgently via the duty list. Don't wait for the ordinary listing process if a child is at risk.

Mention
Court Administration
A short, administrative court appearance at which the judge or registrar checks the status of the matter, gives any necessary directions, and sets the next listing. Mentions are typically brief (5–15 minutes) and are not used for substantive argument.
When it applies: Often the first court event after filing. Self-represented parties must attend in person unless telephone or video attendance has been approved by the court.
Notice of Address for Service
Court Administration
A document filed with the court and served on other parties that provides the address — physical, postal, or electronic — at which a party agrees to receive court documents and correspondence. Parties must keep their address for service current throughout proceedings.
When it applies: Required when commencing or responding to proceedings. If a party's address changes during proceedings, a new Notice of Address for Service must be filed and served promptly.
Notice of Discontinuance
Court Administration
A document filed to formally withdraw an application or proceedings. Once filed, the party is generally bound by the discontinuance and cannot refile the same claim without leave of the court. The other party may seek costs if the discontinuance is unreasonable.
When it applies: Filed when parties have resolved their dispute by agreement and no further orders are needed from the court, or when a party decides not to proceed with their application.
Notice to Produce
Court Process
A formal notice served on the opposing party requiring them to produce specified documents for inspection or use at a hearing. Directed at parties to the proceedings, not third parties.
When it applies: Used when you need documents from the other party that they have not voluntarily disclosed. Failure to comply may result in a court direction, adverse inference, or costs order.

Notice to Produce

Requires the other party to produce specific documents. Unlike a subpoena (which targets third parties), this is directed at a party to the proceedings. Failure to comply may lead to a court direction, adverse inference, or costs order.

📌 vs. subpoena

Use a notice to produce for documents held by the other party. Use a subpoena for documents held by third parties like schools, hospitals, or police.

Notice to Produce vs. Subpoena

A notice to produce requires a party to the proceedings (not a third party) to produce specific documents. Failure to comply may lead to a court direction compelling production or an adverse inference being drawn.

Unlike a subpoena, which compels third parties, a notice to produce is directed at the other party themselves. It is useful for obtaining documents the other party controls — communications, financial records, medical or school documents they hold.

📌 Tip

If the other party fails to produce documents after a notice to produce, you can ask the court to draw an adverse inference — that the documents would not have supported their case. Raising this in submissions can be more powerful than the documents themselves.

Procedural Fairness
Court Administration
A foundational principle of administrative and court proceedings requiring that each party is given adequate notice of the case against them, a reasonable opportunity to respond, and that decisions are made by an impartial decision-maker. Also known as natural justice.
When it applies: Applies at every stage of proceedings. A party who is not given procedural fairness — for example, because they were not served with documents or not given an opportunity to respond to evidence — may appeal the decision on that basis.
Revocation of AVO
Protection
The formal cancellation of an AVO by court order, bringing the order to an end before its expiry date. Revocation requires a court application and is granted at the court's discretion.
When it applies: Either party can apply to revoke an AVO. For revocation, the court will consider whether the protected person still needs protection. If the protected person consents and indicates they no longer fear the defendant, revocation is likely but not automatic. Courts are cautious about revoking AVOs in cases involving serious domestic violence or where children are protected. Revocation ends all conditions — unlike variation, which modifies them. Related: AVO, variation of AVO, revocation.

Can the protected person revoke an AVO?

Yes — either party can apply to revoke an AVO, including the protected person. However, the court is not obliged to grant revocation just because the protected person consents. The court must be satisfied that the protected person no longer needs protection. This prevents defendants from pressuring protected persons into seeking revocation.

Revocation vs Variation

Revocation cancels the order entirely. Variation changes specific conditions while keeping the order in force. If your circumstances have changed but you still need some protection, a variation application may be more appropriate than revocation.

Rule 15.04
Evidence
Rule 15.04 of the Family Law Rules 2021, which deals with the content requirements for expert witness reports in family law proceedings. It sets out what an expert's report must contain to be admissible.
When it applies: Under r 15.04, an expert report must include: the expert's qualifications; the literature or other material relied upon; the assumptions on which the opinion is based; the expert's opinion itself; a statement that the expert understands their duty to the court and has complied with it. Reports that do not comply may be inadmissible or given less weight. The rule reflects the principle that expert evidence must be genuinely independent and based on disclosed reasoning, not advocacy. Related: expert witness, single expert, opinion evidence.
Self-Represented Litigant
Court Administration
A party to court proceedings who appears without legal representation. Also called a litigant in person. Self-represented parties are subject to the same rules and obligations as legally represented parties but are entitled to reasonable assistance and explanation from the court regarding procedure.
When it applies: The FCFCOA has a Self-Represented Litigants Coordinator at each registry who can provide procedural information. The court cannot give legal advice, but will generally take steps to ensure self-represented parties understand what is required of them.
Section 60I Certificate
Court Process
A certificate issued by an accredited Family Dispute Resolution (FDR) practitioner confirming that the parties have attended — or attempted to attend — mediation before commencing parenting proceedings. Required under section 60I of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) before filing most parenting applications.
When it applies: Must be obtained before filing an Initiating Application for parenting orders. Exemptions exist for urgent matters, family violence, child abuse, and where the other party is unable or unwilling to participate. Without the certificate (or a valid exemption), the court may reject the application.

Section 60I Certificate in Practice

The section 60I certificate confirms that parties attempted Family Dispute Resolution before commencing parenting proceedings. It does not indicate who was at fault — it simply confirms participation status.

Exceptions apply in cases involving urgency, family violence, or abuse risk. Without the certificate (or a valid exemption), an application may be rejected. The certificate type matters — a certificate showing one party refused to participate or did not make genuine effort can affect the court's view of that party's conduct.

💡 Getting your certificate

Contact Family Relationships Australia or Relationships Australia to book FDR. Legal Aid can also provide FDR services in most states. Keep your certificate safe — you'll need to file it with your Initiating Application.

Service
Court Administration
The formal delivery of court documents to another party in a manner prescribed by the Family Law Rules. Service may be effected by hand, post, email (where agreed), or through a process server. Documents must be served within the time specified in the court rules or orders.
When it applies: Required whenever a party files a document that affects another party's rights. An Affidavit of Service must then be filed to prove that service occurred correctly and on time.
Setting Down
Court Administration
The process by which a matter is allocated a fixed date for a final hearing. A matter is "set down" once the court is satisfied that all interlocutory steps have been completed and the matter is ready for final determination.
When it applies: Occurs at a compliance and readiness hearing or directions hearing once the court is satisfied the matter is trial-ready. Parties should have all evidence prepared before applying to be set down.
Stamp
Court Administration
The court's official seal or mark applied to a filed document to confirm that it has been accepted for filing. A stamped copy is the official version of a court document and should be retained by each party. Unstamped copies have no official status.
When it applies: When documents are filed electronically via the Portal, the stamped copy is returned as a PDF. Always serve stamped copies on the other party — serving an unstamped draft is not valid service.
Substituted Service
Court Administration
Court-approved service of documents by a non-standard method — such as email, social media, post to a last known address, or service on a relative — when personal service has been attempted and is not reasonably practicable.
When it applies: Applied for by filing an Application in a Proceeding with an affidavit setting out the attempts made to locate and serve the other party, and proposing the alternative method. The court will only grant substituted service if satisfied that the method proposed is likely to bring the document to the other party's attention.

Substituted Service
