Court-approved alternative to personal service — used when a party is evading service, their whereabouts are unknown, or personal service poses a safety risk.

The court may order service by email, social media, post, or through a known associate. You must apply before attempting alternative service — unilateral alternatives are invalid.

💡 Document every attempt first

The court must be satisfied that reasonable attempts at standard service were made. Log every attempt with date, time, and what happened.

When Substituted Service Is Available

Substituted service is a court-approved alternative to standard personal service, available where personal service is impractical — for example, where a party is evading service, their whereabouts are unknown, or personal service poses a safety risk.

The court may approve service by email, social media, through a known contact, or by publication. You must prove that you have made reasonable attempts at personal service first.

💡 Document your attempts first

Before applying, document every attempt at service with dates, times, addresses and outcomes. The court needs to be satisfied that you have genuinely tried before it will approve an alternative method.

Section 102NA
Protection
A provision of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) that restricts direct cross-examination by an alleged perpetrator of family violence of an alleged victim in family law proceedings.
When it applies: Applies where a final AVO, criminal conviction for violence, or charging document exists, or where the court otherwise considers it appropriate. Instead of direct cross-examination, a lawyer must be appointed to conduct the questioning, protecting the victim from retraumatisation while preserving the right to test evidence.

Section 102NA — Cross-Examination Protections

Section 102NA restricts direct cross-examination in family violence cases. It prevents an alleged perpetrator from personally questioning an alleged victim — a lawyer must be appointed instead. This protects vulnerable parties from retraumatisation while still allowing evidence to be tested.

The restriction applies automatically in certain circumstances (existing AVO or criminal conviction) and may also be ordered by the court where it considers direct cross-examination inappropriate.

💡 Know your rights

If you are an alleged victim and the other party is self-represented, raise section 102NA early in proceedings. The court can order that the other party be provided with a lawyer for cross-examination purposes. You do not need to agree to be cross-examined directly by the other party in these circumstances.

If the party does not have a lawyer, the court may appoint one for the purpose of cross-examination only. You do not need to apply for this protection where the statutory conditions are met — raise it with the judge if direct cross-examination is attempted.

Section 117 Costs
Costs
The provision of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) governing the court's discretion to make costs orders in family law proceedings, including the circumstances in which departure from the usual 'each party bears own costs' rule is justified.
When it applies: The court may order costs against a party where their conduct warrants it — including unreasonable litigation behaviour, false allegations, failure to comply with orders, or unjustified refusal to negotiate. Section 117 provides the legal framework for this discretion.

Section 117 — The Costs Framework

Section 117 governs costs discretion in family law. It outlines when departure from the general "each party pays own costs" rule is justified. The court considers:

  • Financial circumstances of each party
  • Conduct during proceedings
  • Whether a party was wholly or partly successful
  • Any offers of settlement made
  • Whether a party has complied with orders and directions
📌 Document your settlement offers

Making reasonable, documented settlement offers protects you from adverse costs orders if the final outcome is no better than what you offered. Keep all without prejudice offers in writing with dates — they may be relied upon in costs submissions at the end of proceedings.

The general rule is that each party pays their own costs. A costs order under section 117 is a significant departure and requires the court to be satisfied that it is appropriate in all the circumstances.

📌 Conduct throughout proceedings matters

Courts look at the entire conduct of the litigation — not just who 'won' at the end. Unreasonable refusal to negotiate, baseless applications, and failure to comply with orders can all attract adverse costs even if you ultimately succeed on the main issues.

Section 69ZW Order
Legislation
A court order under section 69ZW of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) compelling a child protection authority to produce its records to the family court.
When it applies: Sought in parenting proceedings where child protection authorities have been involved. The court balances evidentiary value against privacy considerations.

Section 69ZW Orders

Compels child protection authorities to produce their files — risk assessments, investigation notes, interview records — to the family court. Can be critical evidence for both parties.

📌 Common in abuse and neglect cases

If child protection has been involved with your family, their records are often essential evidence. Applications under s69ZW are standard in contested parenting matters involving these allegations.

Accessing Child Protection Records

A section 69ZW order compels child protection authorities to produce their records to the family court. These records can significantly influence findings relating to risk and parenting capacity — they may contain notifications, investigations, risk assessments and case notes dating back years.

The court carefully balances privacy against evidentiary need. Records are typically provided to the court and then assessed for relevance before being released to the parties.

💡 When to seek these records

If there have been prior child protection notifications, departmental involvement, or welfare checks relating to either parent or the child, these records can be critical evidence. Apply early — production can take time and may affect your hearing timetable.

Timetable Order
Court Administration
A court order specifying the dates by which each party must complete particular steps before the next hearing — such as filing affidavits, serving financial documents, or obtaining an expert report. Compliance with timetable orders is mandatory.
When it applies: Made at early directions hearings to keep proceedings on track. If you cannot comply with a timetable order, apply for an extension before the deadline — not after — and be prepared to explain the reason for the delay.
Transcript
Court Administration
A verbatim written record of court proceedings, prepared by an authorised court reporter. Transcripts are relevant for appeals, for reference during a hearing, and when checking what was said on the record. Parties must pay for transcripts, which can be costly.
When it applies: Essential for any appeal, as the appeal court will rely on the transcript of the original hearing. Transcripts can be ordered through the court's transcript service and are usually available within a few days of the hearing.
Vexatious Litigant
Court Administration
A party declared by a court to have habitually, persistently, and without reasonable cause instituted vexatious proceedings. A vexatious litigant order restricts the person's ability to file further proceedings without leave of the court.
When it applies: Courts apply this declaration when a party repeatedly brings hopeless or harassing claims to abuse the court process. Applying for a vexatious litigant order against the other party requires strong evidence of a pattern of unreasonable litigation conduct.
Vexatious Proceedings
Court Process
Court proceedings that are repetitive, baseless or brought for an improper purpose — primarily to harass or exhaust the other party rather than obtain legitimate relief.
When it applies: Relevant where a party has brought multiple failed applications against the same person. A vexatious litigant declaration requires evidence of a sustained pattern. It restricts but does not eliminate access to the court.

Vexatious Proceedings

Repetitive or baseless applications intended to harass rather than resolve a genuine dispute. Courts may declare a person vexatious and require leave before any new application is filed.

📌 It doesn't prevent all litigation

A vexatious litigant declaration requires court permission before filing — acting as a filter for baseless applications while preserving the ability to bring genuine claims.

Vexatious Litigants

Vexatious proceedings are repetitive or baseless applications intended to harass rather than seek genuine relief. Courts may declare a person vexatious and restrict further filings — requiring leave of the court before any new application can be made.

The threshold for a vexatious declaration is high. The court needs to be satisfied of a pattern of abusive conduct across multiple proceedings. A single unsuccessful application is not enough.

⚠️ The reputational impact

Even without a formal vexatious declaration, repeated meritless applications damage your credibility with the court. Judges have long memories. Every application that fails without good reason erodes your standing in subsequent proceedings.

Adjournment
Court Administration
A postponement of court proceedings to a later date or time. Courts may adjourn for reasons including illness, late filing, unavailability of a party or lawyer, or insufficient time to hear the matter.
When it applies: Common in family law matters where urgent personal circumstances arise. When one party seeks an adjournment, the other may oppose it. Courts weigh fairness, delay, and the impact on any children involved.
Affidavit Filing Fee
Court Administration
The court fee payable when lodging affidavit documents as part of family law proceedings in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia.
When it applies: Fee concessions or waivers may be available for holders of health care cards or those experiencing financial hardship. Always check the current fee schedule on the FCFCOA website before filing.
Approved Form
Court Administration
An official court form approved by the Chief Justice or Rules Committee for use in family law proceedings. Only approved forms are accepted for filing.
When it applies: Using an outdated or unapproved form can result in a document being rejected. Always download forms directly from the FCFCOA website to ensure you have the current version.
Business Day
Court Administration
A day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or public holiday in the relevant state or territory. Court deadlines expressed in business days exclude weekends and public holidays.
When it applies: Critical for calculating filing deadlines. If a deadline falls on a non-business day, it typically rolls over to the next business day. Always confirm with the relevant court registry.
Case Coordinator
Court Administration
A court officer responsible for managing the administrative progress of a case from filing through to hearing, including scheduling, compliance checks, and communications.
When it applies: Case coordinators do not provide legal advice but can explain court procedures and administrative requirements. They are your key contact for questions about your matter's progress.
Case Number
Court Administration
The unique alphanumeric identifier assigned to a matter by the court upon filing. All documents, correspondence, and court appearances must reference the case number.
When it applies: Always include your case number on every document you file or correspondence you send to the court. Matters cannot be tracked or located without the correct case number.
Caveat on Property
Court Administration
A formal notice registered against a property title warning that a person claims an interest in that property. In family law, used to prevent a party from selling or refinancing property during proceedings.
When it applies: Registering a caveat prevents dealing with the property without first notifying the caveator. It does not create a right to the property but preserves the position until the court resolves the matter.
Chambers
Court Administration
The private office of a judge or magistrate. Some procedural or urgent matters are dealt with 'in chambers' rather than open court, meaning without the parties physically present in a courtroom.
When it applies: Directions hearings and urgent applications may sometimes be heard in chambers. Parties are notified of any chambers hearing and have the right to make submissions.
Certified Copy
Court Administration
An official copy of a document that has been certified as a true copy of the original by a justice of the peace, solicitor, or other authorised person.
When it applies: Courts may require certified copies of identity documents, birth certificates, or prior orders. A certified copy must bear the certifier's signature, name, qualification, and date.
Compliance Certificate
Court Administration
A document certifying that a party has complied with a specific court requirement, such as completing a parenting course or filing mandatory financial disclosure documents.
When it applies: Required before certain hearings can proceed. Failure to obtain or file a compliance certificate can result in a hearing being vacated or costs orders being made against the non-compliant party.
Court Directory
Court Administration
An official listing of court locations, contact details, registry hours, and judicial officers for the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia and state-based family courts.
When it applies: Use the court directory to find the correct registry for filing, phone numbers for enquiries, and addresses for attending court. Available on the FCFCOA website.
Court Holiday
Court Administration
A day on which the court does not sit and the registry is closed. Court holidays include public holidays and any additional days declared by the court.
When it applies: Filing deadlines, response periods, and compliance dates are not usually counted on court holidays. Always check whether the court is open before attending or assuming a deadline applies.
Docket
Court Administration
The official list or schedule of matters assigned to a particular judge or courtroom on a given day or period. Also refers to a court's overall caseload.
When it applies: If your matter is on the docket for a given day, you must attend unless formally excused. Check the court's online listings or contact the registry to confirm your matter is listed.
e-Filing
Court Administration
The online submission of court documents through the Federal Circuit and Family Court's Commonwealth Courts Portal (CCP) without attending a registry in person.
When it applies: e-Filing is the preferred method for most family law documents. You must create an account on the CCP before filing. Accepted file formats and maximum file sizes apply to all uploaded documents.
Enforcement Warrant
Court Administration
A court-issued warrant directing a third party, such as a sheriff or employer, to enforce a court order — for example, by seizing property or garnishing wages to satisfy a financial order.
When it applies: Used when a party refuses to comply with a property or financial order. Obtaining an enforcement warrant requires filing a separate application and proving non-compliance with the existing order.
Filing Deadline
Court Administration
The date by which a document must be received and accepted by the court registry to be considered filed in time. Missing a filing deadline may result in the document being refused or the party being in default.
When it applies: Filing deadlines are strictly enforced. If you are at risk of missing a deadline, you must apply to the court for an extension before the deadline passes, not after.
Garnishee Order
Court Administration
A court order requiring a third party who holds money for a judgment debtor — such as a bank or employer — to pay that money to the judgment creditor instead.
When it applies: Used to enforce unpaid financial orders in family law. The garnishee (e.g. the bank) is legally bound to comply once served with the order, regardless of the debtor's wishes.
Index
Court Administration
A document listing the contents of a court book or affidavit annexures in numbered order. Courts may require an index to be filed with large document bundles to assist the judge.
When it applies: Always include an index when filing multiple annexures or when directed to prepare a court book. Items should be numbered consecutively and described clearly in the index.
Judicial Registrar
Court Administration
A judicial officer of the Federal Circuit and Family Court who exercises delegated powers from a judge. Judicial Registrars conduct procedural hearings, consent orders, and some defended hearings.
When it applies: Many routine matters are heard by a Judicial Registrar rather than a judge. Their orders are as binding as orders made by a judge and can only be reviewed by applying for a review by a judge.

Judicial Registrars vs. Judges

Registrars manage case progression and may determine procedural or less complex interim matters; contested issues are typically referred to a Judge. Many self-represented parties first appear at a Case Assessment Conference or directions hearing.

Registrar orders are binding. Prepare as carefully as for a Judge; outcomes can be hard to overturn.

📌 Referral upward

If you believe the matter needs judicial determination, you can seek referral — explain why complexity or dispute warrants a Judge.

Leave of Court
Court Administration
Permission granted by a court to take a step in proceedings that would otherwise not be permitted — for example, to file a document out of time, adduce additional evidence, or amend an application.
When it applies: Leave is not automatic. You must apply for leave and provide reasons why it should be granted. Courts balance the interests of both parties when deciding whether to grant leave.
Matter Number
Court Administration
See Case Number. The unique identifier assigned to a family law matter upon filing, used to track and identify the proceedings throughout their life.
When it applies: Some registries use 'matter number' and 'case number' interchangeably. Always quote your matter number in full on every document and communication with the court.
Notice of Acting
Court Administration
A document filed by a solicitor to formally notify the court and other parties that they are now acting for a party in the proceedings.
When it applies: Must be filed promptly when a party engages a lawyer. Until a Notice of Acting is filed, a self-represented party remains responsible for all correspondence and court obligations.
Notice of Change of Solicitor
Court Administration
A court form filed when a party changes legal representation, notifying the court and opposing parties of the new solicitor's details.
When it applies: Must be filed before the new solicitor can correspond or appear on behalf of the party. The outgoing solicitor also has obligations regarding the handover of the file.
Official Seal
Court Administration
The formal stamp or seal of the court applied to certified court orders and sealed copies of documents. An order bearing the official seal is the enforceable version of the order.
When it applies: Always keep your sealed orders in a safe place. A sealed order is required to enforce compliance. If you lose your sealed orders, you can apply to the registry for a replacement sealed copy.
Overarching Purpose
Court Administration
The principle in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Act 2021 (Cth) requiring that family law proceedings be conducted in a way that is just and efficient — minimising delay and expense.
When it applies: The overarching purpose shapes how judges manage cases and make orders about costs, adjournments, and conduct. Parties who cause unnecessary delay or expense may face adverse costs orders.
Practice Direction
Court Administration
An administrative direction issued by the Chief Justice or a Senior Judge of the FCFCOA setting out procedural requirements, expectations, or guidance for parties and practitioners in family law matters.
When it applies: Practice Directions are binding on all parties. Failure to comply can result in documents being rejected or adverse orders. They are published on the FCFCOA website and updated regularly.
Registry Manager
Court Administration
The senior administrative officer responsible for managing a court registry, overseeing filing, record-keeping, and the day-to-day operation of the registry.
When it applies: Registry managers can assist with procedural queries but cannot give legal advice. They can direct you to the correct forms, explain filing processes, and confirm hearing details.
Sealed Order
Court Administration
A copy of a court order that has been stamped with the official court seal, making it the enforceable version of the order. Unsealed orders have no enforcement effect.
When it applies: Always request a sealed copy of every order made in your matter. You will need the sealed order to enforce compliance, register the order, or take any further court action based on the order.
Self-Represented Litigant (SRL)
Court Administration
A party who conducts their own case in court without legal representation. Also called a litigant in person.
When it applies: SRLs are held to the same procedural and evidentiary standards as represented parties. Courts may make allowances for lack of legal expertise in how they explain procedures, but cannot provide legal advice or overlook non-compliance with rules.
Taxation of Costs
Court Administration
The process by which a court officer (a taxing officer or registrar) assesses and determines the amount of legal costs payable under a costs order, if the parties cannot agree on the amount.
When it applies: If you receive a costs order in your favour, you may need to go through taxation to have the amount assessed if the other party disputes the sum. This is a separate court process with its own filing requirements.
Relevance
Evidence
A fundamental requirement for evidence to be admissible: the evidence must have a rational connection to a fact that is in issue in the proceedings. Evidence that does not assist in proving or disproving a material fact may be excluded as irrelevant.
When it applies: Assessed by the court whenever evidence is tendered or objected to. Family law courts have broad discretion in determining relevance and tend to admit evidence if there is any arguable connection to a material issue. However, evidence that is marginally probative and highly prejudicial may still be excluded.
Relevance Threshold
Evidence
The standard determining whether a piece of evidence has a sufficient connection to the issues in dispute to be admissible or worthy of inclusion. Evidence that does not meet the relevance threshold may be excluded or given no weight.
When it applies: Applied by courts when ruling on the admissibility of evidence and when assessing affidavits. Parties should ask, before including any material in their affidavit, whether it actually helps prove or disprove something that is genuinely in dispute.
Relocation
Parenting
The proposed move of a parent — and potentially the child — to a location that would significantly affect the child's current parenting arrangements and their relationship with the other parent. Relocation can be interstate or overseas.
When it applies: Where the other parent does not consent, the relocating parent must apply to the court for permission. Courts weigh the benefits of the move for the child against the impact on their relationship with the non-relocating parent. The child's best interests — not parental freedom — is the determinative consideration.

Why Relocation Cases Are Complex

Relocation cases arise when one parent seeks to move with a child in a way that substantially affects the other parent's time. There is no automatic right to relocate. The court reassesses the entire parenting arrangement through the best interests framework.

Key considerations include:

  • Impact on the child's relationship with the non-relocating parent
  • Practical travel arrangements
  • Motive and good faith
  • Educational and support opportunities
Factors supporting relocation
  • Genuine employment or family support
  • Good faith, not to exclude other parent
  • Workable contact arrangements proposed
  • Child's expressed wishes (age-dependent)
Factors against relocation
  • Significant impact on other parent's relationship
  • Motive appears to exclude other parent
  • No workable contact alternative
  • Child settled in current school/community

Relocation cases are highly fact-specific and often finely balanced. Early legal advice is strongly recommended.

Return of Subpoena
Evidence
The compliance deadline by which a party or third party served with a subpoena must produce the required documents to the court registry.
When it applies: On the return date, documents are lodged with the registry and both parties are typically given the opportunity to inspect them. If a party objects to production on privilege or other grounds, they must do so before the return date. Late production may require a court order.

The Return of Subpoena Process

Return of subpoena refers to the compliance deadline and process for document production. On the return date, documents are lodged with the registry. Both parties can then inspect and uplift the documents with court permission.

If a third party objects to producing certain documents — on confidentiality, privilege, or relevance grounds — they must file a notice of objection before the return date. Uninspected documents remain with the registry unless uplifted.

💡 Uplift and review promptly

Once documents are returned to the registry, apply to inspect and uplift them promptly. Review the contents carefully — subpoenaed documents often contain far more relevant material than anticipated and can significantly shape your case strategy.

Return of Subpoena — What Happens

Return of subpoena refers to the process by which a person or organisation that has been subpoenaed produces documents to the court. The documents are filed with the registry and parties are notified of their availability for inspection.

Parties must inspect returned documents within the timeframe allowed by the court. You cannot simply assume the documents contain what you hoped — review them carefully and identify anything relevant before the next hearing.

📌 Inspect promptly

Register to inspect as soon as you receive notification that documents have been returned. Subpoenaed documents sometimes contain material that requires urgent action — new allegations, contradictory records, or important corroboration.

Relocation Application
Parenting
A formal application to the court for orders permitting a parent to relocate a child — interstate or overseas — over the other parent's objection. The applicant must demonstrate that relocation is in the child's best interests.
When it applies: Filed when a parent wishes to move with a child and cannot obtain the other parent's agreement. Relocation applications are often urgent and may require interim travel prohibition orders to prevent the child being removed while proceedings are on foot.
Relocation Objection
Parenting
A formal challenge by one parent to the other parent's proposal to relocate with the child to a different area, whether interstate or internationally. The objecting parent must file an application to restrain the relocation.
When it applies: Filed promptly when a parent intends to relocate with a child and the other parent does not consent. Courts will not permit relocation over objection without a hearing. Where relocation is imminent, an urgent injunction or travel prohibition order may be needed to preserve the status quo while proceedings are on foot.
Relocation Urgency
Parenting
A claim that a proposed relocation must occur quickly — for example, due to employment, housing, or safety reasons — requiring the court to consider the application on an accelerated timetable.
When it applies: Raised in urgent listing applications and ex parte applications where delay would defeat the purpose of the relocation or cause significant harm. Courts will accelerate relocation proceedings where genuine urgency is established but are alert to urgency claims that are strategically motivated.
Reserved Judgment
Court Process
A judgment that is not delivered at the conclusion of a hearing but is instead "reserved" by the judge, who takes time to consider the evidence and write a comprehensive decision to be delivered at a later date.
When it applies: Common in complex or lengthy matters. The period of reservation varies — it can be days or months. Interim orders typically remain in force while a judgment is reserved. Parties may enquire about the status of a reserved judgment if delivery has been significantly delayed.
Rice & Asplund Rule
Court Process
A legal principle established in Rice v Asplund (1979) which provides that a court will not reconsider final parenting orders unless there has been a significant change in circumstances since the orders were made. The rule aims to promote stability for children and prevent repeated litigation.
When it applies: Applies to any application to vary or reopen final parenting orders. Before the court will rehear the matter, the applicant must first satisfy the Rice & Asplund threshold — failure to do so will result in the application being dismissed without a full hearing.

What Is Rice v Asplund?

It's a landmark Australian family law case that established a rule: you cannot keep re-litigating parenting orders unless there has been a significant change in circumstances. Courts do not want constant re-opening of parenting arrangements. Stability for children comes first.

🧠 What Is the "Rice & Asplund Rule"?

Before a court will reconsider final parenting orders, the applicant must show:

  1. A material change in circumstances, AND
  2. That it is in the child's best interests to reopen the case.

If you fail at step 1 → the court won't even properly rehear the matter. It acts like a legal gatekeeper test.

📌 What Counts as a "Material Change"?

✓ May qualify
  • Serious new family violence
  • Child safety concerns
  • Relocation plans
  • Long-term non-compliance with orders
  • Significant change in child's needs
  • Evidence not available at original hearing
✗ Usually doesn't qualify
  • "I don't like the orders anymore"
  • Minor disputes
  • Routine parenting disagreements
  • Situations already considered in the original case

⚖️ Why It Matters

The court's priority is stability for children, preventing repeated litigation, and protecting children from ongoing parental conflict. If courts allowed endless re-opening of orders, parenting cases would never end.

🏛 Where It Applies

Applies to
  • Final parenting orders under the Family Law Act
  • Applications to vary existing parenting arrangements
Does not automatically apply to
  • Interim orders (though similar logic can influence decisions)
🧭 Practical Strategy Insight

If you want to change parenting orders, the first legal hurdle is not "best interests" — it's proving a substantial change since the last final orders. Many self-represented litigants miss this and file variation applications that get dismissed early.

Respondent
Court Process
The party who responds to an application in family law proceedings — the person the application has been made against. In appeals, the respondent is the party defending the original orders.
When it applies: Identified from the moment an application is filed and served. The respondent must file a response within the prescribed timeframe or risk having orders made in their absence. Even if the respondent agrees with some of the applicant's requested orders, filing a response ensures their position is formally recorded.
Retaliatory Allegation
High Conflict
An allegation made in response to a previous complaint or court filing by the other party, appearing designed to neutralise that complaint rather than raising a genuinely independent concern.
When it applies: Courts assess whether allegations have been made in direct response to the other party's filings. Where retaliatory patterns are identified, courts may give the allegations reduced weight and may make adverse comments about the party's litigation conduct. Genuine concerns should be raised promptly, not strategically timed.
Revocation
Court Process
The formal cancellation of an existing court order — most commonly an AVO, parenting order, or other family law order. An order can only be revoked by another court order, not by private agreement between parties.
When it applies: An AVO can be revoked if circumstances have changed significantly — for example, if the parties have genuinely reconciled and the protected person consents and no longer fears harm. For parenting orders, revocation requires demonstrating a significant change in circumstances since the original order was made. Parties cannot simply agree to ignore an existing order — doing so while the order remains in force may expose the defendant to criminal liability.

Applying for Revocation

To revoke an AVO, both parties typically attend court and the protected person must indicate they no longer require the protection. A magistrate will assess whether revocation is appropriate — they are not obliged to revoke simply because the protected person consents.

For family law orders, a revocation application is made to the FCFCOA using an Initiating Application or Application in a Case. You must file supporting material demonstrating the changed circumstances that justify revisiting the order.

Courts are cautious about revoking protective orders, particularly where there is a history of family violence. If you are the protected person and feel pressured to consent to revocation, you can seek independent legal advice before attending court.

Risk Assessment
Protection
A structured professional evaluation of the nature and level of risk posed to a child or party. It considers factors such as history of violence, mental health, substance use, and the capacity of each parent to protect the child.
When it applies: Conducted by family consultants, independent psychologists, or child protection workers when safety concerns are raised in parenting proceedings. Findings inform the court's decisions about whether protective orders are needed, whether supervised time is appropriate, and what conditions should be attached to parenting orders.

How Risk Is Assessed

Risk assessment evaluates the likelihood and nature of harm to the child — history, behaviour patterns, substance use, mental health, and protective capacity. Courts look forward as well as back.

Assessments inform interim and final orders.

High-weight risk factors
  • Prior family violence findings
  • Child protection involvement
  • Substance misuse / mental health concerns
  • Hostile or controlling behaviour
Mitigating / lower-risk indicators
  • Treatment or course completion
  • Stable environment
  • Demonstrated protective capacity
  • Consistent compliance with orders
Risk of Emotional Harm
Protection
An allegation that a child is at risk of psychological or emotional damage as a result of a parent's behaviour, the parenting arrangements, or exposure to conflict. Emotional harm can occur without physical violence.
When it applies: Courts must consider risk of emotional harm when assessing parenting orders. Relevant factors include exposure to family violence, a parent's mental health, substance use, and the quality of the parent-child relationship. Expert evidence from a psychologist or family consultant often assists in assessing this risk.
Risk of Physical Harm
Protection
An allegation that a child or party faces a risk of bodily injury or physical harm. It may relate to past incidents of physical violence or a reasonably apprehended future risk.
When it applies: One of the primary safety concerns courts must address in parenting proceedings. Where risk of physical harm is raised, the court may impose supervised time, restrict contact, or make urgent interim protective orders. Evidence of specific incidents, injuries, medical records, and police reports are all relevant.
Routine Disruption
Parenting
Disturbance to a child's established daily patterns — including sleep, meals, school, sport, and social activities — caused by changes in parenting arrangements or the behaviour of one or both parents during proceedings.
When it applies: Courts consider routine disruption as a factor in assessing the impact of proposed parenting changes on the child's wellbeing. A proposal that significantly disrupts established routines requires justification. Evidence of how existing routines support the child's development strengthens arguments for preserving the current arrangements.
s47
Safety Plan
Protection
A documented personal strategy developed with the help of a domestic violence service, counsellor, or legal professional that identifies warning signs of escalating danger and maps out practical steps to protect yourself and your children.
When it applies: A safety plan typically covers: identifying warning signs that the situation is becoming dangerous; creating a code word with a trusted person to signal that help is needed; knowing in advance which police station or service to contact; having documents (passport, birth certificates, medication) and essentials ready to take quickly; planning a safe exit route from the home; and identifying a safe place to go. Courts and domestic violence services encourage all people experiencing family violence to have a safety plan even if proceedings have commenced. A safety plan does not substitute for legal protection — it complements an AVO or family violence order.

Creating Your Safety Plan

1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) can help you create a safety plan over the phone, 24 hours a day. They can also connect you with local services and accommodation if needed.

Keep your safety plan in a location the other party cannot access — not in a shared email account or cloud storage. A trusted friend, family member, or your lawyer should also have a copy.

Update your plan if circumstances change — new address, new phone number, changes to court orders. A safety plan is a living document, not a one-time exercise.

School Attendance Impact
Parenting
The effect of the parenting dispute, arrangements, or conflict on a child's school attendance, academic performance, and engagement with their education.
When it applies: Relevant in parenting proceedings, particularly where changeover logistics, travel, or conflict affect a child's ability to attend school consistently. Evidence from school records, teacher reports, or a family consultant can establish the link between parenting arrangements and school outcomes.
School Continuity Argument
Parenting
A submission that a child should remain at their current school to preserve educational continuity, friendships, and routine. It is often raised in relocation matters or disputes about change of residence.
When it applies: Courts give weight to school continuity, particularly where a child is settled, performing well, and has established social connections. The argument is stronger for older children and where the school change would occur at a disruptive point in the child's educational journey.
Schooling Orders
Parenting
Court orders specifically determining which school a child will attend and who has authority to make decisions about the child's education. They resolve disputes about schooling as a major long-term parenting issue where parents cannot agree.
When it applies: Applied for when separated parents dispute their child's schooling. Courts consider the child's current schooling, proximity of schools to each parent, academic needs, social connections, and the child's own preferences when determining schooling disputes.
Sealed Orders
Orders
Court orders that have been formally stamped with the court's seal by the registry, confirming they are authorised, final, and issued by the court. The sealed copy is the legally operative document — draft or unsigned versions have no legal effect.
When it applies: Required whenever a party needs to enforce orders, take action pursuant to orders (such as a property transfer), or provide evidence of existing orders to a third party such as a school, employer, or government agency. Parties should retain their sealed orders and keep them in a safe place.
Section 65Y
Legislation
Section 65Y of the Family Law Act 1975, which creates the offence of taking a child from Australia, or refusing to deliver a child to a person entitled to custody or access under an Australian order, where an overseas order or agreement applies.
When it applies: s 65Y is part of the international child abduction framework in the Family Law Act. It works alongside the Hague Convention provisions to prevent the removal of children from Australia in contravention of court orders. Related: Hague Convention, s 65Z, international relocation.
Section 65Z
Legislation
Section 65Z of the Family Law Act 1975, which criminalises the taking of a child outside Australia in contravention of a parenting order, or aiding and abetting such removal.
When it applies: Under s 65Z, a person who takes or sends a child outside Australia in breach of a parenting order, or assists another person to do so, commits an offence. The penalty is imprisonment. Section 65Z applies whether or not the destination country is a signatory to the Hague Convention. It is the criminal law complement to the civil remedies available through the Hague Convention and the location/recovery order framework. Related: s 65Y, Hague Convention, recovery order.
Section 79
Legislation
Section 79 of the Family Law Act 1975 — the primary provision empowering the FCFCOA to make orders altering the property interests of the parties to a marriage. It is the legal foundation of almost all property settlement proceedings for married couples.
When it applies: s 79 gives the court a broad discretion to make such order as it considers just and equitable with respect to the property of the parties. This includes transferring property between parties, vesting interests, ordering the sale of assets, and adjusting superannuation interests. The process under s 79 requires the court to: identify and value the asset pool; assess contributions; consider future needs; and ask whether the proposed orders are just and equitable. For de facto couples, the equivalent provision is s 90SM. Related: property settlement, just and equitable, contributions, future needs.
Section 90B
Legislation
Section 90B of the Family Law Act 1975, which provides the legal basis for a financial agreement made by parties to a marriage before the marriage (a pre-nuptial or pre-marital agreement). A section 90B agreement can exclude the court's jurisdiction to make property orders.
When it applies: To be binding under s 90B, the agreement must: be in writing and signed; each party must have received independent legal advice before signing; a certificate of independent advice must be attached; and the agreement must not have been set aside by a court. The grounds for setting aside a financial agreement are set out in s 90K. Related: binding financial agreement, s 90C, s 90D.
Section 90C
Legislation
Section 90C of the Family Law Act 1975, which provides the legal basis for a financial agreement made by parties to a marriage during the marriage (while still married and not separated). A section 90C agreement deals with how property will be divided if the marriage breaks down.
When it applies: A s 90C agreement requires the same formalities as a s 90B agreement — written, signed, independent legal advice, and certificates. It is used where parties wish to reorganise their finances during the marriage — for example, to protect a family business or an inheritance. Related: binding financial agreement, s 90B, s 90D.
Section 90D
Legislation
Section 90D of the Family Law Act 1975, which provides the legal basis for a financial agreement made by parties to a marriage after separation (or after divorce). A section 90D agreement deals with property matters following the end of the marriage.
When it applies: A s 90D agreement is the post-separation alternative to applying for consent orders through the court. It does not require court approval. The same strict formality requirements apply as for s 90B and s 90C agreements. For many couples, consent orders are preferable to s 90D agreements because they receive judicial scrutiny and provide more certainty. Related: binding financial agreement, consent orders, s 90B.
Section 90SB
Legislation
Section 90SB of the Family Law Act 1975, which defines a de facto financial cause — the threshold condition that must be met before the court can exercise jurisdiction to make property orders in relation to a de facto relationship.
When it applies: Under s 90SB, the court must be satisfied of at least one of: the de facto relationship lasted at least 2 years; there is a child of the de facto relationship; one party made substantial contributions and failure to make an order would cause serious injustice; or the relationship is or was registered under state or territory law. This gate-keeping provision means the court cannot intervene in brief or casual relationships without special circumstances. Related: property settlement, de facto relationship.
Serious Contravention
Orders
A breach of a court order that is of significant severity — typically involving intentional, repeated, or harmful non-compliance, such as withholding a child over an extended period or repeated defiance of court authority.
When it applies: Courts distinguish serious contraventions from technical or minor breaches. A finding of serious contravention can result in the most significant enforcement consequences available to the court, including imprisonment. Evidence of intent, repetition, and impact on the child or other party is central to establishing serious contravention.
Service
Court Process
The formal delivery of court documents to another party in a manner prescribed by the court's rules. Service ensures that the other party has proper notice of the proceedings and the documents filed. Proof of service is usually required before the court will proceed.
When it applies: Required at every stage of proceedings when documents are filed. Personal service (direct delivery to the person) is required for initiating documents. Subsequent documents may generally be served by email or post to the party's address for service. Substituted service may be ordered if a party cannot be located.
Service of Documents
Court Process
The formal process of notifying a party of court proceedings by delivering documents in a manner prescribed or approved by the court. Most initiating documents must be personally served.
When it applies: Mandatory before a matter can proceed. Improper or defective service may invalidate steps or result in adjournment. File an affidavit of service once service is effected.

Service of Court Documents

Formally notifies a party of proceedings. Most initiating documents must be personally served. Improper service may invalidate steps or delay hearings.

Once served, file an affidavit of service. Where personal service is impractical, apply for substituted service before attempting any alternative.

💡 Use a process server if needed

If the other party is evading service or personal service creates a safety risk, a professional process server can serve documents on your behalf.

Service Requirements in Family Law

Service formally notifies a party of proceedings or of documents filed. Improper service may invalidate procedural steps or delay hearings. Strict rules govern how and when documents must be served.

Personal service (handing documents directly to the person) is required for certain documents such as Initiating Applications. Substituted service may be ordered where standard service is impractical.

💡 Always get proof of service

Keep an affidavit of service for every document served. If the other party later claims they were not served, your affidavit of service is your evidence. Disputes about service are easily avoided with proper documentation.

Service Affidavit
Court Process
An affidavit sworn by the person who served a document on another party, providing sworn evidence of how, when, where, and on whom the document was served. It constitutes formal proof of service for court purposes.
When it applies: Required before the court will hear a matter on which the other party may not have appeared, or where service is in dispute. Particularly important in applications for enforcement, recovery orders, and divorce proceedings, where proper service is a pre-condition to the court's ability to act.
Settlement Proposal
Dispute Resolution
A written offer made by one party to the other setting out the terms on which they are willing to resolve all or part of the proceedings. When marked "without prejudice," the proposal and any responses generally cannot be disclosed to the court if negotiations fail.
When it applies: Can be made at any stage of proceedings. Making a reasonable settlement proposal and having the other party reject it unreasonably may be relevant to any costs order the court later makes. A settlement proposal that is accepted is then formalised as consent orders or a financial agreement.
Settlement Resistance
High Conflict
A pattern of refusing to engage meaningfully in settlement negotiations or ADR processes, without genuine legal justification. It may reflect a party's desire to continue litigation for reasons unrelated to the merits of their case.
When it applies: Can attract adverse cost consequences. Courts expect parties to make genuine attempts to resolve matters outside of trial. Unreasonable refusal to negotiate, reject a reasonable offer, or engage in court-ordered ADR is conduct the court considers when exercising its costs discretion.
Shared Care
Parenting
A parenting arrangement in which a child spends substantial time living with both parents, though not necessarily equal time. Shared care recognises the child's need for meaningful relationships with both parents while allowing flexibility based on each family's circumstances.
When it applies: Considered in all parenting matters where both parents are seeking meaningful involvement in the child's life. Courts assess whether shared care is practicable and in the child's best interests, having regard to the parents' proximity, work arrangements, the child's school and activities, and the quality of the co-parenting relationship.
Short-Form Judgment
Court Process
A brief oral or written judgment delivered by a judicial officer at the conclusion of an interim hearing, summarising the key reasoning and orders without full written reasons. Extended reasons may be provided later if requested.
When it applies: Common at the conclusion of interim hearings where time is limited. Parties should listen carefully and take notes. If the reasoning is unclear or inadequate, a party may request fuller reasons, which may be relevant to any appeal. Short-form judgments are binding and take effect immediately unless stayed.
Single Expert
Evidence
An expert witness jointly appointed by the parties (or by the court) to provide an independent opinion on a contested matter. Using a single expert avoids a 'battle of experts' and reduces cost.
When it applies: Under r 7.04 of the Family Law Rules 2021, the court may direct that expert evidence on a particular issue be given by one expert only, appointed by agreement between the parties or by the court. The single expert's report is provided to all parties and the expert may be cross-examined at hearing. Single experts are common for property valuations and superannuation valuations. For parenting matters, the family report prepared by a court-appointed family consultant performs a similar function. Related: expert witness, family report.

Single experts in family violence matters

In family law proceedings where AVO allegations intersect with parenting disputes, the court may appoint a single expert — often a psychologist or family consultant — to provide an independent assessment of risk, the child's needs, or a parent's capacity. This replaces the older model where each party retained their own competing expert.

The single expert's report is provided to all parties and the court. Parties may submit written questions to the expert before the report is finalised. The expert may be cross-examined at hearing, but the court gives their evidence significant weight as an independent source.

Sole Parental Responsibility
Parenting
A court order giving one parent sole authority to make decisions about a child's major long-term issues — including education, health, and religion — without needing to consult the other parent. It is ordered where joint decision-making is not in the child's best interests.
When it applies: Considered where there is a history of family violence, abuse, high conflict, or where meaningful consultation between parents is not possible or safe. The court must be satisfied that the child's welfare is better served by removing the obligation to consult. It does not automatically affect the amount of time the child spends with the other parent.

Sole vs. Shared Parental Responsibility

Sole parental responsibility gives one parent exclusive authority over major long-term decisions — schooling, health, religion — without any obligation to consult the other parent. It may be ordered where conflict, violence or inability to cooperate makes shared decision-making unsafe or impractical.

It does not automatically determine time arrangements — a child can still spend significant time with the non-decision-making parent under a sole parental responsibility order.

Grounds supporting sole responsibility
  • History of family violence
  • Entrenched conflict making cooperation impossible
  • History of withholding consent to medical treatment
  • Risk of unilateral decisions harming the child
What it doesn't affect
  • Time spent with either parent
  • Day-to-day parenting decisions
  • The child's relationship with either parent
Speculative Statement
Evidence
A claim in an affidavit or submission that is not grounded in direct knowledge or objective evidence, but rather in assumption, inference, or opinion. Courts give speculative statements minimal weight.
When it applies: Affidavits should be confined to facts within the deponent's direct knowledge. Statements such as 'I believe he must have...' or 'She probably intends to...' are speculative and should be avoided. Courts may expressly note when affidavit material is speculative in reducing its weight.
Spend Time With Order
Parenting
A parenting order specifying that a child spends time with a particular parent or person. Previously called an 'access order' or 'contact order'. A spend time with order sets out when and how the child sees the parent they do not live with.
When it applies: Spend time with orders can specify: regular fortnightly arrangements; school holiday time; special days (birthdays, Father's Day, Mother's Day); and any conditions around handover. Orders can be as specific or general as the parties agree or the court determines. Courts prefer workable, detailed orders that minimise future dispute. Time arrangements are driven by what is in the best interests of the child, not the preferences of either parent. Related: live with order, changeover, parenting order.
Spousal Maintenance
Orders
Financial support paid by one party to the other after separation, distinct from child support. Spousal maintenance is based on one party's inability to adequately support themselves and the other party's capacity to pay.
When it applies: An application for spousal maintenance must satisfy a two-part test: the applicant must establish they cannot adequately support themselves, and the respondent must have the capacity to contribute to their support. Factors include: age, health, earning capacity, the standard of living during the marriage, and the effect of the relationship on earning capacity. Maintenance can be periodic (weekly or monthly payments) or lump sum. It is separate from — and may be adjusted in light of — the property settlement. Related: future needs, property settlement, child support.

Urgent Spousal Maintenance

Courts can make urgent maintenance orders where a party has insufficient funds to meet their immediate needs pending a full hearing. These interim orders are made on an expedited basis and can be sought quickly after separation.

The threshold for urgent maintenance is immediate financial need — for example, inability to pay rent, buy food, or meet children's school fees. Gather evidence of your expenses and the other party's income.

Spousal maintenance is tax-neutral for the payer and recipient in Australia. It does not affect child support calculations directly, but it may affect the court's view of a party's capacity to pay child support.

Stability Argument
Parenting
A submission that maintaining the child's current arrangements — including home, school, community, and relationships — provides important continuity and should be preserved rather than disrupted by proposed changes.
When it applies: Commonly raised in relocation matters and change of residence applications. Courts give genuine weight to stability arguments, particularly for younger children and where the existing arrangements have been in place for a significant period. The argument must be balanced against the benefits of the proposed change.
Stalking
Protection
A course of conduct involving repeated following, surveillance, or monitoring of another person that causes that person to fear for their safety. Stalking is a criminal offence in NSW under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 and is a common ground for an AVO.
When it applies: Stalking can involve physically following someone, loitering near their home or workplace, monitoring their social media, tracking their location through technology, repeatedly driving past their house, sending unsolicited gifts, or using third parties to gather information about them. It does not require physical confrontation. A single incident can be stalking if sufficiently serious. Courts will consider the pattern of behaviour and its impact on the victim. Related: intimidation, harassment, AVO.

Digital Stalking and Technology-Facilitated Abuse

Technology-facilitated stalking is increasingly common. This includes tracking apps installed on phones or cars, repeatedly accessing shared accounts, monitoring social media activity, and using location data from children's devices.

If you suspect you are being tracked digitally, seek assistance from a domestic violence service who can arrange a phone safety check. Evidence of digital stalking — screenshots, location data, access logs — is valuable in court proceedings.

In family law proceedings, evidence of stalking behaviour is highly relevant to parenting matters. Courts treat stalking of a co-parent very seriously, as it creates an environment of fear that directly affects children.

Standard of Proof
Court Process
The level of certainty required by the court.
When it applies: AVO matters use the civil standard — the balance of probabilities — meaning the court must be satisfied that it is more likely than not that the conduct occurred and that an order is needed. This is a lower threshold than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
Statement in Support
Evidence
A written document filed alongside an AVO application setting out the factual basis for seeking the order. It describes the incidents of violence, harassment, or threatening conduct that justify the court granting protection.
When it applies: The statement in support is the foundation of your AVO application. It should be written in chronological order, describe specific incidents (dates, times, locations, what was said or done), explain how the conduct made you feel, and state why you fear for your future safety. Courts are not looking for legal argument — they need factual narrative. For police applications, the statement is prepared by the police officer based on your account. For private applications, you prepare it yourself. Related: affidavit, applicant.

Writing an Effective Statement in Support

Be specific. 'He has been violent many times' is much weaker than 'On 14 March 2024 at approximately 9pm, he grabbed me by the arm, pushed me against the kitchen wall, and said I would regret calling police.' Courts need facts, not general descriptions.

Include the most recent incidents and the most serious incidents, even if they occurred some time ago. Explain what has changed recently that has increased your fear. Courts want to understand the current risk, not just historical conduct.

If English is not your first language, you are entitled to an interpreter. Legal Aid or a domestic violence service can help you prepare your statement. Do not let language barriers prevent you from seeking protection.

Statement of Truth
Evidence
A declaration signed by a party confirming that the contents of a document are true and accurate to the best of their knowledge and belief. It is a formal legal obligation, not merely an acknowledgement.
When it applies: Required on financial statements, certain affidavits, and other prescribed documents in family law proceedings. Providing false information in a document signed with a statement of truth can constitute contempt of court, perjury, or fraud, all of which carry serious legal consequences including criminal prosecution.
Security for Costs
Costs
An order requiring a party (usually the applicant) to deposit a sum of money with the court as security against the possibility that they will not be able to satisfy a costs order made against them.
When it applies: Sought where a party has reason to believe the other party would be unable to pay a costs order — for example, where the other party is overseas, of limited means, or has a history of non-compliance. Courts exercise this discretion carefully to avoid preventing access to justice.

Security for Costs Applications

Security for costs requires a party to provide financial assurance for potential adverse costs. It is used where there is genuine concern that a costs order could not be enforced — because the other party is overseas, has no assets, or has a history of avoiding financial obligations.

Courts apply this remedy cautiously. An order for security that is set too high can effectively prevent a party from pursuing their case — which itself raises access to justice concerns.

📌 Rarely used in pure parenting matters

Security for costs is more common in financial and property proceedings than in parenting matters. In parenting cases, the focus is usually on the child's welfare rather than cost recovery — but it remains a tool in appropriate circumstances.

The court considers the likelihood of a costs order, the applicant's financial position, and whether requiring security would effectively shut out a legitimate claim.

⚠️ Can be used oppressively

Security for costs applications are sometimes made tactically to impose a financial burden on a weaker party. Courts are alert to this and will not grant security where it would effectively end legitimate proceedings.

Settlement Conference
Court Process
A court-facilitated event at which a judicial officer or registrar assists the parties to negotiate a resolution, often by identifying key issues and testing the strength of each party's position.
When it applies: Typically offered before final hearing as a final opportunity to resolve proceedings without a contested hearing. The judicial officer may express preliminary views on the likely outcome, which can assist parties in assessing the merits of settling versus proceeding.

Settlement Conferences — What to Expect

A settlement conference facilitates negotiation with judicial guidance. It may narrow issues or resolve the case entirely. The judicial officer is not the trial judge — they may speak frankly about the strengths and weaknesses of each party's position to assist settlement.

What is said during a settlement conference is generally not disclosed to the trial judge if the matter does not settle. This confidentiality encourages candid discussion.

💡 Come with authority to settle

Know your bottom line before attending. The most productive settlement conferences involve parties who are genuinely prepared to consider realistic compromise. If the judicial officer expresses a preliminary view, listen carefully — it reflects how the case might be decided at trial.

Settlement conferences are not binding, but a judge or registrar may use a shuttle approach and indicate likely outcomes if the matter proceeds to hearing — which often focuses minds on settlement.

💡 Come with authority to settle

Bring a clear sense of your bottom line. Settlement conferences move quickly. If you need to refer every proposal back to someone before deciding, the opportunity passes. Know what you will and won't accept before you walk in.

Status Quo Principle
Court Process
The general tendency of courts, at the interim stage, to maintain existing arrangements for children rather than making significant changes before full evidence is heard. Stability and continuity are given weight in interim decision-making.
When it applies: Applied when courts are making interim parenting orders. The party seeking to change established arrangements carries the burden of showing why change is needed before the final hearing. The status quo is not preserved at all costs — safety concerns or significant changes in circumstances can displace it.

How Status Quo Influences Outcomes

Courts often give weight to existing stable arrangements. If a child has been living under a particular structure for a significant period without issue, the court may hesitate to disrupt it. However, status quo does not override safety concerns.

Delay in challenging arrangements can weaken later objections.

⚠️ Act early if arrangements aren't working

If you accept interim arrangements you're not satisfied with and allow them to continue for months, you may find the court treats them as the effective status quo at final hearing. Challenge unsatisfactory arrangements promptly and document your objections.

Summary Dismissal
Court Process
The dismissal of a case or application at an early stage where it is found to lack reasonable prospects of success, without proceeding to a full hearing.
When it applies: Applied sparingly. Courts are reluctant to deprive parties of a hearing unless the case is clearly hopeless, lacks jurisdiction, or constitutes an abuse of process.

Summary Dismissal

Dismissal at an early stage where a case lacks reasonable prospects of success, without a full hearing. The threshold is deliberately high — courts are cautious about dismissing cases before evidence is fully tested.

It is most commonly applied to clearly hopeless applications — where even on the applicant's own case, the orders sought could not legally be made, or where the application is an abuse of process.

📌 Distinguish from strike out

Summary dismissal disposes of the entire application. Strike out removes a specific pleading. Both curb abuse of process and unnecessary litigation costs.

📌 High bar, but worth knowing

If the other party has brought a clearly meritless application designed to harass, summary dismissal combined with a costs order is a powerful response. Get legal advice before applying — the court takes a dim view of summary dismissal applications that themselves lack merit.

Strike Out
Court Process
A court order removing specific paragraphs, parts or entire documents from proceedings where they are defective, irrelevant, scandalous, vexatious or an abuse of process.
When it applies: Applied where affidavit material contains content that should not be before the court. Proper, focused drafting reduces strike-out risk significantly.

Strike Out Applications

Strike out removes defective or inappropriate pleadings — irrelevant, scandalous, vexatious material, or an abuse of process. It targets specific paragraphs or documents rather than disposing of an entire application.

Proper drafting reduces risk: argument, character attacks, irrelevant history, and naked opinion are vulnerable.

⚠️ Common targets

Unrelated past misconduct, character attacks irrelevant to parenting, hearsay from unnamed sources, inflammatory language. Keep your affidavit tight and relevant.

💡 Drafting to survive scrutiny

Every paragraph should state a fact within your personal knowledge that is relevant to the issues in dispute. Courts need facts, not opinions about the other parent.

Substantial and Significant Time
Parenting
A legislative concept describing a level of parenting time that is less than equal time but still meaningful and substantial. It requires that a child spend time with the non-primary parent during weekdays, weekends, school holidays, and on special occasions — ensuring involvement in the child's routine daily life, not just recreational contact.
When it applies: Considered where equal time is not reasonably practicable or in the child's best interests, but the court still finds that meaningful involvement by both parents is appropriate. The focus is on quality and regularity of involvement across different types of time.

What "Substantial and Significant" Means

If equal shared parental responsibility applies, the court must consider whether substantial and significant time is appropriate. This includes time during:

  • Weekdays
  • Weekends
  • School holidays
  • Special events

It requires meaningful involvement in the child's routine life — not merely recreational contact. Practical feasibility and child stability are central to the analysis.

📌 Key distinction from equal time

Equal time means 50/50. Substantial and significant time might be 6 nights per fortnight, alternate weekends plus one weeknight, or similar — less than half, but genuinely meaningful.

Stay Order
Orders
A court order that temporarily suspends the operation of another court order, typically pending the outcome of an appeal or review. A stay preserves the status quo while the appeal is determined.
When it applies: Applied for urgently once a party announces an intention to appeal, where immediate compliance would cause irreversible harm. The court balances the risk of harm if the stay is refused against the risk of harm if it is granted. A stay is not automatic and must be applied for specifically.

Obtaining a Stay Order

To obtain a stay, the applicant must demonstrate:

  • An arguable case on appeal
  • That harm may occur if the order proceeds
  • That the balance of convenience favours suspension
📌 A stay is not a win

It only delays enforcement while the appeal is heard. Applying for a stay without a strong underlying appeal can damage your credibility.

When Stay Orders Are Granted

A stay order suspends the operation of a court order, often pending appeal. The applicant must demonstrate that there is an arguable case on appeal, that harm may occur if the order is not stayed, and that the balance of convenience favours suspension.

Stays are discretionary and not automatically granted. Courts are reluctant to stay parenting orders where a child's stability may be disrupted by the stay itself.

⚠️ Act quickly

A stay application should be made promptly — once an order has been acted upon (e.g. a child has relocated), courts are less willing to reverse the status quo. File your stay application at the same time as, or immediately after, filing your appeal.

Subpoena
Evidence
A court-issued document requiring a named person or organisation to produce specified documents to the court, or to attend court to give evidence, or both. It is a compulsory legal process — non-compliance without valid reason is contempt of court.
When it applies: Used to obtain documents from third parties such as schools, hospitals, police, child protection agencies, and financial institutions. A party must obtain leave of the court before issuing a subpoena. The person or body served may apply to have the subpoena set aside if it is oppressive, irrelevant, or unduly broad.

How Subpoenas Work in Family Law

A subpoena compels production of documents or attendance to give evidence. It is frequently used to obtain school records, medical records, police reports, child protection notes, and financial records. Non-compliance without valid reason is contempt of court.

A party must obtain leave of the court before issuing a subpoena. The recipient may apply to have it set aside if it is oppressive, irrelevant, or unduly broad.

Common subpoena targets
  • Schools and childcare centres
  • GPs, hospitals, and psychologists
  • Police and child protection agencies
  • Banks and financial institutions
⚠️ Grounds to challenge
  • Too broad or unduly burdensome
  • Not relevant to the issues in dispute
  • Issued for improper purpose (fishing)
  • Privilege (e.g. legal professional privilege)
Substantial Breach
Orders
A significant failure to comply with a court order that materially affects the other party or the children — for example, repeatedly withholding a child or failing to transfer major assets as ordered.
When it applies: Courts treat substantial breaches seriously. Consequences can include make-up time for missed parenting time, financial compensation, community service, or in serious cases imprisonment. Evidence of the specific breach, its impact, and any pattern of repetition is essential in a contravention application.
Superannuation Splitting
Orders
The process of dividing the superannuation interest of one or both parties as part of a property settlement. Superannuation is treated as property under the Family Law Act 1975 and can be split between parties, usually through a superannuation splitting order.
When it applies: Superannuation cannot be accessed before preservation age — it remains in the super fund of the receiving spouse until they too reach preservation age. A superannuation splitting order (or agreement) instructs the trustee of the fund to create a separate interest for the other party, or to roll over a specified amount. It does not provide immediate cash. Not all super funds accept splits from the same fund — in some cases a rollover to a new fund is required. Related: property settlement, consent orders, asset pool.

Valuing Superannuation

Superannuation must be formally valued before it can be split. For accumulation funds, the balance shown on the most recent statement is usually sufficient. For defined benefit funds, a formal actuarial valuation may be required — request a 'family law value' from the fund trustee.

The process involves serving documents on the super fund trustee (called a 'trustee joinder' or 'notice to trustee'). Allow several months for the fund to respond — this is often a bottleneck in settlements.

Superannuation splitting is not always the right approach. Depending on the parties' ages and overall asset pool, offsetting (one party keeps more super while the other takes more equity in the home) may be more practical.

Supervised Time
Parenting
An arrangement in which a child spends time with a parent only in the presence of a specified supervisor — either a nominated trusted adult or a professional at a contact centre. The supervisor's role is to ensure the child's safety during the visit.
When it applies: Ordered when the court has concerns about a child's safety during unsupervised contact — for example, due to allegations of abuse, family violence, substance misuse, or serious mental health concerns affecting parenting capacity. May be an interim measure pending further assessment or a longer-term protective order.

Supervised Time in Practice

Supervised time is ordered where unsupervised contact may expose the child to risk. It may occur at a contact centre with professional supervisors, or under the supervision of a trusted third party agreed by the parties or ordered by the court.

It is usually transitional and subject to review. Where a parent complies with conditions and demonstrates improved capacity, the court may progressively increase time toward unsupervised arrangements.

⚠️ If you are subject to supervised time

Comply strictly with all conditions. Supervisors write reports that may be filed in evidence. Use supervised visits to demonstrate your parenting capacity — stay child-focused, avoid discussing the case, and never attempt to undermine the child's relationship with the other parent during visits.

Supervision Centre
Parenting
A facility providing neutral, professionally monitored contact between a parent and child, typically staffed by trained supervisors who observe and record interactions.
When it applies: Used where unsupervised or informally supervised time is assessed as unsafe. Contact centres provide a neutral environment that removes the risk of confrontation between parents and ensures the child's safety is maintained by an independent third party. A report of the visit may be provided to the court.

Contact Centres — What to Expect

A supervision centre provides neutral monitored contact between parent and child. Staff observe interactions, ensure the child's safety, and may prepare reports for the court. Both parents typically arrive and leave at different times to avoid confrontation.

Supervised time at a contact centre is usually a transitional arrangement — the goal is typically to progress toward less restrictive arrangements as safety is demonstrated over time.

💡 Your conduct is observed

Supervisors write reports that can be filed as evidence. Use every supervised visit to demonstrate positive, child-focused parenting. Avoid discussing the proceedings, speaking negatively about the other parent, or attempting to influence the child's views. Everything you do during supervised contact may appear in a report.

Contact Centres — How They Work

A supervision centre (also called a contact centre) provides a neutral, professionally monitored environment for contact between a parent and child where unsupervised contact is not appropriate. Staff observe interactions and write reports.

Centres typically operate on a booking and fee basis. Wait times can be significant. The court will specify whether contact is to occur at a centre and under what conditions.

⚠️ Reports go to the court

Contact centre supervisors write reports about interactions. These reports are filed as evidence. Be entirely child-focused during visits — avoid discussing the case, asking about the other parent, or behaving in any way you would not want documented.

Supervision Condition
Protection
A condition within a protection order or parenting order requiring that any contact between a specified person and a child or other party be supervised by a named individual or professional service, rather than occurring unsupervised.
When it applies: Attached to orders where the court finds an unacceptable risk of harm in unsupervised contact but does not consider it appropriate to prohibit contact entirely.
