You should seek independent legal advice before relying on any generated document.
Protection Orders

AVO Centre

Apprehended Violence Orders explained in plain language — whether you are applying for protection or you have been served with an order.

What is an AVO?

An Apprehended Violence Order (AVO) is a civil court order that places restrictions on a person's behaviour to protect another person from violence, harassment, intimidation, or stalking. In NSW, AVOs are governed by the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007. AVOs are not criminal convictions — but breaching one is a serious criminal offence.

ADVO — Apprehended Domestic Violence Order

Applies between people who are, or have been, in a domestic relationship — married, de facto, intimate, related by family, or living in the same household. ADVOs are the most common type and are often initiated by police.

APVO — Apprehended Personal Violence Order

Applies between people who are not in a domestic relationship — neighbours, workmates, acquaintances. APVOs are typically applied for directly by the person seeking protection, not by police.

Every AVO contains mandatory conditions: the defendant must not assault, molest, harass, threaten, or stalk the protected person. Additional conditions can be added depending on the circumstances.

AVO / DVO conditions — by state

Protection orders go by different names across Australia, but the core conditions are similar in every jurisdiction. Select your state to see the specific conditions that apply — including mandatory conditions, the most common additional conditions, and what counts as a breach.

🏛️ NSW — Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 Two types: ADVO (domestic relationship — partners, family, household) and APVO (non-domestic — neighbours, colleagues, acquaintances). Conditions are largely the same; the relationship determines which type is issued.
🔴 Mandatory condition — automatic on every AVO
The defendant must not assault, threaten, stalk, harass or intimidate the protected person(s), or damage or destroy their property.

This condition is on every AVO without exception. It cannot be removed, varied, or waived — not even by the protected person's request.

🔵 Additional conditions — common but not automatic
1. No contact
  • No phone calls, SMS, email or social media
  • No messages through friends, family or any third party
  • No indirect contact of any kind

Sometimes worded as: "Must not contact the protected person except through a lawyer."

2. No approaching
  • Cannot come within X metres (typically 100m) of the protected person
  • Cannot approach or attend the protected person's home address
  • Cannot approach or attend their workplace
  • Cannot approach any school or childcare the children attend
3. Exclusion from home
  • Must not enter or remain at a specific residential address
  • Can result in the defendant being removed from the family home immediately

This is particularly common in ADVOs where the parties live together. Police can enforce removal on the day the interim order is served.

4. No stalking or surveillance
  • No following, watching or loitering near the protected person
  • No monitoring their social media accounts
  • No tracking devices of any kind
  • No publishing material online about the protected person
5. Firearms prohibition (automatic in NSW)
  • Firearms licence is automatically suspended upon service of an AVO
  • Defendant cannot possess, use or acquire firearms while the order is in force

This applies regardless of whether a specific firearms condition is listed on the order.

6. Restrictions about children
  • No approaching the children named in the order
  • Contact only if supervised by a specified person
  • Contact only as permitted by a Family Court parenting order
  • Exceptions for changeover at a specified location

⚠️ Important: Family Court parenting orders can override or qualify AVO conditions in some situations. If you have both a parenting order and an AVO, get legal advice on how they interact before each changeover.

7. No intimidation or harassment

Broader than assault. Covers repeated messages, turning up unexpectedly, causing fear, or any behaviour designed to intimidate. Even behaviour that others might consider minor — repeated calls, driving slowly past the house — can constitute harassment under this condition.

8. Tailored / specific conditions

Courts can add custom conditions specific to the situation, including:

  • Not to damage or interfere with specific property
  • Not to approach a specific relative or associate
  • No consumption of alcohol or drugs before contact
  • Not to publish allegations, images or identifying information online
⚠️ What counts as a breach?

The wording of the order is everything. Even seemingly minor acts can be criminal if they breach the specific conditions:

  • Replying to a text from the protected person
  • Liking or reacting to a social media post
  • Driving past their home
  • Asking a mutual friend to pass on a message
  • Standing near their workplace "by coincidence"

Penalty for breach in NSW: up to 2 years imprisonment and/or a fine of up to $5,500.

🧠 The most important practical point

Two AVOs can look identical in name but be completely different in effect. One might allow contact about children; another might prohibit all contact. Always read the exact conditions page of your specific order. The title (ADVO or APVO) tells you almost nothing about what you can and cannot do.

🏛️ QLD — Domestic and Family Violence Protection Act 2012 Queensland uses the term DVO (Domestic Violence Order) rather than AVO. The order can be a temporary protection order (interim) or a protection order (final). A respondent is subject to the order; the protected person is called the aggrieved.
🔴 Mandatory condition — automatic on every DVO
The respondent must be of good behaviour toward the aggrieved and not commit domestic violence against the aggrieved.

This mandatory condition appears on every QLD protection order without exception and cannot be removed.

🔵 Common additional conditions in QLD
No contact
  • No telephone, SMS, email, social media or written contact
  • No contact through any third party
  • No contact of any kind, direct or indirect
No approaching or remaining near
  • Not to approach within a specified distance of the aggrieved
  • Not to attend or remain at the aggrieved's home or workplace
  • Not to attend children's schools or other specified locations
Exclusion from residence
  • Not to enter or remain at a specified residential address
  • Can remove the respondent from a shared home immediately on service
Weapons / firearms surrender (automatic in QLD)
  • Weapons licence automatically suspended on service of a DVO
  • Must surrender all weapons to police within 24 hours of being served
  • Applies to all weapons, not just firearms
No damage to property

Must not damage, destroy or dispose of property belonging to the aggrieved. Also cannot threaten to do so.

Conditions regarding children
  • Children may be listed as named persons on the order
  • Conditions can restrict contact or require supervision
  • Family Court orders may interact with DVO conditions — seek advice if both apply
⚠️ Breach in QLD

Breaching a DVO is a criminal offence in Queensland. Maximum penalty: 5 years imprisonment for a first breach; 7 years for subsequent breaches or where the breach involves violence. The "good behaviour" condition means even low-level intimidating behaviour can be a breach.

📌 QLD practical note

Queensland DVOs can include named persons other than the aggrieved — including children, relatives, and associates. Always check who is listed on the order and what specific conditions apply to each named person. The conditions can differ between named persons on the same order.

🏛️ VIC — Family Violence Protection Act 2008 Victoria uses Family Violence Intervention Orders (FVIOs). Issued by the Magistrates' Court. An interim FVIO can be granted ex-parte (without the respondent present). Victoria also has a dedicated Family Violence Division in the Magistrates' Court.
🔴 Mandatory condition
The respondent must not commit family violence against the protected person.

Appears on every FVIO automatically. Cannot be removed or waived.

🔵 Common additional conditions
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or contact through any third party
No approaching — cannot come within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — must not enter or remain at the family residence, even if the respondent owns or rents it
No publishing on the internet — cannot post material about the protected person online
No locating or tracking — cannot attempt to find the protected person or use any tracking device
No attending specified locations — school, workplace, or other named places
Firearms licence removal — automatic on service of an FVIO; firearms must be surrendered
📌 VIC-specific conditions

Victoria commonly includes a prohibited behaviour condition (broad restriction on intimidating conduct), an exclusion condition (removal from residence), and a family law exception clause which specifies how the FVIO interacts with any existing Family Court parenting orders — essential if both orders apply.

🏛️ ACT — Family Violence Act 2016 The ACT issues Family Violence Orders (FVOs) and Personal Protection Orders (PPOs). FVOs cover domestic/family relationships; PPOs cover non-domestic situations. The ACT Magistrates' Court handles all protection order applications.
🔵 Conditions that may be included
No contact — direct or indirect, including through third parties
No approaching — within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — cannot enter or remain at the family residence
No harassment or intimidation — broad restriction on any behaviour designed to cause fear
No property damage — cannot damage or threaten to damage the protected person's property
No locating attempts — cannot attempt to find the protected person's address or whereabouts
Restrictions on children contact — contact may be limited to supervised or as specified
Firearms prohibition — automatic suspension of licence; must surrender weapons
📌 ACT-specific: electronic monitoring

The ACT allows courts to impose electronic monitoring conditions — including GPS ankle monitoring — in serious cases. This is not available in all jurisdictions and reflects the ACT's more expansive approach to enforcement.

🏛️ SA — Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009 South Australia uses Intervention Orders. They can be issued by police (Police Intervention Orders — immediate, short-term) or by the court (Court Intervention Orders — longer term). SA has a notably broad definition of abuse, explicitly recognising forms of harm that other states do not name separately.
🔵 Conditions that may be included
No abuse — SA explicitly includes physical, emotional, economic and psychological abuse within scope
No contact — direct or indirect
No approaching — cannot come within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — must not enter or remain at the family residence
No attending certain places — school, workplace, or other specified locations
No surveillance — no monitoring, tracking or watching the protected person
Firearms surrender — automatic on service of a Court Intervention Order
📌 SA-specific: broader abuse recognition

SA specifically legislates emotional abuse, economic abuse, and social isolation as forms of abuse that can ground an Intervention Order. This is broader than some other states and means coercive control-type conduct — financial control, isolating a person from family — can be the basis for an order without any physical violence.

🏛️ TAS — Family Violence Act 2004 Tasmania issues Family Violence Orders (FVOs). Notably, Tasmania Police have authority to issue a Police FVO immediately — without a court hearing — where they believe family violence has occurred and urgent protection is needed. Court FVOs are then issued for longer-term protection.
🔵 Conditions
No family violence — core mandatory condition covering all forms of family violence as defined in the Act
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or indirect contact
No approaching — within a specified distance of the protected person
Exclusion from residence — cannot enter or remain at the family home
No locating or tracking — cannot attempt to find the protected person or use surveillance of any kind
No publishing material — cannot post material about the protected person online or elsewhere
Firearms prohibition — firearms licence suspended; must surrender all weapons
📌 TAS-specific: Police FVOs

Police in Tasmania can issue an FVO immediately at the scene of a family violence incident without a court order. These are short-term but take effect immediately. If longer protection is needed, application is made to the Magistrates Court for a court-issued FVO.

🏛️ NT — Domestic and Family Violence Act 2007 The Northern Territory uses Domestic Violence Orders (DVOs). The NT has one of Australia's highest rates of domestic violence and has invested significantly in integrated court responses. The NT also has specialist Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander support services integrated into the court system.
🔵 Conditions
No harm or threats — must not commit any act of domestic violence or threaten to do so
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or contact through any third party
No approaching — cannot approach within a specified distance of the protected person
Exclusion from premises — must not enter or remain at specified premises
No stalking — no following, loitering, or monitoring of any kind
No property damage — cannot damage or threaten to damage the protected person's property
Weapons prohibition — cannot possess or use any weapon; licence suspended
📌 NT-specific: behaviour change programs

NT courts can add a condition requiring the respondent to attend and complete an approved behaviour change program. This is used more frequently in the NT than most other states and can be part of both interim and final DVO conditions. Failure to complete a directed program can itself constitute a breach.

🏛️ WA — Restraining Orders Act 1997 Western Australia has three types of restraining orders: FVRO (Family Violence Restraining Order — domestic relationships), VRO (Violence Restraining Order — non-domestic), and MRO (Misconduct Restraining Order — lower-level conduct). FVROs are the most common in the family law context.
🔴 Core conditions
No violence, threats or intimidating conduct against the protected person.

Applies on all FVROs and VROs automatically.

🔵 Common additional conditions
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or contact through any third party
No approaching — within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — must not enter or remain at the family residence
No attending specific locations — workplace, school, or other named places
No online publication — cannot post material about the protected person on any platform
Weapons surrender — firearms and other weapons licence suspended; must be surrendered to police
📌 WA: three order types compared

FVRO — applies to people in a family or domestic relationship; broadest conditions, most commonly issued. VRO — applies to non-domestic situations; similar conditions. MRO — lower threshold, used for nuisance/harassment conduct that doesn't meet violence threshold; conditions are less restrictive and do not include automatic weapons prohibition.

🇦🇺 National common conditions — across every state
1. No assault or threats
2. No harassment or intimidation
3. No contact
4. No approaching
5. Exclusion from home
6. Restrictions on children
7. Firearms prohibition
8. No surveillance or tracking
9. No online harassment
⚠️ The most important strategic point

The danger is not the order itself — it is the exact wording. Two orders with identical names can have completely different criminal exposure. What matters: whether it allows child contact; whether it permits communication through lawyers; whether it contains a family law exception clause. Small wording differences change your criminal exposure massively. Always read your specific conditions page.

How to apply for an AVO — step by step

1
Report to police or apply at court

You have two routes: (a) Police-initiated AVO — report the conduct to police. They assess and, if appropriate, serve the defendant with an AVO application on your behalf. This is the most common route for domestic violence. (b) Private application — go to your local Local Court registry and file an Application for an AVO yourself. Filing fees are waived in most domestic violence matters.

2
First court date — interim AVO

Your matter will be listed before a Magistrate, usually at the Local Court nearest to where you live. The defendant does not need to be present at this first hearing. If the Magistrate is satisfied there are reasonable grounds, an interim AVO will be granted immediately — giving you protection from that day forward. The defendant is then served with the interim order.

3
Mention date

Both parties appear. The defendant can: (a) consent to the AVO without admission — the most common outcome; (b) contest the AVO — it will be listed for a hearing on a future date; or (c) negotiate conditions — conditions may be varied by agreement. If you have a lawyer, they will appear for you. If self-representing, you will need to be present.

4
Hearing (if contested)

If the defendant contests the AVO, a hearing is scheduled. You will need to give evidence. Your supporting evidence (messages, medical records, police reports, photographs, witness statements) will be relevant. The standard of proof is civil — balance of probabilities — not the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.

5
Final AVO

If the AVO is made (by consent or after hearing), a final AVO is issued. The standard duration is 2 years, but can be shorter or longer depending on circumstances. The order is registered on a national police database. It can be varied or revoked by the court if circumstances change — but only by court order, not by agreement between the parties.

Collecting and presenting your evidence

Strong evidence significantly improves your outcome. Start gathering evidence as early as possible, even before you apply. Courts respond to specific, dated, documented incidents — not general descriptions of behaviour.

💬Text & messaging records

Screenshot all threatening, harassing, or controlling messages. Include the sender's name or number, the date and time, and the platform. Store copies in cloud storage and email them to yourself.

📷Photographs

Photograph injuries, damaged property, or evidence of the defendant's presence (e.g. photos taken at your home, unwanted gifts). Date and metadata of phone photos can corroborate your account.

📋Incident diary

Keep a running log of incidents — date, time, location, what was said or done, who was present, and any immediate impact. A contemporaneous diary is highly credible evidence.

🏥Medical records

If you sought medical treatment after any incident, request copies of the relevant records. GPs, hospitals, and mental health services can provide records showing injuries or stress consistent with your account.

👁️Witness statements

Anyone who has witnessed threatening behaviour, seen your physical state after incidents, or heard relevant conversations may be able to provide a statement or give evidence at hearing. Neighbours, family, and work colleagues can all be witnesses.

📧Email records

Print or export threatening or harassing emails. Ensure the sender address, subject, and date are visible. Forward them to a private email account for safekeeping.

AVOs and Family Court parenting orders — what to know

If you have, or are applying for, both an AVO and Family Court parenting orders, there are important interactions you need to understand.

AVO conditions can conflict with parenting orders

If your AVO prevents the defendant from being near you or your children, but a Family Court parenting order requires handovers, the two orders can conflict. In NSW, if there is a conflict between an AVO and a Family Court order, the Family Court order prevails (s 68R Family Law Act), but only to the extent of the inconsistency. You should seek urgent legal advice if this applies.

You can apply for child-inclusive conditions

You can apply for the AVO to include conditions that prevent the defendant contacting the children, or approaching the children's school or childcare. If you are also in Family Court proceedings, notify your family lawyer immediately so they can apply for consistent interim parenting orders.

The Family Court must consider AVO history

Under s 60CC of the Family Law Act, the Family Court must take into account any family violence order (including an AVO) when determining parenting matters. An AVO is not automatically determinative of a parenting outcome, but it is highly relevant and will be considered carefully.

You've been served — what does this mean?

Being served with an AVO is serious, but it is important to understand what it is and what it is not.

📋An AVO is a civil order — not a criminal charge

Being served or having an AVO made against you does not create a criminal record. It does not appear as a conviction. It does not affect most employment, travel, or licensing — with the exception noted below.

🔴Breaching an AVO is a criminal offence

Breaching any condition of the AVO — including contacting the protected person even if they contact you first — is a criminal offence under s 14 of the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007. Maximum penalty: 2 years imprisonment and/or $5,500 fine.

🔫Weapons & firearms

If an AVO is made against you, you may be required to surrender any firearms licence and weapons. This is an automatic consequence in most cases and applies during the period the AVO is in force.

👨‍💼Employment implications

Certain professions (police, security, childcare, healthcare) require disclosure of AVOs during background checks. If your employment may be affected, seek specific legal advice.

What happens next — the court process for defendants

1
You receive the AVO documents

You will be served with: the Application for AVO, any supporting facts, the interim AVO (if one has been granted), and a court date. Read the conditions of the interim AVO carefully and comply with them from the moment you are served — even if you believe the allegations are false.

2
First mention at court

You must attend the first mention date. If you do not attend, the matter may be heard and orders made in your absence. Arrive early. If you have not yet obtained legal advice, you can ask the Magistrate for an adjournment to obtain legal representation.

3
Your three options at mention

(a) Consent without admissions — you agree to the AVO but do not admit any of the allegations. This is the most common outcome. It ends the matter quickly and limits risk, but the AVO is made on your record as having existed. (b) Negotiate conditions — you may be able to narrow or modify conditions, particularly around co-parenting contact or property access. (c) Contest the AVO — you dispute the need for the order and the matter proceeds to a hearing. See below.

4
If you contest — the hearing

At hearing, the applicant must prove on the balance of probabilities that the protected person has reasonable grounds to fear the defendant's behaviour. You can give evidence, call witnesses, and cross-examine the applicant. A Magistrate will then determine whether to make the order.

5
After the order is made

If a final AVO is made — whether by consent or after hearing — you must comply with every condition at all times. You can apply to vary or revoke the AVO if circumstances change, but only through a formal court application. Do not attempt to negotiate changes directly with the protected person.

⚠️ Critical rules while an interim AVO is in force

✕

Do not contact the protected person — even if they contact you first. Even if you are in an ongoing relationship. Even if they say it is okay. If they contact you, do not respond until you have legal advice about what is safe.

✕

Do not ask others to contact the protected person on your behalf — third-party contact is also a breach. Do not ask family members, friends, or colleagues to pass on messages.

✕

Do not approach the protected person's home, work, or school — if the AVO contains an exclusion zone, stay strictly outside it. If you are unsure what the condition means in practice, ask a lawyer before you approach any location.

✕

Do not post about the protected person on social media — this can constitute harassment and may be treated as a breach. Screenshot and preserve any prior communications but do not continue them.

✓

Co-parenting contact only — if you have children together, child contact and handovers should be addressed in your court application. Until then, use a neutral third party for handovers and communicate only via a documented co-parenting app.

AVO / DVO conditions — by state

Understanding exactly what conditions are on your order — and what they mean in practice — is the most important thing you can do right now. Select your state to see what each condition means and what constitutes a breach.

🏛️ NSW — Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 ADVO (domestic relationship) or APVO (non-domestic). The conditions — not the label — determine what you can and cannot do. Read your specific conditions page.
🔴 Mandatory — on every NSW AVO, cannot be removed
Must not assault, threaten, stalk, harass or intimidate the protected person(s), or damage/destroy their property.

You cannot apply to remove this condition. It is there whether the order is interim or final.

🔵 Additional conditions — check your order for which apply
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or messages via any third party. Replying to a message from the protected person is still a breach.
No approaching — cannot come within the specified distance (check your order) of the protected person, their home, workplace, or the children's school.
Exclusion from home — even if you own or rent the property, you cannot enter or remain. Police can enforce this immediately on service of the interim order.
No stalking or surveillance — no following, monitoring social media, tracking devices, or publishing material online about the protected person.
Firearms prohibition (automatic in NSW) — your firearms licence is suspended from the moment the AVO is served. You must surrender all firearms. This applies even if no firearms condition is listed.
Restrictions about children — check carefully. Contact may only be permitted if supervised, or only as per a Family Court order. If you have parenting orders, get legal advice on how they interact with the AVO before the next changeover.
⚠️ Breach penalty in NSW

Up to 2 years imprisonment and/or a fine of up to $5,500. Even minor acts — liking a post, driving past the house, asking a friend to pass a message — are criminal if they breach the wording of your order.

🏛️ QLD — Domestic and Family Violence Protection Act 2012 Queensland calls these DVOs (Domestic Violence Orders). You are the respondent; the other person is the aggrieved. Temporary protection orders apply immediately; court protection orders are longer-term.
🔴 Mandatory — on every QLD DVO
Must be of good behaviour toward the aggrieved and not commit domestic violence.

The "good behaviour" condition is broad — even low-level intimidating or controlling behaviour can constitute a breach without any physical contact.

🔵 Common additional conditions in QLD
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or contact through any third party, direct or indirect
No approaching or remaining near — cannot come within a specified distance of the aggrieved, their home, workplace or children's school
Exclusion from residence — cannot enter or remain at the family home. Police can enforce removal on service of a temporary protection order.
No locating or attempting to locate — cannot attempt to find where the aggrieved is living or staying
Weapons surrender (mandatory in QLD) — weapons licence automatically suspended; must surrender all weapons to police within 24 hours of being served
⚠️ Breach penalty in QLD

Up to 5 years imprisonment for a first breach. Up to 7 years for subsequent breaches or where the breach involves violence. QLD has some of the strongest breach penalties in Australia.

🏛️ VIC — Family Violence Protection Act 2008 Victoria calls these FVIOs (Family Violence Intervention Orders). You are the respondent. Interim FVIOs are granted ex-parte (without you present) and take effect immediately on service.
🔴 Mandatory — on every VIC FVIO
Must not commit family violence against the protected person.
🔵 Common additional conditions
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or contact through any third party
No approaching — within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — cannot enter or remain at the family residence, even if you are on the lease or title
No online publication — cannot post material about the protected person on any platform
No locating or tracking — cannot attempt to find the protected person or use any device to monitor them
Firearms removal (automatic) — licence suspended immediately on service; all firearms must be surrendered
Family law exception clause — if your FVIO includes a family law exception, it will specify exactly what contact is permitted for parenting purposes (e.g. changeovers at a specific location). Read this clause carefully. It overrides the general no-contact condition for the purposes it describes.
🏛️ ACT — Family Violence Act 2016 ACT issues FVOs (Family Violence Orders) for domestic situations and PPOs (Personal Protection Orders) for non-domestic. You are the respondent. Electronic monitoring (GPS) can be added as a condition in serious cases.
No contact — direct or indirect, including through third parties. Firearms licence suspended automatically.
No approaching — within a specified distance of the protected person or named locations
Exclusion from home — cannot enter or remain at the family residence
No harassment, intimidation, or property damage
No locating attempts or tracking
Restrictions on children contact — contact may be limited to supervised or as specified
Electronic monitoring — the ACT can add GPS monitoring as a condition in serious cases. If this applies to you, get legal advice immediately.
🏛️ SA — Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009 SA uses Intervention Orders. Police can issue a Police Intervention Order immediately (short-term); Court Intervention Orders are issued by the Magistrates Court for longer-term protection. SA has the broadest definition of abuse in Australia.
No abuse — SA explicitly includes physical, emotional, economic and psychological abuse. Economic control and social isolation are legally recognised forms of abuse.
No contact, no approaching, exclusion from home — standard conditions similar to other states
No attending certain places — school, workplace or other named locations
No surveillance — no monitoring, tracking or watching the protected person
Firearms surrender — automatic on service of a Court Intervention Order
🏛️ TAS — Family Violence Act 2004 Tasmania issues FVOs (Family Violence Orders). Notably, Tasmania Police can issue a Police FVO immediately at the scene without a court hearing. Court FVOs are issued for longer-term protection.
No family violence — core mandatory condition covering all forms of family violence as defined in the Act
No contact — no phone, SMS, email, social media or indirect contact
No approaching, exclusion from residence, no locating or tracking, no publishing material
Firearms prohibition — licence suspended; all weapons must be surrendered
🏛️ NT — Domestic and Family Violence Act 2007 The NT uses DVOs (Domestic Violence Orders). NT courts can add behaviour change program conditions — failure to complete a directed program is itself a breach.
No harm or threats — cannot commit any act of domestic violence or threaten to do so
No contact, no approaching, exclusion from premises, no stalking, no property damage
Weapons prohibition — cannot possess or use any weapon; licence suspended
Behaviour change program — NT courts can order attendance at an approved program as a condition. Non-attendance is a criminal breach.
🏛️ WA — Restraining Orders Act 1997 Three types: FVRO (domestic), VRO (non-domestic), MRO (misconduct — lower threshold, no automatic weapons prohibition). Check which type you have been served with.
🔴 Core condition — FVROs and VROs
No violence, threats or intimidating conduct against the protected person.
No contact, no approaching, exclusion from home, no attending specified locations, no online publication
Weapons surrender — firearms and other weapons licence suspended; must be surrendered to police on service
MRO vs FVRO/VRO — if you have been served with an MRO (Misconduct Restraining Order), the conditions are less restrictive and there is no automatic weapons prohibition. Check the header of your order to confirm which type applies.

Should you consent or contest?

This is one of the most important decisions you will make in AVO proceedings. There is no universal right answer — it depends on your circumstances.

Reasons to consider consenting
• Ends the matter quickly with less cost and stress
• You can consent "without admissions" — no concession of wrongdoing
• Avoids cross-examination and the risk of an adverse finding at hearing
• Allows you to negotiate workable conditions rather than having them imposed
• The AVO exists whether you consent or it is proven — strategically the effect is similar
Reasons to consider contesting
• The allegations are false or significantly overstated
• The AVO conditions would prevent you from seeing your children
• An AVO would seriously affect your employment or professional licence
• You have strong evidence that the application is retaliatory or vexatious
• You need the court to make findings for related Family Court proceedings

⚠️ This is a decision that should ideally be made with legal advice. Legal Aid and community legal centres can assist even if you are on a limited income.

💡 Law Access: 1300 888 529 · Legal Aid NSW: legalaid.nsw.gov.au
🤝
FDR Practitioner / MediatorMediation & negotiation

An accredited mediator who helps separated parents negotiate parenting arrangements outside of court. Required before most parenting applications (s 60I).

When you need them: Before filing a parenting application, when communication has broken down.
💡 Government-subsidised FDR via Family Relationship Centres: familyrelationships.gov.au
🧠
Psychologist or CounsellorMental health support

A professional space to process what you're going through — separate from your legal strategy.

When you need them: From day one. Don't wait until you're in crisis.
💡 Your GP can provide a Mental Health Care Plan — up to 10 Medicare-subsidised sessions per year.
💰
Financial Advisor or AccountantFinancial clarity

Separation triggers complex financial decisions — superannuation splitting, asset division, tax implications.

When you need them: Early in property proceedings, when valuing business interests or considering super splitting.
💡 National Debt Helpline: 1800 007 007 — free financial counselling.

New Partners

Introducing a new partner during or after family law proceedings is one of the most delicate decisions you will make. Courts, family consultants, and independent children's lawyers all pay close attention to how new adults are introduced into a child's life. Getting this right protects your case and — more importantly — protects your children.

Timing — when is it appropriate?

There is no legally prescribed waiting period before introducing a new partner to your children. However, family consultants and psychologists who write reports for the court apply a consistent standard: children should not be introduced to a new romantic partner until the relationship is established and stable — generally accepted as a minimum of six to twelve months.

Introducing a new partner too quickly — particularly within weeks or months of separation — can be used as evidence of poor parenting judgment and a lack of child-focus. In contested proceedings, the other party's lawyer will almost certainly raise it. Family consultants will ask the children about it directly.

✓ What helps
Waiting until the relationship is stable and the children have adjusted to the separation before any introduction. Introducing your partner as a friend initially, and allowing the relationship to develop naturally over time without pressure or forced affection.
✗ What damages your case
Introducing a new partner within weeks of separation, having your partner sleep over when the children are present in the early stages, or allowing your partner to take on parenting responsibilities before the children are ready and before orders are in place.

Your partner's role in proceedings

A new partner is not a party to your family law proceedings unless they are seeking to adopt the child, apply for parental responsibility, or are subject to a family violence order. However, they can become relevant to proceedings in a number of indirect ways that you should understand.

Family consultant interviews — If a family report is ordered, the family consultant will interview your children. Children frequently disclose information about a parent's new partner — their name, how often they are there, what they say, how they behave. Children's accounts of new partners are taken seriously in family reports.
Affidavit evidence — The other party may file affidavit evidence about your new partner — their history, character, or behaviour. If your partner has a criminal record, a domestic violence history, or their own child protection involvement, this will almost certainly be raised and will need to be addressed.
Working with children checks — Courts increasingly expect that any adult with significant involvement in a child's life holds a current Working with Children Check. If your partner spends substantial time with your children, ensure they have obtained the relevant check for your state.
Overnight arrangements — Whether your partner stays overnight when the children are present is a common point of dispute, particularly in the early stages of proceedings. Courts do not prohibit this, but they do consider the child's adjustment, the stability of the relationship, and the impact on the co-parenting dynamic.
Step-parent parental responsibility — A step-parent does not automatically acquire parental responsibility by virtue of the relationship. If your partner is to play a significant parenting role, this needs to be specifically addressed in consent orders or parenting plans — particularly for emergency medical decisions, school enrolment, and travel.

Supporting your partner through proceedings

Family law proceedings place enormous strain on new relationships. Your partner did not choose to inherit the legal, financial, and emotional complexity of your separation — they chose you. Understanding what they are experiencing, and managing the impact on the relationship, matters.

🗣️Keep them informed, not overwhelmed

Your partner needs enough information to be supportive, but not so much that they become a surrogate legal advisor or secondary participant in the conflict. Brief them on major developments; protect them from daily detail.

🚧Set boundaries around conflict

Do not conduct arguments, legal calls, or emotionally charged correspondence with the other party in front of your new partner. Exposing them to that conflict entangles them in ways that are difficult to undo and can create unnecessary hostility.

❤️Protect the relationship separately

Your new relationship needs its own oxygen. Schedule time together that is entirely separate from the proceedings — where you are not discussing court dates, affidavits, or the other parent. This requires discipline, but it is essential for the relationship's survival.

🧒Align on parenting approach

Before your partner spends significant time with your children, have explicit conversations about parenting expectations — discipline, boundaries, activities, language used about the other parent. Misalignment on these points is one of the most common sources of conflict in blended families.

💸Be transparent about financial pressure

Legal proceedings are expensive and financially disruptive. Don't hide the cost from your partner — bring them into the reality of it so you can plan together. Surprises about money are one of the most destabilising things for a new relationship under stress.

🧘Acknowledge what they carry

Your partner absorbs stress, adjusts their life around court dates, and supports children who may be struggling — often without recognition. Name what they are doing. Gratitude and acknowledgement matter more than people admit, especially when the road is long.

📌 The most important thing your new partner can do Support you without becoming part of the conflict. The best new partners in this situation are people who are warm to the children, respectful of the co-parenting relationship even when they disagree with it, and a stable, calm presence in your home. Courts reward child-focused households. A partner who understands this is an asset. A partner who cannot contain their own feelings about the other parent is a liability — through no fault of yours.

Grandparents

Grandparents occupy a unique position in Australian family law — they are both a vital support resource for the separating parent and a party with independent legal rights in relation to their grandchildren. Understanding both dimensions helps you protect the relationship and avoid common pitfalls.

Grandparents' legal standing under Australian family law

Under section 65C of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth), grandparents have explicit standing to apply to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA) for a parenting order — including orders for time spent with grandchildren, communication, and specific aspects of parental responsibility. This right exists independently of the parents and does not require the parents' consent.

The court's primary consideration in any parenting matter is the best interests of the child (s 60CA). Within that framework, section 60CC(2) specifically identifies the benefit of the child having a meaningful relationship with both parents and other people significant to the child's care, welfare, and development — a category that courts have consistently applied to grandparents.

The 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act strengthened this framework. Judges now consider a child's connections to culture, community, and extended family as part of the best interests assessment. For grandchildren of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander backgrounds, the Act explicitly requires consideration of their right to connection with their family, community, and culture.

👴 Paternal grandparents

If the father is the non-resident parent, his parents — your children's paternal grandparents — may find their relationship with the grandchildren significantly disrupted by separation. This side of the family often loses contact not through any fault of their own, but through the breakdown of the parental relationship.

What you can do
Facilitate ongoing contact even if your relationship with the other parent is difficult — courts look favourably on parents who support extended family relationships.
If contact is being blocked unreasonably, grandparents can apply under s 65C for a parenting order independently.
Consider including grandparent contact arrangements in any proposed parenting plan to avoid future disputes.

👵 Maternal grandparents

If you are the primary carer, your parents are often the first line of practical support — before paid childcare, before school, and during court dates. Their involvement can be deeply stabilising for children whose world has been upended. However, their proximity to the situation also creates risks if they become too enmeshed in the conflict.

Protecting the role
Grandparents who speak negatively about the other parent in front of children can undermine your credibility in court proceedings.
Set clear boundaries: grandparents should support you and the children, not gather evidence or act as intermediaries.
If grandparents are providing the primary childcare during proceedings, document their role — it may be relevant to your case.

When grandparents should seek their own legal advice

There are specific circumstances where grandparents need to act independently, rather than relying on the separating parent to protect the relationship. These include situations where both parents agree to limit or cut off the grandparent relationship, where family violence means the grandparent's safety is at risk in their own home, or where grandchildren are living with grandparents under informal arrangements and custody is disputed.

Applying for a parenting order
Grandparents can file an Initiating Application in the FCFCOA seeking defined time with grandchildren. They must attempt FDR mediation first (s 60I certificate required).
Grandchildren living with you
If grandchildren are staying with you on an informal basis, consider obtaining parenting orders to formalise the arrangement before it becomes a dispute.
Child protection intersects
If child protection services are involved, grandparents may be considered as carers. Engaging a family lawyer early in this process is strongly advised.
International relocation
If a parent intends to relocate overseas with the children, grandparents can apply for orders that prevent the move until the court considers the children's relationships with extended family.

Grandparents as practical support during proceedings

Beyond their legal rights, grandparents are often the most important practical resource a separating parent has. Understanding how to use that support well — and where its limits are — can make a significant difference to both your wellbeing and your case.

🏠 Housing

If you need to leave the family home quickly, a grandparent's home may be the safest immediate option — especially if you have children. Courts understand emergency housing arrangements.

👶 Childcare during hearings

Court dates are unpredictable in timing. Having a grandparent available for flexible childcare — including last-minute school pickups — is practically invaluable.

💸 Financial support

Legal costs are significant. Grandparents who provide financial assistance should be aware it may be treated as a loan or gift in property proceedings — get any agreement in writing.

📋 Witnessing documents

Grandparents with JP qualifications can witness affidavits and statutory declarations — a practical advantage when you need documents signed quickly.

🚗 School runs and logistics

Proceedings can disrupt the predictability children depend on. A grandparent who can reliably manage the school run, after-school care, and weekend logistics gives your children stability when everything else is uncertain.

🗂️ Helping organise evidence

A trusted grandparent can help you sort through documents, organise timelines, and track correspondence — practical administrative support that reduces overwhelm without requiring legal expertise. Keep them out of strategy discussions.

👴👵
Grandparents — key resourcesSupport & advocacy

National and state-based organisations that provide advice, legal referrals, and peer support for grandparents navigating the family law system.

💡 Grandparents Australasia: grandparents.com.au — advocacy, peer support, legal information
💡 Grandparents Rights Association NSW: gransw.org.au — NSW-specific support
💡 Family Relationships Online: familyrelationships.gov.au — mediation services, parenting plans
💡 National Legal Aid: nationallegalaid.org — find your state Legal Aid for free advice

Siblings

Your siblings — and the other parent's siblings — play roles that are often underestimated. They can be your closest support, your children's beloved aunts and uncles, or — when managed poorly — a source of conflict that complicates your case. This section covers both your own siblings and the other parent's.

Your siblings as support

Unlike parents, siblings often have a more peer-level relationship with you — which makes them valuable for honest conversations, practical advice that isn't filtered through parental anxiety, and emotional support that doesn't come with conditions. They may also have personal experience with their own relationships and legal matters.

Siblings who are lawyers, accountants, teachers, or health professionals can provide informal advice in their area of expertise — but be clear about what you're asking for and acknowledge the limits of informal professional advice. A sibling who is a solicitor can help you understand a document; they shouldn't be your primary legal advisor.

⚠️ Boundaries to set with siblings
Don't use a sibling as a message carrier to the other parent — anything said can become evidence if things escalate.
Be thoughtful about siblings attending court with you. While allowed, a sibling who reacts emotionally in court can create a poor impression.
Siblings who post about your matter on social media — even supportively — can cause real damage to your case. Have this conversation early and explicitly.
Siblings who witness family violence or incidents relevant to your case can provide written statements or affidavits. If their evidence is useful, speak to your lawyer before asking them to write anything down.

Aunts and uncles — your children's relationship with the other side

Your children's aunts and uncles — particularly those on the other parent's side — are often caught in the middle of separation. The other parent's siblings may have been close to your children, and abruptly cutting off that relationship can cause real harm — both to the children and to your standing in proceedings.

Under the Family Law Act, the court considers all people significant to a child's care, welfare, and development — not just parents and grandparents. Aunts and uncles who have played a consistent role in a child's life fall within this category. This means that actively facilitating (or blocking) these relationships can be relevant to how the court views your parenting.

What to facilitate
Birthday cards, phone calls, occasional visits during the other parent's time — these cost you little but demonstrate to a family consultant or court that you support your children's broader family connections.
What to be careful of
An aunt or uncle who regularly questions your children about the other household, or who passes information between parents, should be gently but firmly asked to stop — in writing if necessary.
If there is family violence
If the other parent's siblings are part of a broader family dynamic involving intimidation or harassment, consider applying for AVO conditions that cover extended family members.

Siblings of children — keeping brothers and sisters together

If you have more than one child, sibling relationships become a significant consideration in parenting proceedings. Courts are generally reluctant to make orders that separate siblings, recognising the sibling bond as an important source of emotional stability and identity for children experiencing family disruption.

The principle that siblings should remain together is not absolute — there are cases where different living arrangements serve different children's needs — but courts will require clear evidence of why separation of siblings is in the children's best interests before ordering it.

📌 Key principles for sibling arrangements
Propose parenting orders that allow all siblings to spend time together with each parent — staggered or split arrangements that chronically separate siblings are rarely supported by the court.
Half-siblings and step-siblings who have lived together as part of the same household may also be considered — especially if the children have a significant relationship with them.
If a teenager expresses a strong preference about their living arrangements that differs from a younger sibling, the court may accommodate this — but will still consider how this affects the sibling relationship.
Document evidence of the sibling relationship: photos of siblings together, school events attended as a family, shared activities — this supports any argument that separation would be harmful.

Other personal support

⚠️ Keeping family support healthy

Family members who are angry on your behalf can entrench conflict.
Be careful about family members speaking to your children about the case.

Friends remind you who you are outside of all this. They keep you grounded and help maintain a sense of self.

Be specific about what you need: "I need to vent" vs "I need advice" vs "I just need company."
Be careful sharing case details with friends who also know the other parent.

Children & Parenting

About the Kids

Understanding how separation affects children — and what you can do to protect, support, and reassure them through the process.

How children experience separation — by age

Children's responses to separation are profoundly shaped by their developmental stage. Understanding what is developmentally typical — versus what signals a need for additional support — helps parents respond appropriately rather than reactively.

Regression — Toilet training regression, thumb-sucking, baby talk, increased clinginess, and sleep disturbance are all common responses to family disruption in children under 5. These are not signs of permanent damage — they are signs that the child is under stress and needs additional reassurance and routine.
Separation anxiety — Very young children do not have a reliable understanding of object permanence or time. When a parent leaves, they do not know the parent is coming back. Brief, predictable separations with consistent farewell routines help build trust that the absent parent returns.
Absorbing parental emotion — Infants and toddlers are exquisitely sensitive to parental emotional states. They do not understand words — but they read tone, body language, and nervous system cues. A parent who is visibly distressed at handover communicates to the child that something is wrong. Practice calm handovers even when you do not feel calm.
What helps: Consistent routines across both homes; familiar objects (a stuffed animal, a blanket) that travel between homes; brief, warm, and calm handovers; age-appropriate language ("Daddy/Mummy loves you and will see you on Tuesday"); and maintained contact with grandparents and other significant people.
When to seek professional help: If regression is severe or prolonged, if sleep disturbance is significantly impacting the child or parent, or if the child is consistently inconsolable during transitions, consult your GP or a child psychologist. Early Childhood Intervention Services can also support young children experiencing family stress.
Self-blame — Children in this age group frequently believe the separation is their fault. They may recall a recent conflict or misbehaviour and connect it (incorrectly) to the family breakdown. This belief is almost universal and must be directly, explicitly, and repeatedly addressed: "The separation is a grown-up problem. It is not your fault. Nothing you did caused this, and nothing you do will change it."
Loyalty conflicts — School-age children feel intensely pulled between parents. They may modify their behaviour, opinions, and reports depending on which parent they are with, in order to avoid hurting anyone. This is not dishonesty — it is an attempt to manage an impossible emotional position. Do not debrief your child about the other household.
Internalising and externalising — Some children in this age group internalise distress (appearing fine, becoming anxious, struggling at school, developing physical complaints like stomach aches). Others externalise (becoming aggressive, defiant, or attention-seeking). Both are communication — they need more support, not more discipline.
Impact on school performance — Cognitive bandwidth used for emotional regulation is cognitive bandwidth unavailable for learning. It is normal for school performance to dip during periods of acute family disruption. Alert your child's teacher to the situation (briefly and without detail) so that unexplained absences or behavioural changes are understood in context.
What helps: Age-appropriate, honest explanation that the separation is not their fault; maintained school routine and extracurricular activities; explicit permission to love both parents without guilt; regular, predictable contact with both parents and extended family; and a trusted adult at school who knows the situation. Do not denigrate the other parent when talking about the relationship.
Strong views on arrangements — Adolescents have real, considered opinions about living arrangements and will express them. Under s 60CC(3)(a) of the Family Law Act, the court must consider the child's views, with the weight given depending on the child's maturity and level of understanding. A 14-year-old's clearly expressed views about where they want to live carry significant weight. This does not mean teenagers make the final decision — but dismissing their views is both practically and legally counterproductive.
Risk-taking and acting out — Adolescents experiencing family breakdown are at elevated risk of academic disengagement, substance experimentation, risk-taking behaviour, and social withdrawal. These are not simply teenage phases — they are distress signals. Peer relationships become critically important during this time, and disruption to peer networks (through school changes or relocation) compounds the stress significantly.
Parentification — Teenagers are old enough to understand what is happening, which makes them vulnerable to being treated as confidants or emotional supports by parents. This is called parentification — it is inappropriate, harmful to the child's development, and — if documented by a family consultant — adversely affects parenting assessments. Do not share legal strategy, financial concerns, or hostile feelings about the other parent with your teenager.
Identity and stability — Adolescence is already a period of identity formation. Family breakdown during this stage is particularly disruptive because it occurs when the adolescent needs a stable base from which to explore who they are. Consistency in school, friendships, and activities provides the scaffolding they need.
What helps: Genuine respect for their views without burdening them with adult decisions; maintained peer and social connections; transparency without detail ("We're going through some legal proceedings but you don't need to worry about the details"); consistent expectations and boundaries across both homes; professional support from a youth counsellor or psychologist; and being willing to acknowledge that the arrangements might need to adapt as they get older.

The legal framework — best interests of the child

The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) places the best interests of the child as the paramount consideration in all parenting decisions (s 60CA). This principle governs every parenting order made by the FCFCOA — from interim arrangements through to final orders. No other consideration — including what the parents want — outranks it.

Following the 2023 amendments to the Family Law Act, the court must assess the child's best interests by considering several factors. The two most significant are:

1
Protection from harm

Protecting the child from physical or psychological harm, from being subjected to, or exposed to, abuse, neglect, or family violence (s 60CC(2)(a)). This is now the primary consideration — it outweighs the benefit of having a relationship with both parents where there is a safety concern.

2
Meaningful relationships

The benefit of the child having a meaningful relationship with both of their parents — where it is safe and in the child's best interests to do so (s 60CC(2)(b)). The 2023 amendments removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility.

Additional considerations under s 60CC(3) include: the child's own views (given weight according to their maturity and age), the nature of the relationship with each parent and other significant people, the willingness of each parent to facilitate the child's relationship with the other parent, the practical difficulty and expense of proposed arrangements, the capacity of each parent to meet the child's physical, emotional, and intellectual needs, and any other factor the court considers relevant.

Parental responsibility — what it means and how it works

Parental responsibility is defined under s 61B of the Family Law Act as all the duties, powers, responsibilities and authority which, by law, parents have in relation to children. It concerns decision-making — not where the child lives or how much time they spend with each parent.

Shared parental responsibility

Both parents jointly make major long-term decisions about the child — including education, healthcare, religion, and relocation. This does not mean equal time. It means decisions about these major areas require consultation and agreement. Day-to-day decisions (what the child eats, bedtime, activities during your time) do not require consultation.

Sole parental responsibility

One parent makes all major decisions without consultation with the other. Courts grant sole parental responsibility where shared responsibility is unworkable — typically in high-conflict situations, where there is a history of family violence, or where one parent has been completely disengaged from the child's life.

Specific issues orders

Courts can allocate parental responsibility for specific decisions to one parent — for example, one parent may have sole responsibility for medical decisions while parental responsibility for education is shared. This approach is used where parents can cooperate on some matters but not others.

What children need from both parents during separation

What distinguishes children who do well after family separation from those who struggle is remarkably consistent. The single strongest predictor of positive outcomes is not the specific parenting arrangement — it is the quality of the co-parenting relationship and the level of conflict the child is exposed to. Children are remarkably resilient when they feel safe, loved by both parents, and not caught in the middle.

🛡️To feel safe

Children need to know they are physically safe with both parents and that adult conflict will not escalate in front of them. Witnessing parental conflict — including shouting, crying, or tense exchanges at handover — causes genuine psychological harm regardless of what the conflict is about.

💬To not be the messenger

Children should never carry information, money, or messages between parents. "Tell your dad he needs to pay the school fees" or "Ask your mum when she's picking you up" places children in an impossible position between two people they love equally. This is parental alienation behaviour whether intended or not.

❤️Permission to love both parents

One of the most protective things any parent can say is: "It's completely okay to love [the other parent]. I want you to have a good relationship with them." Research consistently shows this explicit permission significantly reduces loyalty conflict and improves long-term outcomes.

🏠Routine and predictability

Consistent schedules, consistent bedtimes, consistent handover locations, and predictable transitions reduce anxiety and give children a reliable structure to organise their experience around. Unpredictability — even when benign — is inherently stressful for children during family disruption.

👂To be heard without pressure

Children should be able to express how they feel about arrangements without feeling that their opinion will determine the outcome, hurt a parent's feelings, or be used as evidence. "How are you feeling about things?" is appropriate. "Would you rather live with me or your mum/dad?" is not.

🎒Continuity of important relationships

School, sport, music, friends, grandparents, cousins, and pets are all stabilising anchors during a destabilising time. Wherever possible, protect these relationships. Decisions about schooling or activities should prioritise the child's existing connections — not parental convenience or strategic positioning.

🌱To not carry adult burdens

Children should not know the details of court proceedings, affidavit allegations, financial disputes, or legal strategy. They should not feel responsible for either parent's emotional state. They should not be asked to "keep secrets" from the other parent nor pressured into explaining everything that occurred at the other parent's residence. Childhood is not compatible with being a party to adult conflict.

🤝Consistency between homes

Where possible, similar expectations about bedtime, screen time, homework, and behaviour across both homes give children consistency. This does not mean identical — different homes have different rules. But extreme inconsistency creates confusion and gives children leverage to play parents against each other.

🗣️Age-appropriate honesty

Children notice when something is wrong and fill silence with their own explanations — which are almost always worse than the truth. They need honest, developmentally appropriate answers: "Mum and Dad have decided not to live together anymore, but we both love you and that will never change" is enough. They do not need details about why the relationship broke down, what the other parent did, or what is happening in court. The absence of information is not protection — it is a vacuum children fill with fear and self-blame.

🧠Emotional permission

Children need permission to experience the full range of emotions that come with separation — sadness, anger, confusion, relief, anxiety, loyalty conflict, or even moments of happiness. Statements like "You seem upset today" or "It's okay to miss the other parent when you're here" help children feel emotionally safe. Trying to force positivity, minimise their feelings, or treat emotional reactions as disloyalty teaches children to suppress rather than process distress.

📱Protection from adult communication conflict

Children should not be exposed to hostile texts, emails, phone calls, or social media disputes between parents. Reading messages over a child's shoulder, arguing during FaceTime calls, or making sarcastic comments while communicating with the other parent places children inside adult conflict even when they are not directly involved. Parents should communicate privately, calmly, and in ways that minimise the child's awareness of conflict wherever possible.

⏳Time to adjust

Children rarely adapt to major family change immediately. Behaviour changes, clinginess, sleep disruption, school difficulties, emotional outbursts, or withdrawal are often signs of adjustment stress rather than "bad behaviour." Children need patience, reassurance, and stability while they adapt to a new reality. The goal is not to force children to "move on" quickly — it is to help them feel secure enough that adjustment happens naturally over time.

What to do and what not to do

These are not judgements — they are evidence-based guidance on what the research shows improves outcomes for children of separated parents.

✅ Do
Tell children the separation is not their fault — clearly, directly, and repeatedly over time.
Maintain as much routine as possible across both homes — same bedtime, same homework expectations, same basic values.
Speak positively or neutrally about the other parent in front of the children. "Your dad/mum loves you very much" is always appropriate.
Keep handovers calm, brief, and consistent. Practice emotional regulation before handovers. Children read your nervous system.
Allow children to take photos, favourite toys, books, and comfort objects freely between homes without comment.
Support children's relationships with grandparents and extended family on both sides. These relationships provide stability children desperately need.
Seek professional help (child psychologist, school counsellor, GP) if children show sustained signs of distress. Early intervention brings best results. These professionals should be decided between both parents.
Communicate directly with the other parent about the children — via app, email, text or if necessary a third neutral party. Do not route communication through the children. Using a co-parenting communication app (such as OurFamilyWizard or Cozi) keeps all parenting-related messages in one place, timestamped, and separate from your personal life.
Be flexible with arrangements around special occasions — birthdays, events, illness. This models to children that their needs come first.
Acknowledge children's feelings about the separation without giving them adult detail. "I know this is hard and it is okay to feel sad" is far more helpful than an explanation of what went wrong.
Attend the other parent's significant life events — school concerts, sports carnivals, graduations — calmly and without incident. Courts and family consultants notice cooperative co-parenting behaviour.
Keep children's school, GP, extracurricular activities, and social routines intact wherever possible. Continuity in these areas is one of the strongest protective factors for children's wellbeing during separation.
When children return from the other parent's home, greet them warmly. Give them time to transition back before asking about their time away, without interrogation.
Ensure children have age-appropriate ways to contact the other parent — phone calls, video calls, or messages — without needing to ask permission, and without the calls being monitored or cut short.
❌ Don't
Use children to carry messages, money, legal documents, or information to the other parent under any circumstances.
Question children about what happens at the other parent's home, who visited, what was said, or what the other parent is doing.
Expose children to court documents, affidavits, legal proceedings, or adult discussions about the case. Ever.
Make negative comments about the other parent, their new partner, their parenting, their finances, or their character — within earshot of the children or to children directly.
Allow children to feel responsible for either parent's emotional state — through explicit statements or through visible emotional distress at separations and handovers.
Withhold contact with the other parent without a genuine, immediate, documented safety reason. Without such a reason — and where parenting orders are in place — withholding contact can be a contravention and is treated seriously by the court.
Ask children to keep secrets from the other parent — this places children in a loyalty conflict and is a recognised form of emotional harm.
Use children's stated views or preferences as strategic leverage in proceedings. Encouraging children to express particular views for legal purposes is a form of coaching that family consultants are trained to detect.
Involve children in adult financial or legal discussions. Do not show them paperwork, discuss money issues, or explain why the other parent "has to pay".
Introduce a new partner to your children without careful thought about timing and the children's readiness. Rushing this can increase children's anxiety and provide material that may be raised in proceedings.
Permit children to opt out of court-ordered time with the other parent based on their stated preferences alone. Children should not be placed in the position of making decisions that are properly for adults and the court to make.
Discuss your own emotional pain, loneliness, financial stress, or feelings about the other parent with your children or within their hearing. Children should not be your emotional support during proceedings.
Change schools, relocate, or make significant decisions about the children's lives without the other parent's agreement or a court order permitting you to do so. Depending on your parental responsibility, initiating major decisions can constitute a contravention of existing orders.
Tell children that the other parent does not love them, does not want to see them, or is only attending proceedings for strategic reasons. These statements are deeply harmful and are taken seriously by family consultants and courts.
Allow your own conflict with the other parent to spill into how you manage children's contact — delaying pickups, cancelling time at short notice, or making changeover locations hostile. Every incident is potentially documentable.

Understanding parental alienation — and why it matters legally

Parental alienation refers to a pattern of behaviour by one parent that undermines the child's relationship with the other parent. It ranges from subtle (sighing when the other parent's name is mentioned) to severe (actively telling a child the other parent does not love them, is dangerous, or wants to take them away).

In court, what matters is documented conduct and how it affects the child — not whether anyone uses the words "parental alienation." Statutory references on CasePath are for orientation; always check the current Act and obtain independent legal advice for your situation.

Why it matters legally: Under s 60CC(3)(c) of the Family Law Act, the court must consider the willingness and ability of each parent to facilitate, and encourage, a close and continuing relationship between the child and the other parent. A parent who undermines the child's relationship with the other parent is directly affecting a key factor in parenting assessments. Family consultants are specifically trained to identify alienating behaviour.
Why it matters for children: Children who are alienated from a parent consistently show elevated rates of depression, anxiety, difficulties with trust and relationships, and, in adulthood, often describe profound grief about the lost relationship — regardless of which parent they originally aligned with.

Note: Not every child who resists contact with a parent is alienated. Children can have genuine, legitimate reasons to be reluctant to spend time with a parent — including exposure to family violence, parenting that is inconsistent or harsh, or simply normal developmental preferences. The distinction between alienation and legitimate resistance is complex and should be assessed by a professional.

If you are concerned this pattern is affecting your child: keep a factual record (what was said or done, when, and who was present); raise issues through your lawyer or in sworn material where appropriate; and discuss whether a family report or an Independent Children's Lawyer is suitable — these are case-specific decisions. Avoid mirroring the behaviour you complain about (negative talk about the other parent, or coaching children before interviews). Courts treat that as harmful to children and damaging to your own credibility.

Family consultants, ICLs, and how children's voices are heard in court

Children do not give evidence in family law proceedings. Instead, their views, needs, and wellbeing are assessed and represented through specialised processes.

📝Family Report

A report prepared by a court-appointed family consultant (psychologist or social worker) who interviews both parents, the children, and sometimes other significant people. The report makes recommendations about parenting arrangements. It is highly influential — Magistrates and Judges give it significant weight.

👶Child Impact Report

A shorter, earlier report focused on the immediate needs and circumstances of the child. Often ordered at interim stages to assist with short-term arrangements while proceedings continue.

⚖️Independent Children's Lawyer (ICL)

A lawyer appointed by the court to represent the children's interests — not to act on the children's instructions, but to independently assess and present what is in their best interests. ICLs interview children (depending on age), review evidence, and make submissions to the court. They are appointed in serious or complex cases.

🧠Expert witnesses

In complex cases involving alleged child abuse, mental health conditions, or developmental concerns, the court may appoint an independent expert — typically a clinical or forensic psychologist — to assess specific issues. Their evidence is given significant weight.

If you are involved in a family report process: be honest and child-focused, not strategic. Family consultants have extensive experience distinguishing genuine child-focus from parental positioning. Preparing your children for what to say is detrimental to your case and harmful to your children. CasePath provides general information only — seek independent legal advice about your own proceedings.

131 272 · servicesaustralia.gov.au
💡
Freedom from loyalty tests

Children are highly attuned to subtle cues — tone of voice, facial expressions, silence, or what goes unsaid. They quickly learn what earns approval and what creates tension. Even indirect comments like "I guess you had more fun at Dad's" or visible disappointment at transitions can function as loyalty tests. Over time, children adapt by editing themselves — downplaying positive experiences with one parent to protect the other. This is psychologically costly. Children need to be able to move between homes without performing emotional diplomacy.

📱
Low-conflict communication between parents

Children benefit when communication between parents is business-like, predictable, and contained. This does not require warmth or friendship — it requires control. Arguments via text, hostile emails, or conflict at handover all leak into the child's world, even when you think they're shielded. Using structured communication (clear, brief, child-focused) and, where needed, tools like parenting apps creates psychological distance from conflict. The goal is simple: reduce the amount of adult tension the child has to absorb.

🧭
Clear roles and boundaries

Children cope better when the roles in their world are stable and appropriate: parents make decisions, children are children. When boundaries blur — children acting as emotional support, decision-makers, or confidants — anxiety increases and development is disrupted. Statements like "I don't know what I'd do without you" or seeking comfort from a child about the separation places them in a role they are not equipped to carry. Children need parents who are steady, contained, and able to hold the emotional weight of the situation.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to be admitted to practice in Australia?

Yes. Lawyer Portal accounts require a current Australian practising certificate. We verify this during registration.

Can my entire firm use one subscription?

The $699.99/year subscription covers one practitioner. Firm-wide plans with multiple seats are available — contact us for pricing.

What if a client doesn't use CasePath yet?

You can send clients a referral link directly from your portal. They sign up for free and can invite you once their vault is set up.

Is the 7-day trial really free?

Yes — no credit card required to start. You'll be prompted to add payment details before the trial ends if you choose to continue.

How do I get listed in the CasePath lawyer directory?

All active Lawyer Portal subscribers are automatically listed in the directory. You can customise your profile — areas of practice, location, languages spoken — from your account settings.
